p-v-narasimha-rao: Pamulaparthi Venkata Narasimha Rao was born on 28 June 1921 into a Telugu Niyogi Brahmin family in Laknepalli village in present-day Telangana, then part of Hyderabad State. At the age of three he was adopted by Pamulaparthi Ranga Rao and Rukminamma and taken to the village of Vangara. He studied at Osmania University, took a master's degree in law at Hislop College and completed his law studies at Fergusson College in Pune. In 1931, aged ten, he was married to Satyamma, who died in 1970.

He was an active participant in the independence movement and joined full-time politics after independence as a member of the Indian National Congress. He sat in the Andhra Pradesh assembly from 1957 to 1977 and held ministerial posts from 1962 to 1973. As chief minister of Andhra Pradesh from 1971 he applied land reforms and land ceiling acts strictly; President's rule had to be imposed to counter the Jai Andhra movement. In the union government he later held the Defence, Home Affairs and External Affairs portfolios.

In the 1991 general election the Congress under Rao won 244 seats, and with outside support from other parties he formed a minority government. India was then close to bankruptcy. I. G. Patel declined the post of finance minister, and Rao chose the economist Manmohan Singh, a former governor of the Reserve Bank of India. The reforms advanced furthest in opening to foreign investment, reforming capital markets, deregulating domestic business and changing the trade regime. In 1992 the Controller of Capital Issues was abolished. Some socialist nationalists criticised the liberalisation at the time.

On 6 December 1992 members of the Vishva Hindu Parishad demolished the Babri Mosque at Ayodhya. The act led to large-scale communal violence, the most extensive since the Partition of India, in almost every major city. His government introduced the Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, India's first anti-terrorism legislation. In 1993 an earthquake at Latur in Maharashtra killed nearly 10,000 people, and Rao's relief operation drew applause. Voters turned the Congress out in the 1996 election, and Atal Bihari Vajpayee became prime minister on 16 May 1996.

Rao published a novel, The Insider, whose rise of a man through Indian politics resembles events in his own life. He spoke 17 languages, and translated a Telugu work by Viswanatha Satyanarayana into Hindi and a Marathi novel into Telugu. He suffered a heart attack on 9 December 2004 and died 14 days later, aged 83, and seven days of state mourning were declared. Biographies by Vinay Sitapati and studies by Sanjay Baru and Jairam Ramesh examine his role in the reforms of 1991. He was awarded the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian award, posthumously in 2024.
pablo-escobar: Pablo Emilio Escobar Gaviria was born on 1 December 1949 in Rionegro, in the Antioquia Department, and grew up in poverty in the neighbouring city of Medellín. He was the third of seven children. His father was a small farmer and his mother a teacher.

Escobar began his criminal career with a gang that stole tombstones, sandblasted the inscriptions and resold them, and then joined gangs that stole cars. He also had people kidnapped for ransom. His best-known victim, the businessman Diego Echavarria, was kidnapped and killed in 1971.

In May 1976 agents of the Colombian Security Service (DAS) arrested Escobar on his return from Ecuador and found 39 kilograms of cocaine in the spare tire of his car. He changed the first judge in the case and bribed the second, and was released. The agent who had arrested him was killed the following year. His method of bribing officials and murdering those who refused became known as silver or lead, meaning money or death.

With Carlos Lehder he developed a transshipment point on Norman's Cay in the Bahamas, used from 1978 to 1982. He bought some 20 square kilometres of land in Antioquia for the Hacienda Nápoles, which had a zoo, a lake and a private bullring. He also spent millions on housing, parks, football pitches, hospitals and schools in poor districts of Medellín, and was known as the Paisa Robin Hood.

In 1982 he was elected an alternate member of the Chamber of Representatives for the Liberal Party, which gave him parliamentary immunity. The Liberal leader Luis Carlos Galán expelled him from the party, and Escobar announced his retirement from politics in January 1984. The justice minister Rodrigo Lara-Bonilla, who had accused him of criminal activity, was murdered three months later.

In 1991 Escobar surrendered and was held in his own self-built prison, La Catedral, under a deal with President César Gaviria that excluded extradition. He escaped in 1992 when authorities tried to move him, and a nationwide manhunt followed. On 2 December 1993, a day after his 44th birthday, Colombian special forces traced him to a house in Medellín after he made a call to his family. In an exchange of gunfire he was shot while trying to escape over the roof, and a bullet to the head killed him. Whether he killed himself or was shot has been debated.

Over 25,000 people attended his funeral, and some of the city's poor, whom he had helped, consider him a saint. After his death the Cali Cartel came to dominate the cocaine market until the mid-1990s.
pablo-neruda: Ricardo Eliécer Neftalí Reyes Basoalto was born on 12 July 1904 in Parral, about 350 km south of Santiago. His father, José del Carmen Reyes Morales, was a railway employee. His mother, the schoolteacher Rosa Neftalí Basoalto Opazo, died two months after his birth. He grew up in Temuco and composed his first poems in the winter of 1914.

His father opposed his interest in literature, but others encouraged him, among them the future Nobel laureate Gabriela Mistral, who headed the local school. On 18 July 1917, aged 13, he published an essay in the daily La Mañana under the name Neftalí Reyes. By mid-1920 he had adopted the pseudonym Pablo Neruda and was a published author of poems, prose and journalism. He is thought to have taken the name from the Czech poet Jan Neruda.

Neruda held diplomatic posts in Buenos Aires and Barcelona, then succeeded Mistral as consul in Madrid, where he became the centre of a literary circle that included Rafael Alberti, Federico García Lorca and César Vallejo. He later served as Consul General in Mexico City from 1940 to 1943. Back in Chile in 1943, he toured Peru and visited Machu Picchu, which inspired the 12-part poem Alturas de Macchu Picchu, completed in 1945, and later Canto General (1950).

Like many left-leaning intellectuals of his generation, Neruda came to admire the Soviet Union of Joseph Stalin, and he received the Stalin Peace Prize in 1953. His friend Octavio Paz later criticised this loyalty. When President Gabriel González Videla outlawed communism in 1948, a warrant was issued for the Communist senator's arrest. Friends hid him for 13 months, and in March 1949 he crossed the Andes on horseback into Argentina. He returned to Chile in August 1952 to support Salvador Allende's presidential campaign.

Under President Allende, Neruda served as ambassador to France. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1971, though some committee members had not forgotten his praise of Stalinist dictatorship. In September 1973 he was diagnosed with prostate cancer, and after the coup led by Augusto Pinochet he planned to go into exile in Mexico. He died at a clinic in Santiago on 23 September 1973, the day before he was to leave. The official cause was complications of prostate cancer, but the circumstances of his death have been investigated since 2011.

Neruda is often considered the national poet of Chile. His three houses, La Chascona in Santiago, La Sebastiana in Valparaíso and Casa de Isla Negra, are museums, and he and Matilde Urrutia are buried at Isla Negra.
pablo-picasso: Pablo Ruiz Picasso was born on 25 October 1881 in Málaga, Andalusia, the first child of José Ruiz y Blasco and María Picasso y López. His father was a painter of birds and other game and a professor at the School of Crafts. According to his mother, his first word was "piz, piz", short for lápiz, the Spanish word for pencil. From the age of seven he was trained by his father, a traditional academic artist, in figure drawing and oil painting. The family moved to A Coruña in 1891, and an apocryphal story relates that his father, seeing the precision of the thirteen-year-old's technique, felt his son had surpassed him.

His career as a painter can be said to have begun by 1894. The academic realism of the mid-1890s appears in The First Communion (1896), and a Modernist period followed in 1899–1900. After 1906 the Fauvist work of Henri Matisse pushed him towards more radical styles, beginning a rivalry between the two. The commonly accepted periods are the Blue Period (1901–1904), the Rose Period (1904–1906), the African-influenced Period (1907–1909), Analytic Cubism (1909–1912) and Synthetic Cubism (1912–1919). His works include Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (1907) and Guernica (1937). From 1909 to 1928 he made sculptural constructions from diverse materials, such as Guitar (1912) in sheet metal and wire. In 1944 he joined the French Communist Party, and he remained a member until his death.

Picasso died on 8 April 1973 in Mougins, France, of a heart attack, having painted until 3 a.m. the night before. He died without a will, which led to a feud over his estate. At his death there were more than 45,000 unsold works in his estate, among them 1,885 paintings, 1,228 sculptures and 3,222 ceramics. In 1971 he was the first living artist honoured with an exhibition in the Grand Gallery of the Louvre, for his 90th birthday.
pachuca: Pachuca, formally Pachuca de Soto, is the capital and largest city of the state of Hidalgo, about 90 kilometres north of Mexico City. It lies in a small valley almost surrounded by hills, and its nickname, La Bella Airosa, refers to the strong winds that blow through the canyons to the north. In the Otomi language it is Nju̱nthe. Its official name honours Manuel Fernando Soto, a congressman credited with founding the state, and Benito Juárez declared it the capital of Hidalgo in 1869. The origin of the word pachuca is not agreed.

People mined green obsidian in the Sierra de Pachuca, at Cerro de las Navajas, as early as 12,000 BCE. Artifacts from between 200 and 850 CE show Teotihuacan influence, and it has been argued that Teotihuacan monopolised the deposit to control the obsidian trade of central Mexico. The obsidian was prized in pre-Columbian times and traded as far as Spiro Mounds in the United States. The Spanish began mining silver here in the mid-16th century, and the city remained a major mining centre until the mid-20th century.

From 1824 Cornish miners and English investors came to Pachuca and nearby Real del Monte; some founded the Compañía Real de Monte y Pachuca. Ships carrying 125 passengers and about 1,500 tons of equipment sailed from Falmouth and reached Veracruz three months later, and the trek inland killed about half the miners and their families, many from malaria and yellow fever. The survivors brought high-pressure steam pumping engines of the kind designed by Richard Trevithick, which turned flooded mines into large silver producers. They also brought football and the pasty, known in Pachuca as pastes, which became defining features of the city.

A manufacturing sector, set up in the 1950s, has changed the city's mining image. The last Pachuca mine to close was El Álamo, in 1993. The Universidad Autónoma del Estado de Hidalgo, the state's oldest educational institution, began in 1869 as the Instituto Literario y Escuela de Artes y Oficios. The Monumental Clock, 40 metres high, was donated by the Cornishman Francis Rule and inaugurated on 15 September 1910 for the centennial of Mexican independence. The English Cemetery holds about 600 graves, mostly of Cornish miners and their families, and many of their descendants still live in the area.
pacific-ocean: The Pacific is the largest and deepest of Earth's five oceanic divisions. It covers about 165,250,000 square kilometres, taking the definition with an Antarctic southern border, which is about 46% of Earth's water surface. Its mean depth is 4,000 metres, and the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, at 10,928 metres, is the deepest known point in the world. More than 25,000 islands rise above its surface, many of them the remains of volcanoes, and the Ring of Fire, a belt of explosive volcanism above subduction zones, surrounds it.

Modern humans first reached the western Pacific around 60,000 to 70,000 years ago. They crossed from Sundaland to Sahul, a sea journey of at least 80 kilometres, to reach Australia, probably on large bamboo rafts, although the level of maritime technology is not known with certainty. Settlement of Buka by 32,000 years ago and Manus by 25,000 years ago confirms their seafaring skill. Their descendants include the Negritos, Melanesians and Indigenous Australians.

In 1513 the Spanish explorer Vasco Núñez de Balboa crossed the Isthmus of Panama and sighted what he called the Mar del Sur, the Southern Sea. The present name was given by Ferdinand Magellan during the Spanish circumnavigation of 1520, when he met favourable winds and called it Mar Pacífico, the peaceful sea. From 1946 to 1958 the Marshall Islands served as the Pacific Proving Grounds designated by the United States, where 67 nuclear tests were conducted.

The Pacific is divided by the equator into the North and South Pacific. Its marginal seas include the Philippine Sea, the South China Sea, the East China Sea, the Sea of Japan, the Sea of Okhotsk, the Bering Sea, the Tasman Sea and the Coral Sea. The Bering Strait joins it to the Arctic Ocean, and the Drake Passage and Strait of Magellan link it to the Atlantic. It is the only ocean mostly bounded by subduction zones.
pacific-war: The Pacific War was the theatre of the Second World War fought between the Empire of Japan and the Allies in East and Southeast Asia, the Pacific and Indian Oceans and Oceania. It was the largest theatre geographically and included some of the largest naval battles in history. War between Japan and China had begun in 1937, and Japan had invaded Manchuria in 1931, but the Pacific War is more widely held to have begun in 1941, when the United States and the United Kingdom were drawn in. Japanese strategists had concluded as early as 1935 that the oil of the Dutch East Indies was crucial to expansion, and Japan invaded French Indochina in 1940.

On 7 and 8 December 1941 Japan struck simultaneously at Pearl Harbor, the Philippines, Guam, Wake Island, Malaya, Singapore and Hong Kong. At Pearl Harbor eight American battleships were put out of action and 2,403 Americans were killed, but the three American aircraft carriers were at sea. Over six months Japan took the territories it had attacked, together with the Dutch East Indies, Burma and parts of New Guinea.

The Battle of the Coral Sea in May 1942 turned back an invasion force bound for Port Moresby, and the Battle of Midway in June is considered a key turning point. Allied offensives began in August 1942 on Guadalcanal and New Guinea. The Allied strategy of island hopping followed, with landings in the Gilbert and Marshall Islands, the Marianas and Palau, Iwo Jima and Okinawa. After the Battle of Leyte Gulf in October 1944 the Japanese fleet turned to kamikaze attacks. Of the 117,000 Okinawan and Japanese troops defending Okinawa, 94 percent died.

The United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 and Nagasaki on 9 August, and the Soviet Union invaded Manchuria on 9 August. Japan accepted the Potsdam terms on 15 August and signed the surrender document on 2 September. It lost its possessions in Asia and the Pacific and was occupied by the Allies until 1952. Total American losses were 161,000 killed and 248,000 wounded. About 2,121,000 Japanese military personnel died between 1937 and 1945, according to a 1964 Japanese report. Japanese forces killed millions of non-combatants, including prisoners of war, and at least 20 million Chinese died during the Second Sino-Japanese War.
pact-of-steel: Germany and Italy had fought on opposite sides in the First World War. Italy at first opposed German designs on Austria, signed the Rome Protocols of 1934 and joined the Stresa Front. Its isolation after the Abyssinia Crisis left it without major allies, and on 23 October 1936 Italy and Germany signed a secret protocol aligning their policies on the Spanish Civil War, the League of Nations and Abyssinia.

The pact was first drafted as a three-way alliance with Japan, which wished it to be aimed at the Soviet Union, while Germany and Italy wanted it directed at the British Empire and France. Germany feared that an anti-Soviet alliance would risk a two-front war before it could conquer Western Europe, and Japan stood aside. The original name, Pact of Blood, was changed to Pact of Steel when Mussolini was told it would be badly received in Italy.

The foreign ministers Joachim von Ribbentrop and Galeazzo Ciano signed the pact on 22 May 1939. Under the third article, if one party became involved in military complications with another power, the other would come to its side as an ally with all its military might on land, at sea and in the air. The fifth bound both to conclude any armistice or peace only in full agreement, and the seventh set its first period at ten years. A secret supplementary protocol urged closer military and economic cooperation and joint work on the press and propaganda. The treaty rested on the assumption that war would not come within three years.

Together with the Anti-Comintern Pact and the Tripartite Pact, the Pact of Steel was one of the three agreements that formed the main basis of the Axis alliance. When Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, Italy was not prepared and had difficulty meeting its obligations. It entered the Second World War only in June 1940, with an invasion of southern France.

The pact did not last its ten years. After the invasion of Sicily in July 1943 Mussolini was overthrown, and the new government under Marshal Pietro Badoglio signed an armistice with the Allies in September, ending Italy's real part in the pact. The Italian Social Republic, a puppet state under Mussolini in northern Italy, remained a member in name only.
padmasambhava: Padmasambhava, whose name means Born from a Lotus, is described as a tantric Buddhist master whose life is known largely from later tradition. One of the earliest chronicle sources is the Testament of Ba, which records the founding of Samye monastery under King Trisong Detsen. Manuscripts from Dunhuang also mention a tantric master of that name who tames demons. Earlier Tibetologists questioned his historicity; according to Lewis Doney it is now cautiously accepted.

His life story grew mainly from the 12th century. The first full biography, the Copper Palace, is a treasure text said to have been revealed by Nyangrel Nyima Özer (1124–1192). It tells that he appeared as an eight-year-old child in a lotus blossom on Lake Dhanakosha in the kingdom of Oddiyana; other accounts have him born from the womb of Queen Jalendra.

In the Testament of Ba the Indian abbot Śāntarakṣita, invited by Trisong Detsen to Tibet, helped plan the first monastery at Samye, but a flooded temple and a lightning strike on the palace convinced some at court that the local gods were angry. The later hagiographies tell how Padmasambhava was invited, subdued the spirits and demons of Tibet and made them guardians of Buddhism, the deity Pe har becoming protector of Samye. He is also said to have initiated the king into tantric rites.

Because of his part in founding Samye he is regarded as the founder of the Nyingma, the Ancients, school of Tibetan Buddhism. Tradition names Yeshe Tsogyal and Mandarava among his students. Bhutan has many pilgrimage places linked with him, the best known being the Tiger's Nest monastery at Paro, built around a cave where he is said to have meditated.

Tradition holds that his teachings pass down as an oral lineage and as hidden treasure texts, or terma, concealed for later discoverers called tertöns, to whom he is said to appear in visions. The Bardo Thodol, the Tibetan Book of the Dead, is held to be one of these, found by Karma Lingpa (1326–1386). He is closely associated with the kila dagger, and the Vajra Guru mantra and the Seven Line Prayer, which many Tibetans recite daily, are addressed to him. His life is shown in masked cham dances, and he is venerated in Tibet, Nepal, Bhutan and the Himalayan regions of India.
padua: Padua lies on the banks of the Bacchiglione, 40 kilometres west of Venice and 29 kilometres south-east of Vicenza, in the Venetian Plain. The Brenta River, which once ran through the city, still touches its northern districts, and the Euganaean Hills to the south-west appear in poems by Petrarch and Percy Bysshe Shelley. The origin of the Roman name Patavium is uncertain; it may be connected with Padus, the ancient name of the Po, or with a Gaulish word for pine.

According to a tradition at least as old as Virgil and Livy, the Trojan prince Antenor founded Padua around 1183 BCE, leading the Eneti or Veneti to the Euganean plain. When a stone sarcophagus was dug up in 1274, officials of the medieval commune declared its remains to be Antenor's. Attila sacked the city savagely in 450. It then fell to the Gothic kings Odoacer and Theodoric, was reconquered by the Byzantine Empire in 540 and passed to the Lombards in 568. The Magyars sacked it in 899.

In the early eleventh century the citizens established a constitution with a general council and an executive body, and in 1138 the government was entrusted to two consuls. Jacopo da Carrara was elected lord of Padua in 1318, and nine members of the Carrara family ruled until 1405, apart from short periods under the Scaligeri and Giangaleazzo Visconti. Padua came under the Republic of Venice in 1405 and stayed under it until 1797, except for a few weeks in 1509 during the wars of the League of Cambrai.

After 1797 the city passed to the Habsburgs, then to the Kingdom of Italy in 1806 and, from 1814, to Lombardy-Venetia under Austria. It was annexed to Italy in 1866. Padua was the Italian army's main command in the First World War, and the armistice with Austria was signed at Villa Giusti in Padua on 3 November 1918.

Padua is the capital of its province, with 208,202 inhabitants. It has two UNESCO World Heritage entries, its Botanical Garden, the world's oldest, and its fourteenth-century frescoes, among them Giotto's cycle of 1305 in the Scrovegni Chapel. The University of Padua, founded in 1222, is one of the oldest in the world; Galileo Galilei observed Jupiter's moons from Padua in 1610, and in 1678 Elena Lucrezia Cornaro Piscopia became the first woman in the world to graduate from a university.
paestum: According to Strabo, Poseidonia was founded by Achaeans from Sybaris; Solinus calls it a Dorian colony. No ancient source gives a date, but the archaeological evidence points to about 600 BCE. When Croton conquered Sybaris in 510 BCE, Poseidonia probably sheltered refugees. Strabo says the Lucanians conquered the city late in the fifth century BCE, and the evidence suggests that the Greek and Oscan cultures then thrived side by side.

The city became the Roman Paestum in 273 BCE, after the Pyrrhic War, in which the Poseidonians had sided with King Pyrrhus of Epirus against Rome. It stayed loyal to Rome during Hannibal's invasion and was rewarded with special favours, including its own coinage. It became a bishopric around 400 CE. Decline began between the fourth and seventh centuries, probably through changes in drainage that brought malarial swamp, with pirate raids perhaps also a cause. The site was abandoned in the Middle Ages and left largely forgotten until the eighteenth century.

Its fame rests on three temples in the Archaic Doric order, dating from about 550 to 450 BCE and in excellent preservation. The first Temple of Hera, about 550 BCE, is the oldest and was long called the Basilica by eighteenth-century scholars who thought it Roman. The Temple of Athena, about 500 BCE, mixes Doric and Ionic features and was used as a church in the Middle Ages. The second Temple of Hera, about 460 to 450 BCE, keeps most of its entablature. Walls about 4.75 kilometres long, a Roman forum and a small amphitheatre also survive; of about 120 hectares, only 25 have been excavated.

The Tomb of the Diver, found in 1968 and dated to about 470 BCE, is the only known Greek tomb of its period with frescoes of human figures, and it is displayed in the site's national museum. The ruins came to wide notice in the eighteenth century, and Piranesi's etchings of 1778 spread their influence on Greek Revival architecture.
pago-pago: Pago Pago lies at the narrowest part of Tutuila, the main island of American Samoa. Tutuila is a basaltic volcanic dome built by five volcanoes along two or possibly three rift zones. The central feature of its geology is the Pago Volcano, active between 1.54 and 1.28 million years ago, whose caldera, about 6 miles long and 3 miles wide, collapsed 1.27 million years ago. The harbour formed in the partly submerged remnants of that caldera, and the village stands near its centre. Rainmaker Mountain, also called Mount Pioa, shelters the eastern side and helps give the harbour very heavy rainfall.

The area was first settled about 4,000 years ago by Polynesian navigators. The people of Tutuila made a plain clay pottery known as Samoan Plainware, found at sites such as Vaipito, which ceased to be made about 1,500 years ago. Tutuila was part of the Tuʻi Tonga Empire from an invasion around 950 CE until the Tongans were expelled in 1250. Samoan tradition credits a warrior from Pago Pago, Fua'au, with leading the revolt, after his fiancée Tauoloasi'i was kidnapped and taken to Tonga.

Among the early names of the place were O le Fagaloa, or Long Bay, and O le Maputasi, the Single Chief's House, a compliment to the Mauga, the senior chief of the area. The first European ships arrived in the late 18th century, and in 1830 a man from Massachusetts living in the household of High Chief Mauga translated parts of the Church of England Prayer Book into Samoan.

The initial American interest in Tutuila was the use of the harbour as a coaling station, and its strategic position played a direct part in the political separation of Western and Eastern Samoa. On 17 April 1900 the first American flag was raised on Sogelau Hill above the new wharf and coaling facilities at Fagatogo. The Deed of Cession of Tutuila and Aunu'u, written and signed by the chiefs, formalised the relationship between the United States and American Samoa.

Pago Pago is the capital of American Samoa and its main port, the seat of the territorial government and the centre of its commerce. Greater Pago Pago consists of six villages strung along the harbour, among them Fagatogo, the downtown area, which holds the territorial legislature, the Fono, and Utulei, which holds Government House. Sixteen buildings of the former United States Naval Station Tutuila are listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The National Park of American Samoa lies immediately to the north.
paide: Paide is the capital of Järva County, one of the 15 counties of Estonia. Its German name, Weißenstein, originally Wittenstein or Wittensten in Low German, means white stone and comes from the limestone used to build the castle; a Latin translation, Albus Lapis, has also been used. The Estonian name was first recorded in 1564 as Paida and is thought to derive from the word paas or pae, meaning limestone.

Konrad von Mandern, master of the Livonian Order, ordered a castle built at Paide in 1265 or 1266. It was constructed from the beginning around a central tower or keep, locally called the Tall Hermann tower or Vallitorn, which has six storeys and has always been the core of the complex. The fortress was strengthened in the 14th and 15th centuries, when the walls were enlarged and towers added, and it was modernised to meet the threat of firearms. In the 16th century outer bastions were added.

During the Livonian War the castle was repeatedly besieged by Russian troops, and in 1573 troops loyal to Ivan the Terrible occupied it. It then changed hands several times and was involved in the fighting of the Polish-Swedish War of 1600 to 1611, in the so-called Siege of Weissenstein. The central tower was restored in 1895 to 1897. In 1941, during World War II, retreating Soviet troops blew it up, and it was not repaired until after Estonia regained its independence, in 1990 to 1993. The church dates originally from the 16th century but was badly damaged by war and fire on several occasions, and the present building is mainly a reconstruction of 1909 to 1910.

The restored central tower houses a part of the Järva County museum. Among the town's natives are the composer Arvo Pärt, born in 1935, and the Baltic German novelist, poet and painter Alexander von Ungern-Sternberg, who lived from 1806 to 1869.
pakistan: Pakistan is bounded by the Arabian Sea on the south and shares land borders with India to the east, Afghanistan to the west, Iran to the southwest and China to the northeast. The Wakhan Corridor, a narrow strip of Afghanistan, separates it from Tajikistan. It lies where the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates meet, a region of high seismic activity.

The country is divided into three major geographic areas: the northern highlands, the Indus River plain and the Balochistan Plateau. The highlands include the Karakoram, Hindu Kush and Pamir ranges and five of the fourteen peaks over 8,000 metres, among them K2 at 8,611 metres. The 1,609 km Indus River and its tributaries cross the country from Kashmir to the Arabian Sea and sustain the alluvial plains of Punjab and Sindh.

The earliest known stone tools in the region, about 2 million years old, were found in the Soan Valley. The Neolithic site of Mehrgarh dates from 7000 to 4300 BCE, and the Indus Valley Civilisation included Mohenjo-daro and Harappa. After its decline, semi-nomadic Indo-European Aryans migrated into the subcontinent around 2000 BCE, and the Gandhara civilisation later flourished at the crossroads of India, Central Asia and the Middle East.

The western regions became part of the Achaemenid Empire around 517 BCE, and Alexander the Great conquered the region in 326 BCE, defeating King Porus at Jhelum. The Mauryas ruled from 322 BCE to 185 BCE, and Ashoka introduced Buddhism. The Indo-Greek Kingdom founded by Demetrius of Bactria included Gandhara and Punjab, and Greco-Buddhist culture flourished under Menander. Later powers included the Kushan, the Ghaznavids, the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals, and the British Raj from 1858 to 1947.

Pakistan gained independence in 1947 through the partition of British India, which was accompanied by mass migration and loss of life. It adopted a republican constitution in 1956, and East Pakistan seceded as Bangladesh in 1971 after a nine-month civil war. The 1973 constitution established a parliamentary system. Military rule governed in 1958 to 1971, 1977 to 1988 and 1999 to 2008, and the first successful democratic transition took place in May 2013.

The 2023 census counted 247,541,947 people, and the population grew more than sevenfold between 1951 and 2023. The country is ethnically and linguistically diverse and has a very young population, with a median age of 19. Its legislature has a 96-member Senate and a 336-member National Assembly.
palace-of-westminster: The site may have been used by Cnut during his reign from 1016 to 1035, and from about 1045 to about 1050 Edward the Confessor built a palace and the first Westminster Abbey. The oldest surviving part, Westminster Hall, was erected in 1097 for William II, when it was the largest hall in Europe. The palace was the principal residence of English monarchs in the late medieval period. After a fire destroyed the royal apartments in 1512, Henry VIII moved in 1534 to the Palace of Whitehall, and from then on the two houses of Parliament and various courts of law were its main occupants.

On 16 October 1834 a fire broke out when an overheated stove, used to burn the Exchequer's stockpile of tally sticks, set alight the House of Lords Chamber. Both Houses were destroyed. Westminster Hall was saved by firefighting and a change in the wind, along with the Jewel Tower and parts of St Stephen's Chapel.

Charles Barry won the competition to design the new palace and chose the Perpendicular Gothic style, aided by the Gothic architect Augustus Pugin. Work began in 1840 and lasted thirty years, with delays, cost overruns and the deaths of Barry and Pugin. Pugin, displeased with Barry's symmetrical layout, remarked that it was "All Grecian, sir; Tudor details on a classic body". The stone is Anston limestone, carried by canal, sea and river. The Victoria Tower, 98.5 m high, was the tallest secular building in the world on its completion in 1858.

The building has over 1,100 rooms and 100 staircases. It is planned around the Central Lobby, from which corridors lead north to the Commons Chamber, south to the Lords Chamber and west to Westminster Hall.

In the Second World War the palace was hit by bombs on fourteen occasions. In the raid of 10 to 11 May 1941 three people were killed and the Commons Chamber was destroyed, because firefighters could save only one of it and the roof of Westminster Hall; they chose the hall. The chamber was rebuilt in a simplified style and completed in 1950.

The Gunpowder Plot of 1605 aimed to blow up the House of Lords at the State Opening of Parliament, and since then the Yeomen of the Guard search the cellars before each opening. The palace became a Grade I listed building in 1970 and part of a World Heritage Site in 1987. Tsar Nicholas I called it "a dream in stone", and Westminster is now used to mean the UK Parliament and government.
palaiologos-dynasty: The Palaiologoi were a Byzantine Greek noble family whose origins are unclear. Their own medieval stories traced them to Roman patricians who accompanied Constantine the Great to Constantinople in 330, but they more probably arose in Anatolia. The earliest known member, possibly the founder, was Nikephoros Palaiologos, a commander in the second half of the 11th century. In the 12th century the family belonged to the military aristocracy and often intermarried with the ruling Komnenos family. When the Fourth Crusade took Constantinople in 1204, the Palaiologoi fled to the Empire of Nicaea, ruled by the House of Laskaris, and held high office there.

Michael Palaiologos, born in 1223, was mistrusted by the Laskaris emperors. After Theodore II Laskaris died, Michael led a coup against the regent George Mouzalon, seized the guardianship of the child emperor John IV Laskaris and was proclaimed co-emperor. After the recapture of Constantinople from the Latin Empire in 1261, John IV was deposed and blinded. Michael VIII and his successors ruled the empire at its weakest, with decline caused partly by Bulgarians, Serbs and Ottoman Turks and partly by civil wars within the family. The war between Andronikos II Palaiologos and his grandson Andronikos III lasted until 1328.

In 1394 Manuel II stopped paying tribute to the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I, who besieged Constantinople for more than a decade. Manuel signed a peace with Mehmed I in 1403. By the 15th century the empire was effectively a client state of the Ottomans. The dynasty ended in 1453, when Mehmed the Conqueror took Constantinople and the last emperor, Constantine XI Palaiologos, died in its defence. His brothers Thomas and Demetrios kept the Morea as Ottoman vassals until a civil war between them led Mehmed to annex it in 1460.

The Palaiologoi were not well liked by their subjects, partly because of their religious policy. Michael VIII achieved a union of the Orthodox and Catholic churches at the Second Council of Lyons in 1274, which the Byzantine people opposed passionately. It broke down in 1281 when Pope Martin IV excommunicated him, and he died condemned as a traitor and heretic. Constantine XI's death in battle, however, led Greeks to remember him as a hero and improved the dynasty's reputation.

A branch in Italy, the Palaeologus-Montferrat, ruled the March of Montferrat until 1536. The senior imperial line probably died out in the 16th century, and many later claims of descent were fabricated. Thousands of people, particularly in Greece, still bear the name.
palau: Palau is an archipelago of about 340 islands in the western Pacific Ocean, the western part of the Caroline Islands, with a total area of 466 square kilometres. Its most populous islands are Angaur, Babeldaob, Koror and Peleliu, and about two-thirds of the people live on Koror. North of them lies the coral atoll of Kayangel, and west lie about 200 uninhabited Rock Islands. A remote group of six Southwest Islands, some 604 kilometres away, make up the states of Hatohobei and Sonsorol.

The Palauan name for the islands, Belau, derives from the word for village, beluu, or from aibebelau, meaning indirect replies, which relates to a creation myth. The name Palau came into English from the Spanish Los Palaos through German. An older English name was the Pelew Islands.

The islands were first settled in the 3rd or 2nd millennium BCE by Austronesian peoples, most likely from what is now the Philippines or Indonesia. In December 1696 sailors from the Caroline Islands were stranded on Samar, where the missionary Paul Klein met them. They showed him with pebbles the position and size of their islands, and he drew from this the first European map of the Palau area.

The islands became part of the Spanish East Indies in 1885. After Spain's defeat in the Spanish-American War they were sold to Germany in 1899 and administered as part of German New Guinea. After the First World War they fell within the Japanese-ruled South Seas Mandate of the League of Nations. In the Second World War American and Japanese troops fought in the Mariana and Palau Islands campaign, including the major Battle of Peleliu.

In 1947 Palau became part of the United States-governed Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands. A referendum in 1978 rejected joining the Federated States of Micronesia, and Palau adopted a constitution in 1981. It gained full sovereignty in 1994 under a Compact of Free Association with the United States, and the United Nations General Assembly admitted it on 15 December 1994.

The Republic of Palau is a presidential republic with a bicameral Palau National Congress. Its capital, Ngerulmud, is on Babeldaob, the largest island, and its most populous city is Koror. The official languages are Palauan and English, and the currency is the United States dollar. Palauan society follows a strict matrilineal system, seen in funerals, marriages, inheritance and the passing of traditional titles.
palawan: Palawan is an archipelagic province of the Philippines in the region of Mimaropa and the largest province in the country by area, at 14,649.73 square kilometres. Its islands stretch between Mindoro in the north-east and Borneo in the south-west, lying between the South China Sea and the Sulu Sea. The province takes its name from its largest island, 450 kilometres long and 50 kilometres wide. It comprises roughly 1,780 islands and islets, including the Calamianes group in the north-east, Balabac Island off the southern tip and the Cuyo Islands in the Sulu Sea. Unlike most of the Philippines, Palawan belongs biogeographically to Sundaland, with fauna and flora related to those of Borneo.

Researchers led by Robert Bradford Fox found evidence in the Tabon Caves that humans have lived on Palawan for more than 50,000 years, along with the bone fragments of an individual known as Tabon Man. The oldest inhabitants are the Palaw'an, Batak, Tagbanwa and Tau't Bato of the interior and highlands and of the Calamianes Islands, who traditionally practise animist anito religions. Later groups settled the coasts. In the 1200s Palawan, Calamian and parts of Luzon came under the nation of Sandao, a vassal of the more powerful Ma-i in Mindoro. The Molbog of the south, and the Cuyonon and Agutaynon, arrived later.

The northern Calamianes Islands were the first to come under Spanish authority. In the early 17th century Spanish friars sent missions to Cuyo, Agutaya, Taytay and Cagayancillo, but met resistance from Moro communities, and churches enclosed by garrisons were built against Moro raids. The Spanish census of 1818 recorded 4,486 native families and 29 Spanish-Filipino families on Palawan, then called Isla de Paragua. In 1902, after the Philippine–American War, the United States established civil rule in northern Palawan as the province of Paragua. In 1905 the province was reorganised to include the south, renamed Palawan, and given Puerto Princesa as capital.

During the Japanese occupation guerrillas, called Palawan's Fighting One Thousand, resisted, helped escaping American prisoners of war and guided the landings of the 8th Army. Palawan also felt the effect of martial law, declared by Ferdinand Marcos in 1972. Later settlement from Luzon and elsewhere changed the island's population and languages.

Palawan has about 968,795 people, according to the 2024 census. The capital and largest city, Puerto Princesa, is administered independently of the province. Tagalog is spoken by more than half the people, and the native Cuyonon and Palawano are also used. The economy is basically agricultural, with palay (rice), corn and coconut the main crops, along with fishing, logging and mining. The Puerto Princesa Subterranean River National Park, listed by UNESCO in 1999, and the Tubbataha Reef Marine Park, listed in 1993, are World Heritage Sites.
palembang: Palembang occupies a wide lowland east of the Bukit Barisan Mountains in southern Sumatra, at an average elevation of about 8 metres and some 105 kilometres from the coast at the Bangka Strait. The Musi River, one of the largest in Sumatra, runs through it and divides the city into Seberang Ilir, the downstream bank, and Seberang Ulu, the upstream bank. The city stands where two major tributaries, the Ogan and the Komering, join the Musi, and in the rainy season the tide of the river floods many areas.

The oldest inscription found in Palembang, the Kedukan Bukit Inscription, is dated 682 CE. It tells of a king who acquires magical powers and leads a large force over water and land, setting out from the Tamvan delta and arriving at a place called Matajap, and, in the reading of some scholars, founding the polity of Srivijaya. Matajap is believed to be Mukha Upang, a district of Palembang. George Coedes wrote that in the second half of the 9th century Java and Sumatra were united under a Sailendra ruler reigning in Java, with his centre at Palembang.

Prince Parameswara fled the city after Javanese forces crushed it, and pirates then plagued it. In 1407 the returning treasure fleet of Admiral Zheng He confronted the pirate Chen Zuyi there. A local Chinese informant revealed Chen's plan for a surprise attack, and in the battle that followed the Ming fleet destroyed the pirate fleet and killed 5,000 of its men. Chen was taken to Nanjing and executed, and Shi Jinqing was installed as Palembang's ruler.

Islam became the dominant religion after a Demak nobleman, Geding Suro, fled to Palembang with his followers and founded a new dynasty. The Sultanate of Palembang was proclaimed in 1659, and its Grand Mosque was built between 1738 and 1748. The Dutch abolished the sultanate in 1825 and made the city the capital of the Residency of Palembang. It was chartered as a city on 1 April 1906.

Palembang is the capital of the Indonesian province of South Sumatra and the second most populous city of Sumatra after Medan. It is known for songket, a hand-woven silk or cotton cloth patterned with gold or silver thread, which was used at court under Srivijaya. Local cooking relies on freshwater fish and prawn from the Musi, and pempek is among its best-known dishes. The city co-hosted the 2018 Asian Games with Jakarta.
palencia: Palencia lies on the left bank of the Carrión river, near its confluence with the Pisuerga, in the north of the Meseta Central at an altitude of 749 metres. It is about 190 kilometres north of Madrid and 40 kilometres north of Valladolid. The old city stands on the left bank, on higher ground, and the modern suburbs on the right; the first inhabitants probably settled on the right bank and moved because of frequent flooding. A 21-metre statue of Christ, the Cristo del Otero, stands on a hill north-east of the city.

As Pallantia, the town was a fortified Celtiberian settlement and the chief town of the Vaccaei. The Romans starved it into submission in the 2nd century BCE and incorporated it into Hispania Tarraconensis. According to the chronicler Idatius, it was all but destroyed in 457 in the Visigothic wars against the Suevi. The Catholic bishopric was founded in the 3rd century or earlier. Under Visigothic rule the Arian bishop Maurila, installed by Leovigild, followed King Reccared's conversion to Catholicism in 587 and attended the Third Council of Toledo in 589.

After the Moors arrived in the early 8th century the see was a title only, until Froila, Count of Villafruela, retook the area in 921; Sancho III of Navarre was the true restorer of Christian power, and Bernardo, said to be the first prelate of the restored see in 1035, rebuilt the cathedral over the crypt of Saint Antolín.

Alfonso VIII founded a studium generale here in 1208, which did not long survive him; Saint Dominic and the poet Gonzalo de Berceo studied there. Jews are first documented in Palencia in 1175, when Alfonso VIII brought 40 Jews to the town, and most moved to Portugal in 1492 after the expulsion. In 1212 Bishop Tello took part in the battle of Las Navas de Tolosa, where the city won the right to put a cross over its castle emblem.

Palencia is the capital of its province, on an economic axis with Valladolid and Burgos. Its Gothic cathedral, dedicated to San Antolín, was built from 1321 to 1504 over a Visigothic crypt, and its museum holds a twelve-panel retablo by Juan de Flandes, court painter to Queen Isabella I of Castile. Thirteen kilometres south, at Baños de Cerrato, stands a 7th-century basilica built by the Visigothic king Reccaswinth, the oldest church on the peninsula. The Roman villa of La Olmeda, a 4th-century house with 27 rooms, is known for its mosaics. The Canal de Castilla runs close to the city, and lechazo, roast suckling lamb, is the local speciality.
palenque: Much of Palenque's history has been reconstructed from the hieroglyphic inscriptions on its monuments, which give a long sequence of rulers. The first king known to the inscriptions, K'uk' Bahlam I, governed from 431. The city's kings competed with the states of Calakmul and Toniná. Under Yohl Ik'nal, troops from Calakmul invaded and sacked Palenque in 599, and in 611 the king of Calakmul entered the city in person, a disaster followed by political disorder. An inscription records that annual ceremonies went unperformed in 613 and laments the loss of the divine lady and the king.

The city recovered under K'inich Janaab' Pakal, who came to the throne at the age of 12 and reigned from 615 to 683. His mother Sak K'uk' had ruled for about three years and remained a force in his early reign. Most of the palaces and temples were built in his time, and the Palace was enlarged and remodelled in 654, 661 and 668. In 711 Palenque was sacked by Toniná and K'inich K'an Joy Chitam II was taken prisoner, and for some years the city had no king; K'inich Ahkal Mo' Nab' III was crowned in 722.

In the 8th century Palenque came under increasing stress, as did most Classic Maya states. There was no new elite construction in the ceremonial centre sometime after 800, an agricultural population stayed for a few generations, and the site was then abandoned.

Palenque, known in the Itza' language as Lakamha, meaning big water, stands in the Mexican state of Chiapas near the Usumacinta River, 150 metres above sea level. It is a medium-sized site, smaller than Tikal, Chichen Itza or Copán, but holds some of the finest Maya architecture, sculpture and bas-relief carving. The Palace, the largest complex, measures 97 by 73 metres at its base and has a four-story tower. An aqueduct with a three-metre-high vault diverts the Otulum River under the main plaza.

The Temple of the Inscriptions holds the second longest glyphic text known from the Maya world. In 1952 Alberto Ruz Lhuillier lifted a slab in its floor and found a stairway to the tomb of Pakal, whose sarcophagus held the richest jade collection seen in a Maya tomb, including a mosaic mask. John Lloyd Stephens and Frederick Catherwood visited in 1840. Archaeologists estimate that only about 10 percent of the city has been uncovered. Palenque National Park was designated in 1981.
palermo: Palermo lies in a basin formed by the Papireto, Kemonia and Oreto rivers, which the Arabs named the Conca d'Oro, the Golden Basin, in the 9th century. A mountain range forms a cirque around the city and faces the Tyrrhenian Sea, and historically it made the interior of Sicily hard to reach. Monte Pellegrino, which stands apart in front of the sea, is the historically most important of the mountains, and Goethe called its cliff the most beautiful promontory in the world. Cave drawings at nearby Addaura show settlement perhaps around 8000 BCE.

The original inhabitants were the Sicani, who according to Thucydides arrived from the Iberian Peninsula. In the 8th century BCE the Phoenicians built a settlement on the natural harbour, one of their three main colonies in Sicily along with Motya and Soluntum, and the city later passed to Carthage. As Panormus it was part of the Roman Republic and Empire for over a thousand years. The Vandals under Geiseric took it in 440 CE, and in late 535 Belisarius laid siege to the city, which had refused to surrender, and eventually prevailed. From 831 to 1072 Palermo was under Arab rule and for the first time the capital of Sicily.

After the Norman conquest it became the capital of the Kingdom of Sicily, which lasted from 1130 to 1816. Spain ruled the city from 1479 until 1713, with brief interruptions, and Austria from 1720 to 1734. Charles III chose Palermo for his coronation as King of Sicily, but the royal court resided in Naples. In 1866 Palermo was the seat of a week-long popular rebellion against annexation by the Savoy kingdom, which was crushed under martial law, and the Teatro Massimo opened in 1897.

Allied bombing in 1942 and 1943 destroyed the harbour and much of the city, with heavy civilian casualties, until the Allied invasion of Sicily captured it on 22 July 1943. In 1946 Palermo became the seat of the Regional Parliament, and in 1948 the element technetium was discovered at its university.

Palermo is the capital and largest city of Sicily. Its inhabitants speak Italian and the Palermitano dialect of Sicilian. The city is the main seat of the World Heritage Site Arab-Norman Palermo and the Cathedral Churches of Cefalù and Monreale, and its markets of Vucciria, Ballarò and Capo are known for fruit, vegetables and fish. Its patron saint is Saint Rosalia, whose feast day is 15 July.
palermo-stone: The Palermo Stone is one of seven surviving fragments of a stele known as the Royal Annals of the Old Kingdom. The stele listed the kings of Egypt from the First Dynasty through to the early part of the Fifth Dynasty and noted significant events in each year of their reigns. It may originally have been about 60 centimetres high and 2.1 metres wide, and is made of a hard black stone, probably basalt. The Palermo fragment is irregular and shield-shaped, 43.5 centimetres high, 25 wide and 6.5 thick at most.

Its front has six horizontal registers of hieroglyphs. The first lists the names of predynastic kings of Lower Egypt, identified by the Red Crown. Later registers give the annual events for kings of the First to Fourth Dynasties, and the back continues down to Neferirkare Kakai, third ruler of the Fifth Dynasty. Where a king is named, his mother's name is also recorded, such as Betrest, mother of Semerkhet, and Meresankh I, mother of Seneferu.

The annals record the height of the annual Nile flood, festivals such as the Sed festival, taxation, sculpture, buildings and warfare. They name pharaohs including Djer, Den, Semerkhet, Nynetjer, Peribsen, Khasekhemwy, Djoser, Huni, Sneferu, Khufu, Djedefre, Shepseskaf, Userkaf, Sahure and Neferirkare Kakai, and they preserve names of royal family members of the first five dynasties not otherwise recorded.

New Kingdom king lists such as the Turin Canon and the Abydos king list name Menes, probably Narmer, as the first king of the First Dynasty. The top register of the annals names at least fourteen earlier rulers, which may be preserved through oral tradition or may be fictitious; their identification with historical persons is controversial. The historian Manetho may have used information like that of the stele for his chronology.

The stele's original location is unknown, and no fragment has a secure archaeological provenance. A Sicilian lawyer, Ferdinand Guidano, bought the Palermo Stone in 1859, and his family presented it to the Palermo Archaeological Museum on 19 October 1877. Five fragments are in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, four acquired between 1895 and 1914 and one bought in 1963, and one small fragment is in the Petrie Museum in London. A visiting French archaeologist recognised its importance in 1895, and Heinrich Schäfer published it fully in 1902.

The date of the text is uncertain. It was probably made in the Fifth Dynasty, but it has been suggested that it was carved much later, perhaps in the Twenty-fifth Dynasty, though it would still rest on an Old Kingdom original. It is also unknown whether the fragments come from one stele or from separate copies, and some small Cairo fragments may not be genuine.
palestine-liberation-organization: At its first summit meeting in Cairo in 1964 the Arab League initiated the creation of an organisation to represent the Palestinian people. The Palestinian National Council convened in Jerusalem on 28 May 1964, and the PLO was founded on 2 June 1964, with the stated complementary goals of Arab unity and the liberation of Palestine. It initially sought an Arab state over the entire territory of the former Mandatory Palestine, and launched guerrilla attacks on Israel from Jordan, Lebanon, Egypt and Syria. In 1968 the founding charter was replaced by a revised version calling for a Palestinian state in which Christians, Muslims and Jews would have equal rights.

Fatah's founder, Yasser Arafat, was elected chairman in Cairo on 4 February 1969. In September 1970, in the events known as Black September, Jordan assaulted the PLO's armed groups, and by July 1971 it had been expelled to Lebanon. Israel drove it out in the 1982 Lebanon War; about 8,000 fighters evacuated Beirut, and the PLO moved to Tunis. In 1974 the United Nations General Assembly granted it observer status, on 22 November. In 1988 the National Council proclaimed a Palestinian Declaration of Independence in Algiers, and the PLO endorsed a two-state solution.

In the Oslo Accords of 1993, signed on 20 August and publicly on 13 September, the PLO recognised Israel's right to exist and accepted United Nations Security Council Resolution 242, and Israel recognised the PLO as the representative of the Palestinian people. The accords created the Palestinian Authority, with Arafat at its head, to govern Gaza and Jericho. In 1996 the PLO nullified the parts of its charter that called for Israel's destruction.

The PLO is formally an umbrella organisation of resistance movements, political parties and popular organisations. It was designed as a government in exile, with a parliament, the Palestinian National Council, as its highest authority and an elected Executive Committee. The Council has 740 members and the Committee 18. The Oslo Accords created a separate Palestinian Authority for the occupied territories, which came to replace the PLO as the prime Palestinian political institution.
palk-strait: The strait stretches for about 137 km and is between 64 and 137 km wide. Its waters are shallow: around the shoals of Ram Setu they are typically only 1 to 3 metres deep, the central part is typically around 20 metres deep, and the greatest depth is 35 metres. To the north, in the Bay of Bengal, the waves are mostly swells, while in Palk Bay to the south they are mostly smaller wind waves. In the Hindu epic Ramayana the shoals are part of a bridge built by the vanara army of Rama to rescue his wife Sita from the Asura king Ravana.

During the Last Glacial Period, when sea levels fell to as much as 120 metres below their present values, the whole of the shallow strait was dry land. It was submerged again as the sea rose during the Holocene, by around 7,000 years ago.

The construction of a shipping channel through the strait was first proposed to the British government of India in 1860. Pamban Island was linked to the Indian mainland by the Pamban Bridge, opened for traffic on 24 February 1914. Trains ran from Madras to Dhanushkodi at the southern tip of the island, where a ferry crossed to Talaimannar on Mannar Island and another train carried passengers on to Colombo. The railway line to Dhanushkodi was destroyed in the 1964 Dhanushkodi cyclone together with a passenger train, killing around 200 people. A ferry between Rameswaram and Talaimannar continued into the 1970s and was discontinued by the Indian government in 1984.

The shallows, small islands and reefs make the strait difficult for large ships, though fishing boats and small craft navigate it. The Sethusamudram Shipping Canal Project, commissioned by the Government of India in 2005 to dredge a channel, met opposition on religious grounds. A road bridge beside the Pamban Bridge was opened in 1988, and a new railway bridge was completed in 2024 after rail traffic on the old bridge was suspended permanently in February 2023 over concerns about its stability. A combined undersea tunnel and bridge linking India and Sri Lanka, the Palk Strait Bridge, was first discussed in 2002 and has been examined several times since.
palm-oil: Palm oil is an edible vegetable oil taken from the reddish pulp of the fruit of the African oil palm, Elaeis guineensis, which is native to the wetlands of western Africa. Humans have used oil palms for about 5,000 years. In the late 1800s archaeologists found in a tomb at Abydos, dating to 3,000 BCE, a substance that they concluded was originally palm oil. It has long been used as a cooking oil in West and Central African countries, where it features in dishes such as egusi soup and okra soup, and European merchants trading with West Africa occasionally bought it for the same purpose.

The oil is naturally red because of its high beta-carotene content, and it takes its name from palmitic acid, a saturated fatty acid that it contains in unusually high concentration. It should not be confused with palm kernel oil, which comes from the kernel of the same fruit, or with coconut oil. It is traditionally and still industrially produced by milling the fruit; since the 1990s some has also been cold-pressed, and this artisanal oil keeps its red colour. Refined, bleached and deodorized palm oil, the basic form sold on commodity markets, contains no carotenes. Because it is highly saturated it is solid at room temperature in temperate regions, which makes it a cheap substitute for butter or hydrogenated fats in pastry and baked goods.

Palm oil became sought after by British traders during the Industrial Revolution as an industrial lubricant for machinery, and it formed the basis of soaps such as Lever Brothers' Sunlight and the American Palmolive. It is now used in food, in personal care products and as a biofuel.

Its production has drawn criticism. Forests have been cleared in parts of Indonesia and Malaysia for oil palm monoculture, reducing the habitat of the three surviving orangutan species, and journalists and researchers have reported violations of indigenous land rights in fast-growing producing regions. Supporters point out that an oil palm plantation yields about ten times more oil per hectare than soybean, sunflower or rapeseed. The Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil was established in 2004 to promote global standards for its sustainable production.
palmyra: Palmyra lies in central Syria, 215 kilometres north-east of Damascus, in an oasis surrounded by palms. Two mountain ranges overlook it, and to the south and east it is exposed to the Syrian Desert. A small wadi, al-Qubur, crosses the area, and south of it rises the Efqa spring. Pliny the Elder, writing in the 70s CE, described the town as noted for its desert location, the richness of its soil and the springs that made agriculture and herding possible.

The city entered the written record about 2000 BCE, when Puzur-Ishtar the Tadmorean agreed to a contract at an Assyrian trading colony at Kültepe. At the beginning of the 11th century BCE Tiglath-Pileser I of Assyria recorded a defeat of the Arameans of Tadmar. The Hebrew Bible places a desert city Tadmor under Solomon, but its description does not fit the archaeology, since Palmyra was then a small settlement. Under the Seleucids, between 312 and 64 BCE, it became prosperous. In 217 BCE a force led by Zabdibel fought for Antiochus III at the Battle of Raphia.

Palmyra was autonomous before 273 CE and attached to the Roman province of Syria. It became a Roman colonia in the third century and a monarchy in 260. Its wealth, drawn from caravan trade, paid for the Great Colonnade, the Temple of Bel and the tower tombs of the Valley of Tombs, where the most recent tower is dated to 128. The Palmyrenes spoke Palmyrene Aramaic, used Greek in commerce and diplomacy, and worshipped Semitic, Mesopotamian and Arab deities.

Aurelian razed the city in 273, and Diocletian later restored it at a reduced size. The Palmyrenes became Christian in the fourth century. Khalid ibn al-Walid took the city for the Rashidun Caliphate in 634, and in the following centuries the inhabitants adopted Islam and Arabic. The Timurids reduced it to a small village in 1400. In 1932, under French Mandatory rule, the inhabitants were moved to the new village of Tadmur, and the ancient site was opened to excavation.

The ruins include the Temple of Bel, the Great Colonnade, a senate building and the funerary monuments of the Valley of Tombs, over a kilometre of necropolis with more than 50 monuments. Palmyrene funerary art is known above all for the bust reliefs that sealed burial chambers, which stress clothing, jewellery and a frontal pose. The site was damaged in the Syrian civil war, which began in 2011.
pamir-mountains: The Pamirs stand at a junction with several other great ranges: the Tian Shan, the Karakoram, the Kunlun, the Hindu Kush and the Himalayas. Much of the range lies in the Gorno-Badakhshan region of Tajikistan. To the south they border the Hindu Kush along Afghanistan's Wakhan Corridor, to the north they join the Tian Shan along the Alay Valley of Kyrgyzstan, and to the east they extend to the range that includes China's Kongur Tagh. The highest peak of the core is Ismoil Somoni Peak, 7,495 metres, known from 1932 to 1962 as Stalin Peak and from 1962 to 1998 as Communism Peak.

About 12,500 square kilometres, roughly a tenth of the Pamirs, is glaciated, and the Vanch-Yakh Glacier, 77 kilometres long, is the longest glacier outside the polar regions. Winters are long and bitterly cold and summers short and cool. Annual precipitation of about 130 mm supports grassland but few trees.

The lapis lazuli found in Egyptian tombs is thought to come from the Pamir area of Badakhshan. About 138 BCE Zhang Qian reached the Fergana Valley northwest of the Pamirs, and Ptolemy vaguely describes a trade route through the area. From about 600 CE Buddhist pilgrims travelled on both sides of the Pamirs to reach India from China, and in 747 a Tang army was on the Wakhan River. In Old and Middle Chinese the range was called the Onion Range, after the wild onions growing there. The Northern Silk Road, about 2,600 kilometres long, connected the Chinese capital Chang'an with Kashgar and crossed the Pamirs towards the west.

In 1838 Lieutenant John Wood reached the headwaters of the Pamir River. The British and Russians agreed in 1873 that the Afghan frontier would run along the Panj. Russian military-scientific expeditions mapped most of the Pamirs between 1871 and about 1893. In 1892 a Russian battalion under Mikhail Ionov camped near the present Murghab, and in 1893 the Russians built a fort there. The last blank areas around the Fedchenko Glacier were mapped in 1928 by the German-Soviet Alay-Pamir Expedition.

Sheep herding in the upper meadows is the main source of income of the region, and coal is mined in the west. The Pamir Highway, one of the highest international roads in the world, runs from Dushanbe in Tajikistan to Osh in Kyrgyzstan and is the main supply route of the isolated region.
pamplona: Pamplona lies at about 450 metres above sea level in a rounded valley, the Basin of Pamplona, on the flood plain of the Arga river, a tributary of the Ebro. The basin links the mountainous north of Navarre with the Ebro valley, and its position at a crossroads has served as a commercial link between those very different parts of the region. The historical centre stands on the left bank of the Arga.

Early settlement there goes back to the late Bronze Age or early Iron Age. In the winter of 75 to 74 BCE the area served as a camp for the Roman general Pompey in the war against Sertorius, and he is considered the founder of Pompaelo. Later research found that it was already the chief town of the Vascones, who called it Iruña, meaning the city. During the Visigothic period it became an episcopal see, and a staging ground for the Christianization of the area. The Franks raided it in 541.

From the 11th century economic recovery revived urban life, and the pilgrimages to Santiago de Compostela renewed commercial and cultural exchange with Christian Europe. In the 12th century two new boroughs, San Cernín and San Nicolás, were added to the original nucleus, the Navarrería, and the population there was swelled by Occitan merchants and artisans. Charles III decreed the union of the three places under a single municipality in 1423.

After the Castilian conquest of Navarre in 1512, Pamplona remained the capital of the semi-autonomous kingdom, which kept its own institutions and laws, but it became a Castilian-Spanish outpost. In 1513 King Ferdinand V ordered the demolition of the medieval castle and the city's monasteries and the building of a new castle nearby. Its southern walls were destroyed only in 1915.

Pamplona is the capital of the Chartered Community of Navarre. Its Gothic cathedral, of the 14th century, has an outstanding cloister, and the citadel and three of the four sides of the city walls survive. The city is known for the running of the bulls during the San Fermín festival, held each year from 6 to 14 July and brought to literary renown by Ernest Hemingway's novel The Sun Also Rises of 1926.
pan-africanism: Pan-Africanism aims to strengthen solidarity among all indigenous peoples of Africa and all peoples of African descent. It is said to originate in the struggles of sub-Saharan Africans against enslavement and colonization, from resistance on slave ships to plantation uprisings and the Back to Africa movements of the 19th century. Its core belief is that African people, on the continent and in the diaspora, share a common history and a common destiny.

The end of the 19th century produced an intercontinental political movement, alongside numerous slave insurrections in the New World, of which the Haitian Revolution is the best known. Ethiopianism gave a religious form to the same outlook. In London the Sons of Africa, addressed by Quobna Ottobah Cugoano in 1791, wrote letters to Granville Sharp, William Pitt and King George III.

Modern Pan-Africanism began around the start of the 20th century, led first by people of the diaspora. Henry Sylvester Williams, a barrister, established the African Association around 1897 and called the First Pan-African Conference, held in London's Westminster Hall in 1900, to protest the seizure of colonial lands and racial discrimination. The Pan-African Congress series followed, with meetings in Paris in 1919, London in 1921 and 1923, New York in 1927 and Manchester in 1945, pressing the cause of decolonisation.

Ghana's independence in March 1957 made Kwame Nkrumah its first prime minister and president, and he became a leading advocate of the unity of independent Africa and of regional integration for the whole continent. Under him Pan-Africanism moved beyond a movement of black Africa to a political discourse of regional unity. Pan-African thought influenced the founding of the Organisation of African Unity in 1963, since succeeded by the African Union. Most newly independent states opposed Nkrumah's wish for political union because they saw it as a threat to their sovereignty, and Félix Houphouët-Boigny was a staunch opponent.

The movement has produced many organisations and symbols, among them Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association, which adopted the red, black and green flag on 13 August 1920 in New York, and Robert Sobukwe's Pan Africanist Congress in apartheid South Africa. Flags in Malawi, Kenya and South Sudan draw on those colours, while green, yellow and red come from Ethiopia's 1897 flag. Women such as Amy Jacques Garvey and Claudia Jones were prominent, although scholarship has given them little attention. Critics, among them the journalist Philip Ochieng in 1971, have called it a movement of a self-interested educated elite that did not concern ordinary Africans.
pan-islamism: Pan-Islamism advocates the unity of Muslims under one Islamic state, often a caliphate or an international organisation with Islamic principles. It differs from pan-Arabism by focusing on religion rather than ethnicity, and it takes the ummah, the Muslim community, as the focus of allegiance. Classical scholars such as al-Mawardi and al-Ghazali discussed the ummah in a political sense, and the ideology draws on the early Islam of Muhammad and the Rashidun Caliphate. Many scholars see its doctrines in earlier states such as Islamic Iberia and the Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal empires.

In the 18th century reformers such as Shah Wali Allah of Delhi, Muhammad Ibn 'Abd al-Wahhab and Uthman dan Fodio called for puritanical renewal. They are regarded as precursors of modern pan-Islamism, but their influence stayed local, in South Asia, Arabia and West Africa, since they did not call for an international Islamic entity.

In the last quarter of the 19th century Sultan Abdul Hamid II promoted pan-Islamism in the Ottoman Empire, after Ottomanism, to prevent secession movements among the empire's Muslim peoples. The movement's major thinkers were Jamal al-Din al-Afghani, Muhammad Abduh and Rashid Rida, who opposed European penetration of Muslim lands. Afghani feared that nationalism would divide Muslims and sought the replacement of rulers subservient to foreigners by strong patriotic ones. His student Abduh preferred gradual reform through education and distanced himself from Afghani's political path.

Rida believed unity required restoring a caliphate that applied the Sharia, and in the 1920s he set out his doctrine in al-Khilafa aw al-Imama al-'Uzma. His journal Al-Manar promoted Islamic revival and anti-British revolt. Lothrop Stoddard noted in 1921 that the pan-Islamic press had grown from about 200 journals in 1900 to over 1000 by 1914.

After the abolition of the caliphate in 1924, pan-Islamism mobilised traditionalist and reform movements alike. After the Second World War, Arab nationalist parties such as the Ba'ath and Nasserist parties took power in Egypt, Libya, Iraq and Syria, and Islamists faced repression. Sayyid Qutb was imprisoned and later executed, and Nasser took control of the mosques. After the Arab defeat in the Six-Day War, pan-Islamism regained ground against pan-Arabism. Nasser dropped his opposition to a pan-Islamic platform, and the first summit of Muslim heads of state met at Rabat in 1969, leading to the Organisation of Islamic Conference.

During the Cold War Saudi Arabia and allied states led the pan-Islamist effort against communism. The Iranian Revolution of 1979 and the Afghan mujahideen's success against the Soviet Union in 1989 raised the popularity of Islamists. Sunni thinkers such as Abul Ala Maududi embraced a new caliphate, while Ruhollah Khomeini envisaged a united Islamic state led by a Shia scholar of law.
panama-canal: The idea of a canal across the Isthmus of Panama dates back to 1513, when the Spanish conquistador Vasco Núñez de Balboa first crossed the isthmus and noted the possibility in his journal. The earliest proposal for action dates to 1534, when the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V ordered a survey for a route through the Americas to ease the voyage of ships between Spain and Peru. In 1668 the English physician and philosopher Sir Thomas Browne proposed the isthmus as the most convenient place for such a canal.

The French diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps, who had built the Suez Canal, and the engineer Philippe Bunau-Varilla led the French attempt, begun in 1881. A concession from the Colombian government, obtained in 1878 and valid for 99 years, allowed the company to dig and exploit a canal. The French stopped in 1889 because investors lost confidence after engineering problems and a high death rate among workers. The United States took control of the canal property on 4 May 1904, inheriting a depleted workforce and a mass of equipment, much of it in poor condition.

The canal is an artificial waterway 82 kilometres long that connects the Caribbean Sea with the Pacific Ocean at the narrowest point of the isthmus. Because of the shape of the isthmus its general direction from the Atlantic to the Pacific is from north-west to south-east. Locks at each end lift ships up to Gatun Lake, an artificial lake 26 metres above sea level, created in 1913 by damming the Chagres River; locks at the other end lower them again. At its creation Gatun Lake was the largest human-made lake in the world. The original locks are 33.5 metres wide and admit ships of the Panamax size. A third, wider set of locks, built between 2007 and 2016, takes larger vessels.

The United States built the canal under the Isthmian Canal Commission, which also controlled the Panama Canal Zone. In 1907 Stevens resigned as chief engineer and President Theodore Roosevelt appointed Major George Washington Goethals of the US Army Corps of Engineers, who finished the work in 1914, two years ahead of the target date. The canal opened on 15 August 1914.

It shortened voyages between the oceans and spared ships the long and hazardous route around the southern tip of South America. Traffic rose from about 1,000 ships in 1914 to 14,702 vessels in 2008. The United States kept control of the canal and the Panama Canal Zone until the Torrijos–Carter Treaties of 1977 provided for its handover to Panama. After a period of joint American and Panamanian control, the Panamanian government took over in 1999, and the canal is now run by the Panama Canal Authority.
panama-city: Pedro Arias Dávila, also called Pedrarias, founded the city on 15 August 1519. Within a few years it became a launching point for the exploration and conquest of Peru, and the expeditions that conquered the Inca Empire set out from it in 1532. It was also a transit point for the gold and silver sent back to Spain through the isthmus, on a route that led to the fairs of Nombre de Dios and Portobelo.

On 28 January 1671 the privateer Henry Morgan attacked the city with a band of 1,400 men, looted it and set it on fire. The ruins, known as Panamá Viejo, still stand and are now a World Heritage Site. The city was rebuilt on a peninsula about 8 kilometres to the southwest, the site now called the Casco Viejo, which was planned as a walled city against further pirate attacks.

The Panama Railroad ran fully from 1855, and between 1848 and 1869 about 375,000 people crossed the isthmus from the Atlantic to the Pacific and 225,000 in the other direction, which brought the city prosperity. Panama declared independence from Colombia on 3 November 1903. The Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty of that year gave the United States a strip of land ten miles wide for a canal, and the canal was completed in 1914. William Gorgas, the chief sanitary officer, ordered the fumigation of homes and the cleansing of water, and yellow fever was eradicated by November 1905. Tension over the Canal Zone broke out on 9 January 1964, remembered as Martyrs' Day, and in 1999 the United States transferred full control of the canal to Panama.

Panama City is the capital and largest city of the Republic of Panama, at the Pacific entrance of the Panama Canal. About 410,354 people live in the city proper and over a million in the Panamá District. It is the country's political and administrative centre and a hub of banking and commerce. Panamá Viejo and the Casco Viejo, which UNESCO designated a World Heritage Site in 2003, hold the city's colonial past, and the old quarter mixes Spanish colonial, French, Antillean and art deco buildings.
pancho-villa: Villa told conflicting stories about his early life. According to most sources he was born on 5 June 1878 as José Doroteo Arango Arámbula, the eldest of five children of a sharecropper, Agustín Arango, and Micaela Arámbula. He grew up on the Rancho de la Coyotada, one of the largest haciendas in Durango, and had little schooling beyond basic literacy. He worked as a sharecropper, muleskinner, butcher, bricklayer and foreman for a US railway company. His dictated memoirs say that he became a hill-country thief after killing a hacienda owner who had raped his sister; the record shows that on 22 September 1894 he shot the man in the foot.

Villa joined the rebellion that Francisco Madero called in 1910 against President Porfirio Díaz, after Abraham González reached out to him in Chihuahua, and Madero promoted him to colonel. After Madero was murdered in the coup of February 1913, Villa joined Venustiano Carranza's Constitutionalist Army against Victoriano Huerta. That year local commanders elected him provisional governor of Chihuahua against Carranza's wishes, and he carried out a significant land reform, confiscating estates and expelling their owners. In 1914 Carranza diverted him from a direct advance on Mexico City, and Carranza's army entered the capital first in August.

After Huerta's fall, Villa and Emiliano Zapata allied against Carranza after the Convention of Aguascalientes, and a civil war followed. Álvaro Obregón decisively defeated Villa in 1915, and he split his remaining forces into guerrilla bands. At Namiquipa he rounded up the wives of men who had formed a home guard and allowed his soldiers to rape them, although some historians argue that crimes he did not commit were attributed to him.
