On 9 March 1916 nearly 100 of his men attacked Columbus, New Mexico, in which 18 Americans and about 80 Villistas died. President Wilson sent 5,000 soldiers under General Frederick Funston, and John Pershing's force, using aircraft and trucks, pursued Villa fruitlessly until February 1917.

After Carranza's fall in 1920 Villa negotiated an amnesty with the interim president Adolfo de la Huerta and received a landed estate on condition that he retire from politics. On 20 July 1923 he was shot dead in an ambush in Parral, most likely on the orders of Plutarco Elías Calles and President Obregón. His body was stolen from its grave in 1926 and the head removed. In 1976 his remains were reburied in the Monument to the Revolution in Mexico City.

He is generally regarded in Mexico as a hero who stood up to the United States, the subject of corridos, films and novels, while some American media call him a murderer. His biographer Friedrich Katz judged that his time as governor of Chihuahua might in some ways be called the first welfare state in Mexico.
pandara-vanniyan: Kulasegaram Vairamuthu Pandara Vanniyan was a native of the Vanni and is said to have reigned there from 1785. Much about his family is unclear, but reports give him a sister, Nallanachal Vanniyan, and two younger brothers who served as his minister and his commander. He married into the family of Kumarasinghe Maha Vanniya of Nuwara Wewa, and so gained political power in the southern Vanni as well as the north. He is said to have lived at Kumulamunai, in the present Mullaitivu District.

The Vanni served as a buffer zone between the north and south of Sri Lanka. After the Portuguese captured the Jaffna Kingdom in 1621 the region was under their nominal control, and around 1782 the Dutch defeated the Vanniar chieftains.

Pandara Vanniyan is said to have defeated the Dutch officer Lieutenant von Driberg several times. Against the British, the Vanniars carried on a predatory warfare in Mannar and Trincomalee and reached the Jaffna Peninsula, and the British built forts to keep them at bay. In alliance with the Kandy Kingdom he rose to expel the British from his district. On 25 August 1803 he attacked the Government House at Mullaitivu, drove out the garrison under Captain Edward Mudge of the 19th Regiment and seized the fort and its cannons. He then overran the northern districts as far as Elephant Pass.

He turned from conventional warfare to guerrilla tactics, but the British organised a three-pronged attack from Jaffna, Mannar and Trincomalee. Von Driberg, who had stayed on after the British ousted the Dutch, defeated him on 31 October 1803 at Katsilaimadu, capturing a cannon given to him by the Kandyan king Sri Wickrema Rajasinghe. His houses were burned and his people dispersed into the jungle and out of the Vanni.

No longer a ruler, Pandara Vanniyan withdrew to areas near the Kandy Kingdom. Accounts of his end differ: by one he died fighting the British, by another he remained there until September 1810, when British forces ambushed him, and later died of his injuries. Von Driberg set up a granite monument at Katsilaimadu recording the defeat; in 2010 it was found broken. Prime Minister Ranasinghe Premadasa declared him a national hero in 1982, and a statue stands in Vavuniya. Tamil nationalists honour him as an epic hero, and he is the subject of a novel by M. Karunanidhi and of a play by Mullaimani Ve Cuppiramaniyam that won a prize from the Ceylon Art Council in 1964.
pandavas: The name Pandava means descendants of Pandu. According to the Adi Parva of the Mahabharata, Pandu was crowned king of the Kuru kingdom although he was younger than his blind brother Dhritarashtra. Cursed by a sage to die if he touched a wife in desire, he withdrew to the forest with his wives Kunti and Madri. Kunti had received a boon from the sage Durvasa allowing her to have a son by any god, and at Pandu's request she used it and shared her mantra with Madri.

Yudhishthira was fathered by the god Dharmadeva, Bhima by Vayu, Arjuna by Indra and the twins Nakula and Sahadeva by the Ashvins. After Pandu's death Kunti brought the boys to Hastinapura, where they were raised with their cousins the Kauravas, the hundred sons of Dhritarashtra.

Duryodhana, the eldest Kaurava, resented his cousins. When Yudhishthira was named crown prince, Duryodhana and his uncle Shakuni had a palace of flammable lac built at Varnavarta, but Vidura warned the Pandavas and they escaped by a tunnel. Arjuna then won the hand of Draupadi, princess of Panchala, in an archery contest, and all five brothers married her. Dhritarashtra partitioned the kingdom and gave them barren Khandavaprastha, which they built into the city of Indraprastha.

Shakuni then drew Yudhishthira into a game of dice, in which he lost his kingdom, his brothers, himself and Draupadi. In a last game the loser was to spend twelve years in exile and a thirteenth in disguise, and the Pandavas lost. They spent that year as servants at the court of King Virata of Matsya, and when they returned the Kauravas refused to give back the kingdom.

The Kurukshetra War lasted eighteen days. All hundred Kauravas and their army were killed, and the Pandavas, aided by Krishna, won at great cost. Yudhishthira was crowned, and the brothers ruled Hastinapura for thirty-six years before setting out with Draupadi for Mount Kailash.

The Harivamsa Purana, of the 8th century CE, tells the Jain version of their story. In the Garhwal region of Uttarakhand villagers perform the Pandav Lila, a ritual re-enactment of episodes from the epic in song, dance and recitation.
pannonia: Pannonia was a province of the Roman Empire bounded on the north and east by the Danube, on the west by Noricum and upper Italy, and on the south by Dalmatia and upper Moesia. It included western Hungary, western Slovakia, eastern Austria, northern Croatia, north-western Serbia, northern Slovenia and northern Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the Early Iron Age Transdanubia was inhabited by the Pannonians, a collection of Illyrian tribes. Celtic groups, the Scordisci, the Boii and others, later held much of the region, and the Dacian king Burebista overcame several of them between 65 and 50 BCE.

Rome's advance began with the foundation of Aquileia in 181 BCE. In 35 BCE Octavian captured Siscia after a month-long siege and occupied much of the Sava valley. In 15 BCE the future emperor Tiberius defeated the Scordisci, and his operations of 12 to 9 BCE almost certainly brought the whole of Transdanubia under Roman control. Augustus later claimed in his Res Gestae that Tiberius had brought the Pannonian peoples under Roman authority. The Bellum Batonianum, a revolt led by the Breuci under Bato the Breucian and the Daesitiates under Bato the Daesitiate, lasted three years until the last rebel laid down arms in 9 CE. Illyricum was then divided into Dalmatia and Pannonia.

Claudius finished the occupation and began building the frontier, the limes. Under Trajan, between 103 and 107, the province was divided into Pannonia Inferior and Pannonia Superior, the latter with most of the urbanised areas and three legions. Wars with the Marcomanni and Quadi under Marcus Aurelius, from 166, brought heavy destruction and loss of life to Pannonia. Diocletian and his successors divided it into four provinces, Prima, Valeria, Savia and Secunda. In 324 Constantine I annexed the plains to the east up to a new limes, the Devil's Dykes.

Rome lost the province in stages. In 433 Flavius Aetius ceded part of it to the Huns, and after the Hunnic empire collapsed in 454, Emperor Marcian settled large numbers of Ostrogoths there as foederati. Justinian I's Eastern Roman Empire held southern parts in the 6th century, the Avars invaded in the 560s, and Slavs settled over time. In the 790s the Franks invaded and used the name Pannonia for a new frontier province, the March of Pannonia.

Roman Pannonia was fairly productive, with oats and barley its chief crops, and timber an important export until the forests were cleared. Native settlements were organised in cantons, while most large towns were of Roman origin, among them Carnuntum, Vindobona, Aquincum, Savaria, Sirmium and Siscia. Christianity began to spread in the province in the 2nd century. A dialect called Pannonian Latin developed and went extinct around the 6th century. The ancient name survives in the modern term Pannonian plain.
paolo-veronese: Veronese took his usual name from Verona, where he was born in 1528, the fifth child of a stonecutter named Gabriele and his wife Caterina. He was first known as Paolo Spezapreda, after his father's trade, and later took the surname Caliari because his mother was the illegitimate daughter of a nobleman, Antonio Caliari. By 1541 he was apprenticed to Antonio Badile, later his father-in-law, and in 1544 to Giovanni Francesco Caroto, both leading painters in Verona. Trained in the Mannerism then popular in Parma, he soon developed a preference for a more radiant palette.
In 1551 the Giustiniani family commissioned an altarpiece from him for the church of San Francesco della Vigna in Venice, and in 1552 Cardinal Ercole Gonzaga commissioned one for Mantua Cathedral.

Veronese moved to Venice in 1553 after receiving his first state commission, ceiling frescoes in the Hall of the Council of Ten in the Doge's Palace. His ceilings of 1557 in the Marciana Library won a prize judged by Titian and Jacopo Sansovino.

In the late 1550s he decorated the Villa Barbaro at Maser, a new building by Andrea Palladio, with frescoes that combine portraits of the family, mythological figures and ceilings opening to blue skies. His Wedding at Cana, painted in 1562–1563 for the monastery of San Giorgio Maggiore, was to cover 66 square metres; the contract required premium pigments and as many figures as possible, and it includes portraits of Titian and Tintoretto and a self-portrait. In 1565 he married Elena Badile, the daughter of his first master. He headed a family workshop that included his brother Benedetto and his sons Carlo and Gabriele, which went on after his death in 1588, signing its works Haeredes Pauli.

In 1573 Veronese completed a Last Supper for the refectory of the Basilica of Santi Giovanni e Paolo, replacing a painting by Titian that had been burnt in a fire. At 5.55 by 12.80 metres, it showed a banquet that included German soldiers, dwarves and animals.

On 18 July 1573 the Venetian Inquisition summoned him to explain these figures, which it considered extraneous to the Last Supper. He told the tribunal that painters take the same liberties as poets and madmen. The Inquisition ordered him to repaint the scene; he opposed this remedy but was compelled to retitle the work The Feast in the House of Levi. The interrogation is described as cautionary rather than punitive. His admirers have included Rubens, Watteau, Tiepolo, Delacroix and Renoir, though his work has been felt not to permit expression of the profound.
papacy: According to Catholic tradition, the apostolic see of Rome was founded by Saint Peter and Saint Paul in the first century. The Catholic Church teaches that the bishop of Rome succeeded Saint Peter, to whom, in its reading of Matthew 16, Jesus gave the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the powers of binding and loosing. Cyprian of Carthage, in his Letter 55 of about 251 CE to Pope Cornelius, recognised the bishop of Rome as Peter's successor.

The word pope comes from the Greek páppas, father. In the early centuries it was applied, especially in the East, to all bishops and senior clergy. It became reserved in the West to the bishop of Rome during the reign of Leo I (440 to 461), though this was made official only in the 11th century.

In ancient times popes helped spread Christianity and intervened in doctrinal disputes. In the Middle Ages they played a role of secular importance in Western Europe, often arbitrating between Christian monarchs, and their influence eventually rivalled that of territorial rulers. From the 8th century until 1870 the pope was sovereign of the Papal States, and since the Lateran Treaty of 1929 he has headed the much smaller Vatican City State. Between 1309 and 1378 the popes lived in Avignon, France, a period often called the Babylonian captivity. The First Vatican Council defined the pope's authority on 18 July 1870, and in 1870 the dogma of papal infallibility was proclaimed for the rare occasions when the pope speaks ex cathedra on faith or morals.

The pope was originally chosen by the senior clergy in and near Rome. In 1059 the electorate was restricted to the cardinals, and in 1179 the votes of all cardinal electors were made equal. The last pope elected when not yet a bishop was Gregory XVI in 1831, and the last not a cardinal was Urban VI in 1378. Popes adopt a new name on accession.

His official seat is the Archbasilica of Saint John Lateran, and his residence the Apostolic Palace. Antipopes are claimants not canonically elected; briefly in the 15th century three separate lines of popes claimed authenticity. Eastern Orthodox churches and the Anglican Communion accept apostolic succession and a primacy of honour but reject the pope as Peter's successor in any other sense than other bishops.
papiamento: Scholars dispute where Papiamento came from, and its precise history has not been established. Its parent language is West Iberian Romance, but some derive it from Portuguese and the Portuguese-based creoles, others from Spanish. Most linguists now believe it emerged from the Portuguese-based creoles of the West African coasts, since it shares many features with Cape Verdean Creole and Guinea-Bissau Creole. Bart Jacob has argued that it is a relexified offshoot of an early Upper Guinea Portuguese Creole carried to Curaçao from Senegambia in the second half of the 17th century, when the Dutch held the slave-trading island of Gorée. A local-development theory instead proposes a Portuguese-African pidgin formed in the Caribbean, with later Dutch and Spanish influences.

In 1634 the Dutch West India Company took possession of the islands, deporting most of the remaining Arawak and Spanish population and making them a hub of the Dutch slave trade between Africa and the Caribbean. After 1654 the Jewish and Portuguese-speaking population of the islands grew substantially, as Portuguese-speaking Jews and their allies fled Northeast Brazil. The Sephardic community became the main merchants, and everyday trading was conducted in Papiamento. The language itself dates from about 1650.

About 80 per cent of the vocabulary is Iberian in origin and about 20 per cent Dutch, with some words from Native American and African languages. Many Iberian words cannot be assigned to Portuguese or Spanish, such as por fabor and señora. Words of Taíno and Arawak origin, mostly for plants and animals, include maishi, corn, and kunuku, farm; African ones include pinda, peanut, from Kongo mpinda. The grammar is typical of Atlantic creoles: time and aspect markers are used instead of tenses, there is no grammatical gender, and the plural is marked by the suffix -nan on definite nouns.

There are two main dialects, Papiamento on Aruba and Papiamentu on Curaçao and Bonaire. Curaçao and Bonaire adopted the phonetic Römer-Maduro-Jonis spelling in 1976, and Aruba approved a more etymological one in 1977.

Widespread use in official documents is first seen in the early 18th century. The oldest preserved texts are letters, the earliest of 1775. In the 19th century most materials on the islands were written in Papiamento, including Roman Catholic school books and hymnals. The Catecismo Corticu of 1837, the first printed book in the language, was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2009, and the first newspaper, Civilisadó, appeared in 1871. Papiamento became an official language of Aruba in 2003 and of the Netherlands Antilles in 2007. The anthems of Aruba, Bonaire and Curaçao are in it.
papua-new-guinea: The country covers 462,840 km2 and includes a large mainland and hundreds of islands in Melanesia, north of Australia. It lies where the north-moving Indo-Australian plate meets the west-moving Pacific plate, which gives it a highly variable geography, active volcanoes and frequent earthquakes. Mountains cover at least 72% of the country, and the highest point is Mount Wilhelm, at 4,509 metres. The Torres Strait, 152 kilometres wide, separates it from Australia's Cape York Peninsula. This terrain helps explain why the population is largely rural and divided into many small communities.

Archaeological evidence indicates that modern humans first reached what became New Guinea around 42,000 to 45,000 years ago. Agriculture was developed independently in the New Guinea highlands around 7000 BCE, making it one of the few areas where people domesticated plants without outside influence. Austronesian-speaking peoples of the Lapita culture had reached the Bismarck Archipelago by about 3,300 years ago. Communities were linked by trade, and bananas and sugarcane probably passed from New Guinea to other regions along these networks, but each community otherwise functioned largely independently.

European names for the island date from the 16th century: Jorge de Menezes called it Ilhas dos Papuas in 1526, and Yñigo Ortiz de Retez named it Nueva Guinea in 1545. In 1884 the eastern half was divided between German New Guinea in the north and British New Guinea in the south. The British territory was ceded to Australia in 1902 and became the Territory of Papua. Australia occupied German New Guinea during the First World War and then ruled it as a League of Nations mandate. The two territories were united in 1949, after fierce fighting there in World War II, and the country became independent in 1975. Europeans brought together communities that had sometimes been hostile or had no relationship at all.

Papua New Guinea is a Commonwealth realm with a governor-general representing the monarch and a unicameral National Parliament of 118 seats, in a Westminster system. Its capital and largest city is Port Moresby. There are 840 known spoken languages, the most of any country, and English and Tok Pisin serve as common languages. Most people live in customary communities, and the constitution protects traditional communities and lifestyles.
papyrus: Papyrus was first manufactured in Egypt as far back as the 3rd millennium BCE, and it is known to have been used at least as early as the First Dynasty. The earliest archaeological evidence was excavated in 2012 and 2013 at Wadi al-Jarf, an ancient Egyptian harbour on the Red Sea coast: the Diary of Merer, dated about 2560 to 2550 BCE, at the end of the reign of Khufu, describes the last years of the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza. The Egyptians also used papyrus reeds for boats, mats, rope, sandals and baskets. The Greek word biblos, from which bibliography and bible derive, referred to the inner part of the plant.

Papyrus was made from the stem of the sedge Cyperus papyrus. The outer rind was removed and the sticky inner pith cut lengthwise into strips about 40 centimetres long. The strips were laid side by side with their edges slightly overlapping, and a second layer was placed across them at right angles. While still moist, the layers were hammered into a single sheet, which was dried under pressure and polished with a rounded object. Sheets were glued together into a roll, a scroll, and texts were normally written first on the side where the fibres ran along the roll.

Pliny the Elder and Isidore of Seville described six grades sold in the Roman market. Papyrus is stable in a dry climate such as Egypt's, but humid conditions let mould destroy it, and in Europe it seems to have lasted only decades. It was cheap and easy to produce, but fragile, and it was not pliable enough to fold without cracking.

Late in its history papyrus began to be gathered into codices, which early Christian writers soon adopted. Parchment, made from animal skins, gradually overtook it in West Asia and Europe. By the beginning of the 4th century CE the most important books were being made on parchment, which was more durable in moist climates and could be written on both sides. As trade networks declined, papyrus lost its cost advantage outside Egypt. The latest certain uses in Europe are a papal decree of 1057 and an Arabic document of 1087. In Egypt it continued in use until the cheaper paper introduced from the Islamic world replaced it.

Papyri give the only surviving copy of Menander, as well as the Egyptian Book of the Dead and the Ebers, Edwin Smith, Rhind and Westcar papyri. The first modern discovery of papyrus rolls was made at Herculaneum in 1752, and the Dutch historian Caspar Reuvens began scholarly study with the Leyden papyrus, published in 1830.
parachute: The earliest recorded attempt to slow a fall with fabric is that of Armen Firman, an Andalusian who in 852, at Córdoba, jumped from a tower wearing a large cloak. It was recorded that there was enough air in the folds of the cloak to prevent great injury. The earliest evidence of a purposely designed parachute dates from the Renaissance. The manuscript of the 1470s attributed to Francesco di Giorgio Martini shows a free-hanging man clutching a crossbar frame attached to a conical canopy, with four straps running to a waist belt. The canopy looks too small to give effective resistance, but the basic concept is apparent.

In 1691 Simon de La Loubère reported that at the court of King Narai of Ayutthaya a man would jump from a high place holding two large umbrellas, landing in trees, on rooftops and sometimes in rivers. The French physicist Louis-Sébastien Lenormand read the report a century later. He made the first recorded public jump in 1783 and in 1785 coined the word, joining the Italian para, from parare, to ward off, to the French chute, a fall.

In 1911 Grant Morton made the first parachute jump from an aeroplane, a Wright Model B flown by Phil Parmalee at Venice Beach, California, holding a throw-out parachute in his arms. In the same year Gleb Kotelnikov invented the first knapsack parachute, although Hermann Lattemann and his wife Käthe Paulus had already jumped with bagged parachutes in the last decade of the 19th century. On 4 February 1912 Franz Reichelt died jumping from the Eiffel Tower while testing a wearable parachute.

The first military users were artillery observers on tethered balloons in the First World War. A waist harness pulled the lines and canopy from a bag hung on the balloon as they jumped. The Germans adopted them on a large scale for balloon crews, then the British and the French. In fixed-wing aircraft the lines often tangled in a spinning machine, and no parachutes were issued to the crews of Allied heavier-than-air aircraft.

After the war Major Edward L. Hoffman of the United States Army led an effort to combine the best features of several designs. The resulting Airplane Parachute Type-A had a soft pack worn on the back, a ripcord and a pilot chute that draws out the main canopy. Leslie Irvin tested it by jumping from an aeroplane in 1919, and it went into production. After the Second World War parachuting became a popular sport, and nylon replaced silk.
paraguay: Paraguay lies between latitudes 19° and 28°S in the central region of South America and is divided by the Río Paraguay into two regions. The eastern region has mostly grassy plains and wooded hills, while the western region, known as the Chaco and part of the Gran Chaco, has mostly low, marshy plains. The far eastern forest belt receives an average of 170 centimetres of rain a year, the western Chaco no more than 50 centimetres. Although landlocked, Paraguay reaches the Atlantic Ocean by the Paraná–Paraguay Waterway, a system of navigable channels shared by five countries.

The Guaraní had lived in eastern Paraguay for at least a millennium when the Spanish arrived. The Gran Chaco in the west was inhabited by nomads, of whom the Guaycuru peoples were most prominent, and the Paraguay River roughly divided the agricultural Guaraní from them. The Mbayá were known for their warrior traditions and were not fully pacified until the late 19th century. Juan de Salazar de Espinosa founded Asunción on 15 August 1537, and it became the centre of the Spanish colonial province of Paraguay.

In the eighteenth century Jesuit missions developed reductions to gather Guaraní populations and protect them from virtual slavery by Spanish settlers and Portuguese slave raiders, the bandeirantes. The reducciones flourished in eastern Paraguay for about 150 years, until the Spanish Crown expelled the Jesuits in 1767. Paraguay overthrew the local Spanish administration on 14 May 1811. José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia, nicknamed El Supremo, ruled from 1814 until his death in 1840 with very little outside contact, intending a utopian society based on Rousseau's Social Contract. The Triple Alliance War of 1864 to 1870 cost the country half its prewar population and around a quarter to a third of its territory. Paraguay then prevailed in the Chaco War with Bolivia of 1932 to 1935.

Asunción is the capital and largest city. Paraguay is a unitary presidential republic of seventeen departments and a capital district. The population was 6,109,944 at the 2022 census, and most people live in the east. Paraguayan culture is a fusion of European and Southern Guaraní traditions: more than 80% of Paraguayans speak both Spanish and Guaraní. The ruins of two eighteenth-century Jesuit missions, La Santísima Trinidad de Paraná and Jesús de Tavarangue, are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Paraguay is a founding member of Mercosur, the United Nations and the Organization of American States.
paraiba: Paraíba is a state in the Brazilian Northeast, bordered by Rio Grande do Norte to the north, Ceará to the west, Pernambuco to the south and the Atlantic Ocean to the east. Its coast reaches Ponta do Seixas, the easternmost point of the mainland Americas, and the interior rises to the Borborema Plateau, where Pico do Jabre, at 1,208 metres, is the state's highest peak. Most of its territory has a hot semi-arid climate. It takes its name from the Paraíba river, and its area is about 56,467 square kilometres.

Before Europeans came, the Potiguara, part of the Tupi group, lived between the coast and the Borborema Plateau along the Paraíba do Norte river, and the Kiriri and Ariús lived further west. Colonisation began in 1534, when King John III of Portugal divided Brazil into fifteen captaincies. Most of what is now Paraíba fell under the Captaincy of Itamaracá, which was troubled by French piracy, especially of wood, animal skins and amber. Its sugar made the captaincy one of the most successful regions of Portuguese America.

The Dutch, who had seized Salvador in 1624, first appeared on Paraíban soil on 20 June 1625, in the Bay of Traição. Admiral Boudewijn Hendricksz allied with the Potiguara, but troops from Paraíba, Pernambuco and Rio Grande and from indigenous peoples defeated the Dutch on 1 August, at a cost to the Potiguara of 600 to a thousand dead. From 1670 colonists, led by bandeirantes such as Domingos Jorge Velho, pushed into the interior, with the enslavement and massacre of indigenous peoples. The captaincy was annexed to Pernambuco in 1756 and restored in 1799. Paraíba joined the Pernambuco Revolution of 1817, which sought Brazilian independence and spread through the Northeast, and it became a federal state in November 1889 when the republic was proclaimed.

João Pessoa is the coastal capital, and Campina Grande, in the interior, is among the fifteen largest municipalities of the Northeast. The 2022 census counted 3,974,687 people, and Portuguese is the language of the state. The economy has long drawn on sugarcane, cattle, shoes and leather goods, and tourism. A copper-bearing tourmaline of vivid blue-green colour was found in the Batalha mine in 1987. The Festa Junina, the Saint John festival brought by the Portuguese, is a major celebration.
paramaribo: Paramaribo lies on the banks of the Suriname River, about 15 kilometres inland from the Atlantic Ocean, in the Paramaribo District. The city is named for the Paramaribo people who lived at the mouth of the river, and the name is from the Tupi-Guarani para, large river, and maribo, inhabitants. The name is probably a corruption of the name of a native village, spelled Parmurbo in the earliest Dutch sources. It has a tropical rainforest climate with no true dry season.

The first Dutch settlement at the site was a trading post established in 1613 by Nicolaes Baliestel and Dirck Claeszoon van Sanen. English and French traders also tried to settle in Suriname, including a French post founded in 1644 near the present city. All these early settlements were abandoned before English settlers, sent by the governor of Barbados, Lord Francis Willoughby, arrived in 1650. They founded a town on the site, protected by Fort Willoughby, and in 1662 King Charles II granted Willoughby the settlement and its surrounding lands. Around 1665 the village of Paramaribo was expanded and quickly outranked the earlier settlement of Torarica.

In 1667, during the Second Anglo-Dutch War, a squadron under Abraham Crijnssen conquered Paramaribo, and the Treaty of Breda in 1667 confirmed it as the leading town of the Dutch colony of Suriname. The fort was renamed Fort Zeelandia after the Dutch province that had financed the fleet. The population has always been diverse. Many of the first British settlers were Jews, and the Neveh Shalom Synagogue, one of the oldest synagogues in the Americas, stands in the city. The population grew greatly after 1873, when formerly enslaved people, freed in 1863, were allowed to stop working for their former masters and to leave the sugar plantations.

Fires repeatedly devastated the old town, notably in January 1821, when over 400 buildings were destroyed, and in September 1832, when nearly 50 were lost. The enslaved men Kodjo, Mentor and Present were found guilty of arson and burnt alive. Paramaribo has remained the capital of Suriname through its colonial days and the independence of 1975.

Paramaribo is the capital and largest city of Suriname and holds almost half of the country's population. The Dutch colonial town of the 17th and 18th centuries along the left bank of the river became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2002, and its original architecture and street plan have largely remained intact. Landmarks include Fort Zeelandia, the Presidential Palace, the Roman Catholic cathedral of St Peter and St Paul, the Suriname Mosque and the Kwakoe memorial to the abolition of slavery. The city is the business and financial centre of the country.
parana-entre-rios: Paraná stands on the eastern shore of the Paraná River, opposite the city of Santa Fe, capital of the neighbouring Santa Fe Province. Its original name was Bajada, meaning landing. The climate is Pampean, classed as humid subtropical, with an average annual temperature of 18 °C. Winters have mild days and very cold nights, with occasional frosts, while summers are hot and bring most of the rain, about 1,069 millimetres in a year. The city and the whole province lie in an area of high tornado risk, particularly in spring and summer.

In 1730 inhabitants of Santa Fe settled on the other shore of the river and called the place Baxada del Paraná. The first settlers had been forced out of Santa Fe by raiding Payaguá and Muños peoples. They settled in what is now the Square of the first of May, where they built a fort, other defences and a series of huts. Their numbers eventually became stable enough for them to move from defence to offence, and they almost wiped out both peoples. In the middle of the 19th century the city served for some years as the capital of the Argentine Confederation, until 1861.

Paraná is the seat of the provincial government of Entre Ríos and an important river port for the transshipment of cereals, cattle, fish and lumber from the surrounding region. Its industries include the manufacture of cement, furniture and ceramics. The city centre combines colonial churches with buildings in European styles such as the 3 de Febrero Theatre and the Government House, and the Cathedral blends several architectural styles. The Hernandarias Subfluvial Tunnel, inaugurated in 1969, links the city to Santa Fe beneath the river. Its main sports clubs include the basketball team Atlético Echagüe and the football clubs Patronato and Atlético Paraná.
paris: Paris lies in northern central France, in a north-bending arc of the river Seine, whose crest includes two islands, the Île Saint-Louis and the larger Île de la Cité, which form the oldest part of the city. The Seine's mouth on the English Channel is about 375 kilometres downstream. The city is relatively flat, with its lowest point 35 metres above sea level, and the highest of its hills, Montmartre, rises to 130 metres. Excluding the outlying parks, it covers an oval of about 87 square kilometres, enclosed by the 35-kilometre ring road, the Boulevard Périphérique, and since an annexation in 1860 it has had 20 arrondissements.

The Parisii, a Gallic tribe, inhabited the Paris area from around the middle of the 3rd century BCE. A major north–south trade route crossed the Seine on the Île de la Cité, which gradually became an important trading centre, and the Parisii traded with river towns as far away as the Iberian Peninsula and minted their own coins.

Julius Caesar conquered the Paris Basin for the Roman Republic in 52 BCE, and the Roman town of Lutetia grew on the Left Bank into a prosperous city with a forum, baths, temples, theatres and an amphitheatre. By the end of the Western Roman Empire it was known as Parisius. According to legend, Saint Denis, the first Bishop of Paris, introduced Christianity in the middle of the 3rd century CE and was beheaded on the hill later called Montmartre.

For almost all of its history, except for a few brief periods, Paris was governed directly by representatives of the king, emperor or president of France. In the 17th century the Académie royale de peinture et de sculpture was established in 1648, and urbanism laws have been strictly controlled since the early 17th century. Between 1853 and 1870 Napoleon III and his Prefect of the Seine, Baron Haussmann, rebuilt the city centre, creating wide boulevards, standard facades of cream-grey Paris stone and major parks around the centre.

Paris is the capital and largest city of France, with a city population of 2.04 million and a metropolitan population of 13.3 million. The National Assembly granted it municipal autonomy in 1974, and Jacques Chirac became its first elected mayor in March 1977. Its population peaked at 2.9 million in 1921. In the 19th and early 20th centuries artists including Manet, Monet and Renoir worked there, and Impressionism, Cubism and Art Deco all evolved in the city. It hosts UNESCO, whose headquarters have been there since November 1958, and the OECD, and it has hosted the Summer Olympics in 1900, 1924 and 2024.
paris-peace-conference-1919-1920: In 1917 US president Woodrow Wilson commissioned about 150 academics to research the topics likely to arise in peace talks and to develop principles for the negotiations. Their work was summarised in the Fourteen Points, which became the basis of the terms of the German surrender and of the Armistice of 11 November 1918. The conference brought together diplomats from 32 countries and nationalities. Germany, Austria-Hungary, Turkey and Bulgaria were given no voice in the deliberations, and Russia was represented, though not by its actual government.

The conference formally opened on 18 January 1919 at the Quai d'Orsay in Paris, a date chosen because it was the anniversary of the proclamation of William I as German Emperor in 1871. Delegates were assigned to 52 commissions, which held 1,646 sessions on topics ranging from prisoners of war to undersea cables. The five great powers, France, Britain, Italy, Japan and the United States, controlled it, and the Big Four leaders, Georges Clemenceau, David Lloyd George, Wilson and Vittorio Emanuele Orlando, met informally 145 times and agreed all major decisions before they were ratified.

Clemenceau's chief aim was to weaken Germany militarily, strategically and economically. Italy sought the territories promised in the secret Treaty of London. Japan proposed a racial equality clause for the League's Covenant on 13 February and claimed Germany's concessions in Shantung. The Western powers transferred those concessions to Japan, which sparked student protests in China on 4 May, later known as the May Fourth Movement; the Chinese delegation was the only one that did not sign the Treaty of Versailles.

The main result was the Treaty of Versailles with Germany, which had 15 chapters and 440 clauses. Article 231 of the treaty placed responsibility for the war on "the aggression of Germany and her allies", a provision that humiliated German leaders and citizens, and Germany stopped paying reparations after 1931, having delivered only a small portion. German and Ottoman overseas possessions passed as mandates chiefly to Britain and France, and new boundaries were drawn, sometimes after plebiscites. Delegations from Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania won recognition of their independence, while Ukraine, Ireland, Korea and Vietnam were effectively ignored.

The senior statesmen stopped working personally on the conference in June 1919, but historian Michael Neiberg notes that the formal peace process did not end until the Treaty of Lausanne of July 1923. The settlement is considered one of the great watersheds of 20th-century geopolitics, and its exclusion of the defeated powers later gave rise to political resentments that lasted decades.
parmenides: Parmenides was born in the Greek colony of Elea in southern Italy to a wealthy and aristocratic family. Diogenes Laërtius gives his father's name as Pires. The same writer passes on two divergent accounts of his teacher. One, following Sotion, says he first studied with Xenophanes but did not follow him, and later preferred the Pythagorean Aminias. Another, following Theophrastus, makes him a disciple of Anaximander.

The date of his birth is not known. Apollodorus, as transmitted by Diogenes Laërtius, puts his prime in the years 504 to 500 BCE, which would place his birth about 40 years earlier. Plato's dialogue Parmenides shows him visiting Athens at about the age of 65, when Socrates was a young man, which would suggest a birth around 515 BCE. Most modern classicists regard that visit and meeting as fiction, and some scholars prefer other dates. He is generally thought to have been in his prime around 475 BCE.

Plutarch, Strabo and Diogenes Laërtius, following Speusippus, agree that Parmenides took part in the government of his city, organising it and giving it an admirable code of laws. In 1969 the plinth of a statue of the 1st century CE was excavated at Velia, the later Elea. It names Parmenides, son of Pires, and calls him a physicist, the word then used for philosophers who studied nature. Its third word, ouliadēs, may mean simply a native of Elea or a member of a medical school devoted to Apollo Ulius, which would make him a physician as well as a legislator. Other specialists hold that the plinth shows only his social importance in the city.

The only known work is a poem in dactylic hexameter, later titled On Nature. About 160 verses survive from an original total probably near 800, largely through long excerpts made by Sextus Empiricus and Simplicius of Cilicia. It had three parts: a proem with an allegorical narrative, the Way of Truth and the Way of Opinion, of which only small fragments and prose paraphrases remain.

In the Way of Truth, a goddess teaches that what is cannot have come from what is not, since non-Being cannot be thought or spoken of. Being is therefore eternal, indivisible, unchanging and without time, and it cannot move, because that would require space it does not already occupy. The Way of Opinion describes the world of appearances, built on the opposites of light and dark, where the senses lead mortals into false conceptions. He is credited with first defining ontology as a discipline separate from theology.

Parmenides founded the Eleatic school, continued by Zeno of Elea and Melissus of Samos. Zeno devised arguments to defend his views against critics, and Plato counted him among his main influences, alongside Socrates and the Pythagoreans.
parthenon: The first attempt to build a sanctuary for Athena Parthenos on the site began shortly after the Battle of Marathon. The Older Parthenon was still under construction when the Persians razed the Acropolis in 480 BCE. In the mid-5th century BCE, when the Acropolis had become the seat of the Delian League, Pericles started a building project that produced the Parthenon, the Propylaia, the Erechtheion and the Temple of Athena Nike. The Parthenon was built in thanksgiving for the victory in the Greco-Persian Wars, and like most Greek temples it also served as a treasury. Phidias had general supervision and charge of the sculpture, and the architects Ictinos and Callicrates began work in 447 BCE.

The Parthenon is an octastyle peripteral Doric temple, with eight columns at each end where six was usual and seventeen along the sides, and an Ionic two-chambered cella. Its lines deviate slightly from strict straightness: the stylobate bulges upward at the centre by 10.3 centimetres over 70 metres, and the columns swell and incline inward. The cella housed the gold and ivory statue of Athena Parthenos by Phidias, dedicated in 439 or 438 BCE and now lost. The frieze of the entablature had 92 metopes showing the battles of gods and Giants, of Athenians and Amazons, and of Lapiths and Centaurs. An Ionic frieze around the cella, carved about 443 to 438 BCE, is thought to show the Panathenaic procession.

A fire shortly after the middle of the 3rd century CE destroyed the roof and much of the interior. The building later became a church of the Virgin Mary, and after the Ottoman conquest a mosque with a minaret and mihrab. Cyriacus of Ancona in 1436 was the first person since antiquity to describe it as a temple of Athena. On 26 September 1687, during the Morean War, a Venetian mortar round blew up the gunpowder magazine the Ottomans kept inside, blowing out the central part of the building. From 1800 to 1803 the 7th Earl of Elgin removed many sculptures, now in the British Museum. Greece formally asked for their return in 1983. A conservation effort began in 1975.
partition-of-india: In 1905 the Viceroy, Lord Curzon, split the Bengal Presidency into the Muslim-majority province of Eastern Bengal and Assam and the Hindu-majority province of Bengal, which transformed nationalist politics. When World War II began in 1939, Lord Linlithgow declared war on India's behalf without consulting Indian leaders, and the Congress provincial ministries resigned in protest. The Muslim League held Deliverance Day celebrations and supported Britain.

At a press conference on 3 June 1947 Lord Mountbatten announced 14 August 1947 as the date of independence and set out the Mountbatten Plan. The legislative assemblies of Punjab and Bengal would meet by religious group and vote on partition, Sind and Baluchistan would decide for themselves, the North-West Frontier Province and the Sylhet district of Assam would hold referendums, and a boundary commission would be set up. The separate independence of Bengal was ruled out.

The Indian Independence Act 1947 ended the British Raj, and the Union of India and the Dominion of Pakistan came into legal existence at midnight on 14 to 15 August 1947. Bengal and the Punjab were divided according to district-wide Muslim or non-Muslim majorities, and the army, navy, civil service, railways and treasury were shared. The princely states were released from their obligations to Britain and left their rulers to accede to India or Pakistan or to stay independent; the rulers of Hyderabad and of Jammu and Kashmir, among others, chose independence.

The boundary was revealed only on 17 August, two days after independence. The commission had taken longer than the partition itself. Mountbatten was accused of rushing the process and is alleged to have influenced the Radcliffe Line in India's favour. Murshidabad and Malda, though Muslim-majority, went to India, and Hindu-majority Khulna to Pakistan.

No one had expected population transfers: minorities were supposed to stay where they were, except in Punjab, where a transfer was organised because of communal violence. The new governments were unequipped for a two-way migration of such magnitude, and massive violence occurred on both sides of the border. Total migration across Punjab is estimated at 12 million, about 6.5 million Muslims into West Punjab and 4.7 million Hindus and Sikhs into East Punjab, and some describe the violence there as a retributive genocide. Sindh saw no mass violence.

On 13 January 1948 Mahatma Gandhi began a fast to stop the violence, and by 18 January, when he ended it, religious leaders had pledged harmony; the fast is credited with ending communal violence. Estimates of the dead remain disputed. East Bengal became East Pakistan in 1955 and Bangladesh after the war of 1971. The violence created an atmosphere of hostility and suspicion between India and Pakistan.
pashto: Pashto is an Eastern Iranian language of the Indo-European family, sharing features with Eastern Middle Iranian languages such as Bactrian, Khwarezmian and Sogdian. Some linguists derive it from Avestan or a close relative, others place it nearer to Bactrian, and neither view is universally accepted. Loanwords have been traced in Pashto as far back as the third century BCE and include words from Greek and probably Old Persian. After the 7th century most borrowings came from Persian and Hindi-Urdu, with Arabic words arriving mostly through Persian.

In the 16th century Bayazid Pir Roshan introduced 13 new letters to the Pashto form of the Arabic script, which was further modified over the years and now has 45 to 46 letters. The Pata Khazana, a manuscript presented in 1944 by Abdul Hai Habibi as an anthology of Pashto poets reaching back to the 8th century, has been discredited by linguistic analysis and its authenticity is disputed.

Pashto is natively spoken in north-western Pakistan and in southern and eastern Afghanistan, mainly by ethnic Pashtuns, with estimates of 35 million to 55 million speakers. In historical Persian literature it was also called Afghani. It is one of the two official languages of Afghanistan alongside Dari, and the regional language of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and northern Balochistan in Pakistan. Pashto is a subject-object-verb language with split ergativity, two genders, two numbers and four cases, and it uses prepositions, postpositions and circumpositions. Its dialects fall into a soft southern group and a hard northern group, and no single standard form is agreed.

Pashto has a long oral tradition of proverbs, stories and poems. From the 16th century written poetry became popular, and it rose further in the 17th century with Khushal Khan Khattak (1613 to 1689), who used verse to call for Pashtun unity against Mughal rule, and Rahman Baba (1650 to 1715), both regarded as leading poets. Others include Pir Roshan, Nazo Tokhi and Ahmad Shah Durrani, founder of the Durrani Empire.

Persian remained the language of the Afghan royal court and government. King Amanullah Khan began promoting Pashto as a marker of ethnic identity after the Third Anglo-Afghan War of 1919, and a royal decree of 1936 under Zahir Shah gave it official status. In 1964 the constitutional assembly reaffirmed it, when Afghan Persian was renamed Dari. In British India, Bacha Khan founded in 1921 the Anjuman-e Islah al-Afaghina to promote Pashto, and about 80,000 people attended its annual meeting in 1927.
passau: Passau is known as the Dreiflüssestadt, the City of Three Rivers, because the Danube is joined there by the Inn from the south and the Ilz from the north. The old town lies at the confluence, and its position makes it liable to flooding: the peak levels of floods as far back as 1501 are marked on a wall of the Old City Hall, and flood water reaches the base of that wall on average about once every five years. The city is dominated by the Veste Oberhaus and the Veste Niederhaus, parts of the former fortress of the bishop on the crest between the Danube and the Ilz.

In the 2nd century BCE many of the Boii, pushed north across the Alps by the Romans, founded a capital that the Romans called Boiodurum, now in the Innstadt district of Passau. The Romans also held a castrum called Batavis, named for the Batavi, a Germanic tribe who often served as auxiliaries; it stood in the province of Raetia, while the late Roman castrum of Boiotro lay in Noricum. In the second half of the 5th century St. Severinus established a monastery there, and the site suffered repeated raids by the Alemanni.

The bishops of Passau also exercised secular authority as prince-bishops in the area around the city. By the Treaty of Passau in 1552, Archduke Ferdinand I, representing Emperor Charles V, secured the agreement of the Protestant princes to submit the religious question to a diet, which led to the Peace of Augsburg in 1555. In the Renaissance and early modern period the city was one of the most prolific centres of sword making in Germany after Solingen. Smiths stamped blades with the Passau wolf, which superstitious warriors believed made the bearer invulnerable, and the practice of placing magical charms on swords was for a time called Passau art.

A fire in 1662 destroyed most of the city, which was rebuilt in the Baroque style. Passau was secularised in 1803 and divided between the Electorate of Bavaria and the Electorate of Salzburg; the Salzburg portion became part of Bavaria in 1805.

Passau has about 50,000 inhabitants, some 12,000 of them students at the University of Passau. St Stephen's Cathedral, a work of Italian Baroque built by the architect Carlo Lurago, has an organ with 17,774 pipes that was long held to be the largest church pipe organ in the world. Many Danube river cruises begin in the city.
passover: According to the Book of Exodus, God commanded Moses to tell the Israelites to slaughter a lamb and mark their doorframes with its blood. God would then bring the tenth plague, the death of all the firstborn in Egypt, but would pass over the marked homes, which gives the festival its name. Modern scholars widely believe that Passover originated separately from the Exodus narrative. They suggest that it formed from the merger of a pastoral protective rite, in which the blood of a sheep was daubed on the lintels and doorposts to keep demonic forces out of the home, and a spring agricultural festival of unleavened bread connected with the barley harvest. Some scholars disagree with the theory of two merged festivals.

The practice is also attested outside the Bible. A 5th-century BCE Aramaic papyrus letter from Elephantine in Egypt refers to the removal of leaven. The work Jubilees, from the Ptolemaic period, and the Herodian-era writers Josephus and Philo mention the slaughter of the lambs on the 14th of Nisan, and Philo says the banquet included hymns and prayers.

Passover begins on the 15th day of the Hebrew month of Nisan, which is considered the first month of the year. Because the Hebrew day begins at sunset, the holiday starts on the evening before. In Israel it lasts seven days, with the first and last days major holidays; outside Israel, Orthodox and Conservative communities keep eight days. It is one of the Three Pilgrimage Festivals.

Jews are forbidden to own or eat leavened foods, called chametz, during the holiday. On the night of the 14th of Nisan households search for any remaining leaven, and on the following morning it is burned.

While the Tabernacle and later the Temple in Jerusalem stood, the focus of the festival was the Passover sacrifice. Every family large enough to eat a young lamb or goat offered one at the Temple on the afternoon of the 14th of Nisan and ate it that night, roasted, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs; no bone could be broken and no meat left until morning.

Families now gather on the first night, or the first two nights outside Israel, for the seder, a ritual meal whose name means order. The story of the Exodus is retold from the Haggadah, four cups of wine are drunk, and the youngest child asks the four questions, beginning with why this night differs from all other nights. Matzah, unleavened bread, and maror, bitter herbs standing for the bitterness of slavery, are eaten. From the second night Jews begin counting the Omer, the fifty days until Shavuot.
pasto: Pasto, officially San Juan de Pasto, lies in the Atriz Valley on the Andes cordillera, at the foot of the Galeras volcano, which rises to 4,276 metres. Most of the city lies between 2,520 and 2,700 metres above sea level, and some settlement on the volcano's flanks exceeds 3,000 metres. Although it is close to the equator, its altitude gives it a mild climate, with average highs of only 15 to 18 degrees and about 800 millimetres of rain a year. The Pan-American Highway links it northwards with Popayán and southwards with Ipiales, 78 kilometres away on the border with Ecuador, and a paved road of 284 kilometres leads west to the Pacific port of Tumaco.

The city takes its name from the Pastos, the Indigenous people who lived in the region when the Spanish arrived, although the Atriz Valley itself was inhabited by the Quillacingas. The conquistador Sebastián de Belalcázar founded Pasto in 1537. In 1539 another conquistador, Lorenzo de Aldana, moved it to its present site and gave it the name San Juan de Pasto. A man of Italian origin, Guido Bucheli, was a major contributor to its economy and expansion.

Pasto has been an administrative, cultural and religious centre of the region since colonial times, and for this reason is known as the theological city of Colombia. During the wars of independence against Spain it was a royalist city. Partly because of that stance and partly because of its geographical position, it remained isolated from the rest of Colombia for a long time after independence.

Pasto is the capital of the department of Nariño and had a population of 392,930 in the census of 2018. The larger companies of the department are based there, working in food, beverages and furniture, and it trades chiefly with Ecuador. The University of Nariño is one of several universities in the city.

The Blacks and Whites' Carnival, held between 2 and 7 January each year, is one of its most important events, with floats portraying legends and traditions. A local craft, Barniz de Pasto, is a pre-Columbian technique in which the natural rubber of the mopa-mopa tree is coloured, stretched over woodwork and cut into designs. Lake Guamuez, or La Cocha, lies 27 kilometres away, with the island of La Corota, a National Forest Sanctuary. Chaza, a traditional ball game played with heavy wood and leather drums on a rectangular court, is practised in Nariño and parts of Ecuador.
pataliputra: Pataliputra stood where the Ganges, the Gandhaka and the Son rivers met, a position that made it a water fort, or jaldurga, and let it dominate the river trade of the Indo-Gangetic Plain. One traditional etymology derives the name from the pāṭalī tree; another makes it the son of Pāṭali, daughter of a Raja Sudarsan. The city was also called Kusumapura, city of flowers. The Greek ambassador Megasthenes, who lived there under the Maurya Empire and called it Palibothra, described a city in the shape of a parallelogram, surrounded by a ditch and a wall with 570 towers and 64 gates. Strabo adds that the walls were of wood.

The place began as a village, Pataligrama, fortified by the Magadha ruler Ajatashatru; the date given is 490 BCE. Jain and Hindu sources name his son Udayabhadra as the king who moved the capital there from Rajgriha. Archaeological evidence shows urban growth no earlier than the 3rd or 4th century BCE. Under Ashoka it was one of the world's largest cities, with an estimated population of 150,000 to 400,000, and early Buddhist texts record the Third Buddhist council there.

Faxian, visiting about 400, found the people rich and described hospitals where the poor were treated without charge. Xuanzang in 637 found the old city in ruins, with a small walled town of about 1,000 people by the river. Suggested causes of the decline are a shift in the course of the Ganges, a flood on the Son recorded in a later Jain work and placed in the late 500s, and destruction by Hunas in the early 500s. An inscription of the Pala king Dharmapala from the early 800s describes it as a river port and royal camp. Sher Shah Suri later made it his capital under the name Patna.

Much of the ancient city lies buried under modern Patna. Its site was first identified in modern times by Laurence Waddell in 1892, and excavations have been made at Kumhrar, Bulandi Bagh and Agam Kuan. They have found stretches of the wooden palisade over several kilometres, but no stone fortifications. At Kumhrar the remains thin out from the 300s and stop about 600, and a thick layer of ash in the hall of 80 pillars suggests that it was burnt.
pathankot: Pathankot lies in the northernmost part of Punjab, close to the Kangra district of Himachal Pradesh, and is known as the gateway to Himachal. It stands at an average elevation of 332 metres between the Ravi and Chakki rivers, with the Shiwalik foothills to the south and east and the snow-capped Himalayas to the north. The city is the headquarters of Pathankot district.

The Mahabharata and the grammarian Panini mention the region as Audumbara, classed as an ayudhajivi sangha, a warrior community, and many ancient coins of the Audumbara kingdom have been found at sites in Pathankot. Alexander Cunningham of the Archaeological Survey of India held that its fort was originally built in the ancient period.

From the 11th to the 16th century Pathankot was the first capital of Nurpur State, which was earlier known as Dhameri, a corruption of Audumbari. The city takes its name from the Pathania clan of Pahadi Rajputs, chieftains of Nurpur. In Mughal India the name Dhameri was changed to Nurpur during the reign of Shah Jahan. Under the Sikh Empire, Jarnail Jai Singh Kanhaiya of the Kanhaiya Misl invaded Pathankot and annexed it from the Pathania Rajputs, and it was merged with Punjab under Maharaja Ranjit Singh. Moran Sarkar, a Muslim dancing girl whom Ranjit Singh married, lived in a fortress at Pathankot from 1811 until her death.

After the First Anglo-Sikh War in 1845 the British annexed the hill regions from the Sikhs, and Pathankot was part of Kangra until it was merged with Gurdaspur district in 1853. At the partition of India the border demarcation committee's initial plan was to place Pathankot, then in Gurdaspur district, in Pakistan and Shakargarh district in India. In the end Shakargarh went to Pakistan, and Gurdaspur district, with Pathankot, went to India.

Pathankot is a major railway junction, where the lines from Amritsar and Delhi meet and all services to Jammu pass. It is also the lower terminus of the narrow-gauge Kangra Valley Railway, built by the British, which runs 128 km to Joginder Nagar and links the mountainous regions of western Himachal Pradesh to the national network. Its economy rests on agriculture, trade and transport, and the area produces wheat, maize and litchi. The most common languages are Punjabi, Pahari and Hindi. Keshopur Chhamb, near the city, is the only major natural wetland in the state.
patna: Ancient Patna, known as Pataliputra, was the capital of the Magadha Empire under the Haryanka, Nanda, Mauryan, Shunga, Gupta and Pala dynasties. Traditional Buddhist literature has Ajatashatru, the king of Magadha, choose a site on the bank of the Ganges and fortify it so that he could better fight the Licchavis of Vaishali, and says that Gautama Buddha passed through in the last year of his life.

The Chinese Buddhist traveller Faxian, who visited India between 399 and 414 CE, stayed in the city for many months translating Buddhist texts. Pataliputra was home to scholars including Aryabhata, Vātsyāyana and Chanakya. After the Gupta Empire broke up the city passed through uncertain times, and Bakhtiar Khilji's capture of Bihar in the 12th century ended its standing as a political and cultural centre.

Sher Shah Suri revived Patna in the middle of the 16th century, building a fort of which nothing survives and a mosque that does. Akbar reached the city in 1574 to put down the Afghan chief Daud Khan, and Abul Fazl described a flourishing trade in paper, stone and glass and in the rice later known in Europe as Patna rice. In 1704 Aurangzeb agreed to his grandson Prince Muhammad Azim's request to rename it Azimabad. Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, was born in Patna on 22 December 1666, and Patna Sahib is one of the most sacred Sikh pilgrimage sites.

In the 17th century Patna became a centre of international trade. The English East India Company set up a factory there in 1620 for calico and silk, and it grew into a trading centre for saltpetre; Portuguese traders had a factory there from at least 1580. In 1763 Nawab Mir Qasim ordered the killing of 45 mostly British employees and 200 sepoys of the Company in the Patna massacre. The Company annexed the city in 1793. In 1912, when the Bengal Presidency was partitioned, Patna became the capital of the province of Bihar and Orissa.

Patna is the capital and largest city of the Indian state of Bihar and the seat of the Patna High Court. It lies mainly on the southern bank of the Ganges, at the meeting of rivers that include the Son, Gandak and Punpun, and covers about 250 square kilometres. The pilgrimage centres of Vaishali, Rajgir, Nalanda, Bodh Gaya and Pawapuri are nearby. It remained the capital of Bihar after independence in 1947, including after Jharkhand became a separate state in 2000.
patrice-de-macmahon: The MacMahon family is of Irish origin. After losing much of its land in the Cromwellian confiscations of 1652, a branch supported the deposed James II in 1688 and settled in France, applying for French citizenship in 1749. Patrice de MacMahon was born on 13 June 1808 at the Château de Sully near Autun in Burgundy, the sixteenth and second-youngest son of Baron Maurice-François de Mac Mahon. The family, a military one, had decidedly royalist politics. He entered the military school at Saint-Cyr on 23 October 1825 and joined the army in 1827.

MacMahon served in the French conquest of Algeria from 1830, was commended at the seizure of Algiers and was wounded at the Siege of Constantine in 1837. He became a colonel in December 1845 and a general of brigade in 1848, and in 1852 he organised in Algeria the plebiscite that approved the coup d'état of 1851. In the Crimean War he won a victory at the Battle of Malakoff in September 1855, where he is reputed to have said 'Here I am; here will I stay!' At Magenta in 1859 he advanced his troops without orders at a critical moment, which assured the French victory; Napoleon III made him a Marshal of France and Duke of Magenta.

He was Governor General of Algeria from 1864, a post in which he did not distinguish himself and which drew numerous complaints. In 1870 he led the main French army in the Franco-Prussian War, suffered defeats in Alsace and was seriously wounded at Sedan; with the Emperor he was made prisoner on 1 September. In May 1871 he led the Semaine Sanglante, the week-long campaign that defeated the Paris Commune.

In May 1873 the royalist and conservative majority of the National Assembly elected MacMahon President, with one vote against. Many hoped he would hold office until a Bourbon pretender could restore the monarchy, but he refused to meet the Count of Chambord and accepted a seven-year mandate on 9 November 1873. He remained above parties during the Constitutional Laws of 1875. After the Republican victory of 1876 he reluctantly accepted governments under Jules Dufaure and Jules Simon.

In the crisis of 16 May 1877 he dismissed Simon, had the Senate dissolve the Chamber of Deputies and campaigned across the country, but the elections of 14 October gave the Republicans a majority of 120 seats. He resigned on 30 January 1879, succeeded by Jules Grévy. He died on 17 October 1893 and was buried at the Invalides after a state funeral.
patrice-lumumba: Patrice Lumumba was born Isaïe Tasumbu Tawosa on 2 July 1925 in Onalua, in the Kasaï province of the Belgian Congo, to Julienne Wamato Lomendja and François Tolenga Otetshima, a farmer. He belonged to the Tetela ethnic group. Raised in a Catholic family, he attended a Protestant primary school, a Catholic missionary school and finally the government post office training school, where he passed the one-year course with distinction. He was known as a vocal, precocious young man who pointed out his teachers' errors in front of his classmates, and he spoke Tetela, French, Lingala, Swahili and Tshiluba.

Lumumba helped found the Mouvement National Congolais in 1958 and quickly became its leader. Unlike other Congolese parties, it did not rest on an ethnic base, and its platform of independence, gradual Africanisation of government, state-led economic development and neutrality in foreign affairs drew a large popular following. In December 1958 he represented it at the All-African Peoples' Conference in Accra, hosted by Kwame Nkrumah. Independence was set for 30 June 1960, after elections held in May in which the MNC won a plurality, and Lumumba became the first prime minister.

On 5 July 1960 troops of the Force Publique mutinied against their commander, General Émile Janssens, and the mutiny spread; this opened the Congo Crisis. Katanga and South Kasai declared independence, and Lumumba sent the army to put down the secessions. On 5 September President Joseph Kasa-Vubu announced Lumumba's dismissal, and Lumumba in turn declared the president deposed over the radio. On 14 September Mobutu Sese Seko announced a coup. Lumumba was captured while trying to reach Stanleyville, held at the barracks at Thysville from 3 December, and sent to Katanga in January 1961.

Lumumba was killed on 17 January 1961 by the separatist Katangan authorities of Moïse Tshombe, with two associates, Maurice Mpolo and Joseph Okito. Belgian officers dug up and dissolved the bodies. Katangan radio announced on 13 February that he had been killed by villagers after escaping. His killing caused protests in at least twenty countries. Letters of Belgian ministers show that they wanted his elimination and facilitated his transfer to Katanga. In 2002 Belgium formally apologised for its role, admitting moral responsibility. In 2022 a tooth of his, the only remains, was returned to his family. He is widely seen as a martyr of anti-colonial liberation and the pan-African movement.
patrick-henry: Patrick Henry was born on 29 May 1736 on the family farm, Studley, in Hanover County, Virginia. His father John Henry was an immigrant from Aberdeenshire, and his mother Sarah Winston Syme was a wealthy widow from a prominent local family. Henry was tutored at home by his father after about the age of ten. Because custom gave the family's land, stock and slaves to his older half-brother John Syme Jr., he had to make his own way. At sixteen he opened a store with his brother William, which failed.

While helping at Hanover Tavern he studied law on his own, and in April 1760 he passed the examination at Williamsburg, although his knowledge of procedure was scant. He soon became prominent through his victory in the Parson's Cause against the Anglican clergy.

Henry won a seat in the Virginia House of Burgesses in May 1765. In 1774 he was a delegate to the First Continental Congress. At the Second Virginia Convention in March 1775 he urged that a militia be raised independent of royal authority, and on 23 March he defended this in the speech for which he is best known. In May he led militia towards Williamsburg after the royal governor, the Earl of Dunmore, had marines seize the colony's gunpowder, and he stopped only when a member of the Governor's Council agreed to pay for it.

In May 1776 the Fifth Virginia Convention passed unanimously a resolution based largely on his, declaring Virginia independent and instructing its delegates in Congress to press for American independence. He served on the committee that drafted the Virginia Declaration of Rights and the state's first constitution, and he was elected the first governor of the new state. He served five one-year terms in all, the last two from 1784.

Henry feared a strong federal government. He declined appointment as a delegate to the 1787 Constitutional Convention, and he actively opposed ratification of the Constitution, both because he feared a powerful central government and because it had as yet no Bill of Rights. He was a slaveholder throughout his adult life and hoped to see slavery end, but he had no plan beyond ending the importation of slaves.

Henry wrote little, and only a handful of his papers and a few of his speeches survive, which has frustrated his biographers. Thomas Jefferson filled the gap with his own, often negative, recollections, and these have adversely affected Henry's historical reputation. He helped found Hampden-Sydney College, and the Red Hill Patrick Henry National Memorial preserves his final home and gravesite.
patrick-white: Patrick Victor Martindale White was born in Knightsbridge, London, on 28 May 1912, to Australian parents who were on an extended honeymoon. The family returned to Sydney when he was six months old. White developed asthma at the age of four, a condition that had killed his maternal grandfather, and his health was fragile throughout childhood.

From 1932 he studied French and German literature at King's College, Cambridge. After graduating in 1935 he was determined to stay in England and become a writer, supported by an allowance of £400 a year from his father. In London he met the Australian painter Roy de Maistre, who encouraged him to break from naturalistic prose and write from the inside out.

White's first published novel, Happy Valley (1939), won the Gold Medal of the Australian Literature Society. In the Second World War he served as an intelligence officer in the Royal Air Force; in Alexandria in 1941 he met Manoly Lascaris, who became his life companion. They settled in February 1948 on a small farm at Castle Hill, then semi-rural, outside Sydney. Discouraged by the reception of The Aunt's Story, White had a religious experience in late 1951 that gave him a belief in God and the inspiration to resume work on The Tree of Man (1955), which he described as an attempt to suggest every possible aspect of life through the lives of an ordinary man and woman.

That novel and Voss (1957) established his reputation in Britain and the United States, though Australian critics were divided; the poet A. D. Hope called his prose pretentious verbal sludge. Voss won the first Miles Franklin Award, and Riders in the Chariot (1961) won it again. The Eye of the Storm was published in August 1973, and in October White received the Nobel Prize in Literature, cited for an epic and psychological narrative art which had introduced a new continent into literature.

White's fiction concerns individuals, often alienated from society, who try to grasp a higher reality: pioneer settlers, explorers, artists, the simple-minded. He portrayed Australian society as materialistic and conformist, and in 1958 satirised what he called the Great Australian Emptiness. His style drew on the modernism of Joyce, Lawrence and Woolf, shifting between past and present and between the viewpoints of different characters. From the late 1960s he opposed the Vietnam War and supported Aboriginal self-determination, nuclear disarmament and environmental causes. In 1975 he founded the Patrick White Award with the prize money from his Nobel Prize.
paul-doumer: Joseph Athanase Doumer, commonly known as Paul, was born on 22 March 1857 at Aurillac in the Cantal department into a family of modest means. A former student of the Conservatoire national des arts et métiers, he became a professor of mathematics at Mende in 1877 and taught at Remiremont from 1879 to 1883, leaving on health grounds to become chief editor of a regional newspaper, the Courrier de l'Aisne. In 1878 he married Blanche Richel. They had eight children, four of whom were killed in the First World War. He was initiated into Freemasonry in 1879 and became Grand Secretary of the Grand Orient de France in 1892.

Doumer entered politics in 1885 as chef de cabinet to Charles Floquet, president of the Chamber of Deputies, and was elected Radical deputy for the Aisne in 1888. Defeated in 1889, he was returned in 1890 by the arrondissement of Auxerre. As minister of finance in 1895–1896 he tried without success to introduce an income tax.

When he arrived in Indochina the colonies were losing millions of francs a year, and his taxes were meant to put them on a paying basis. Vietnamese, Cambodians and Laotians who could not or would not pay lost their houses and land and often became day labourers. He made Indochina a market for French products and a field for French investment. In 1898 he persuaded the French government to approve the railway to Yunnan, with a view to annexing the south of that province.

Back in France he was elected deputy for Laon, refused to support the ministry of Émile Combes and led a group of dissident Radicals that eventually helped bring it down. He was president of the Chamber from 1902 to 1905, minister of finance again in 1925 and president of the Senate from 1927. On 13 May 1931 he was elected president of the Republic, defeating the better-known Aristide Briand.

On 6 May 1932, at the opening of a book fair at the Hôtel Salomon de Rothschild in Paris, Doumer was shot by Paul Gorguloff, a Russian émigré, while talking to the author Claude Farrère. He died in hospital at 04:37 on 7 May, the second French president to be assassinated and the first to be shot. Gorguloff wrote that the act was a protest on behalf of exiled White Russians and against France's relations with the Soviet Union; he was guillotined four months later. Doumer wrote L'Indo-Chine française (1904) and Le Livre de mes fils (1906).
paul-gauguin: Gauguin was born in Paris on 7 June 1848, the son of Clovis Gauguin, a liberal journalist who had to flee France when his newspaper was suppressed, and Aline Chazal, daughter of the engraver André Chazal and of the author and early socialist activist Flora Tristan. In 1850 the family settled in Peru, where he had a privileged childhood until the age of six. After schooling in France he signed on as a pilot's assistant in the merchant marine and then served two years in the French navy. In 1873 he married the Dane Mette-Sophie Gad, and they had five children.

He worked as a stockbroker and began painting in his spare time, befriending Camille Pissarro, who introduced him to other Impressionist artists. The financial crisis of 1882 damaged his brokerage career and led him to paint full time. He showed 19 paintings and a wood relief at the eighth and last Impressionist exhibition in May 1886.

Under the influence of folk art and Japanese prints, his work moved towards Cloisonnism, with flat areas of colour and heavy black outlines, as in The Yellow Christ of 1889, and later towards Synthetism. In 1887 he travelled with the painter Charles Laval to Panama, where he worked as a labourer on the French canal, and then to Martinique. Vincent van Gogh and his brother Theo, a dealer with the firm Goupil & Cie, admired his Martinique paintings, and Theo bought three of them for 900 francs.

After a successful auction at the Hôtel Drouot in February 1891, Gauguin sailed for Tahiti on 1 April, stating his aim of escaping European civilization and everything artificial and conventional. He returned to France in August 1893 and left for Tahiti again on 28 June 1895.

In the Marquesas Islands he found a society that, as in Tahiti, had lost much of its cultural identity; the population had fallen from some 80,000 in the 18th century to 4,000, largely through Western diseases. In 1903 he campaigned against the island's gendarmes and on 27 March was fined 500 francs and sentenced to three months' imprisonment for libel. Weak, in great pain and using morphine, he died suddenly on 8 May 1903.

Retrospective exhibitions at the Salon d'Automne in Paris in 1903 and 1906 strongly influenced the French avant-garde, above all Pablo Picasso, whose work of 1906 led to Les Demoiselles d'Avignon in 1907. In the 21st century critics have described his Primitivist depictions of Tahiti as colonialist and have pointed to his sexual exploitation of Tahitian girls.
paul-henri-spaak: Paul-Henri Spaak was born on 25 January 1899 in Schaerbeek into a prominent family. His mother, Marie Janson, was a socialist and the first woman to enter the Belgian Senate, and his father, Paul Spaak, was a poet and playwright. In 1914 he tried to join the Belgian army during the German invasion, was captured and spent two years as a prisoner of war in Germany. He then studied law in Brussels and played tennis for Belgium in the 1922 Davis Cup. As a lawyer he defended Communists accused of conspiracy and the Italian anarchist student Fernando de Rosa, who had tried to kill Crown Prince Umberto of Italy.

He joined the Belgian Labour Party in 1920, was elected deputy in 1932 and became Minister of Transport in 1935. From February 1936 he was Foreign Minister, keeping to Belgium's neutrality, and from May 1938 to February 1939 he was prime minister for the first time. After the German invasion of May 1940 he and Hubert Pierlot, with part of the government, reached London in October 1940. In exile he promoted a customs union with the Netherlands and Luxembourg, which became Benelux. After the war he was prime minister from 13 to 31 March 1946, the shortest government in Belgian history, and again from March 1947 to August 1949, when women received the vote.

He chaired the first session of the United Nations General Assembly and was the first President of the Council of Europe's Consultative Assembly, resigning in December 1951 after it rejected a proposal for a European political authority. In 1955 the Messina Conference made him chairman of the committee whose Spaak Report led to the Treaties of Rome, signed on 25 March 1957.

From 1957 to 1961 Spaak was Secretary General of NATO, succeeding Lord Ismay, and clashed repeatedly with Charles de Gaulle. He was Belgium's foreign minister for eighteen years between 1939 and 1966. He retired from politics in 1966, published his memoirs, Combats inachevés, in 1969 and died at Braine-l'Alleud on 31 July 1972. Nicknamed Mr. Europe, he is counted among the founding fathers of the European Union, and a building of the European Parliament in Brussels bears his name.
paul-kruger: Stephanus Johannes Paulus Kruger was born on 10 October 1825 at Bulhoek, a farm in the Steynsburg area of the Cape Colony, the third child of the farmer Casper Jan Hendrik Kruger. As a child he took part in the Great Trek. He had almost no education apart from the Bible, which he took literally and knew in large part by heart. He became a burgher at sixteen, settled near Rustenburg and married Maria du Plessis in 1842.
