As field cornet he took part in the Battle of Dimawe against the Tswana chief Sechele I in 1852, when the Boer commando wrecked David Livingstone's mission at Kolobeng.

A protégé of the Voortrekker leader Andries Pretorius, Kruger witnessed the signing of the Sand River Convention in 1852. In 1863 he was elected Commandant-General, a post he held for a decade. He became vice president in March 1877, shortly before Britain annexed the republic as the Transvaal, and led two deputations to London against the annexation. He was the leading figure in the movement to restore independence, which ended in the Boers' victory in the First Boer War of 1880 to 1881, and he served in an executive triumvirate until he was elected president in 1883.

In 1884 Kruger led a third deputation to London, which secured the London Convention, under which Britain recognised the South African Republic as fully independent. After gold was found on the Witwatersrand in 1886, the uitlanders, mostly British, provided almost all tax revenue but had no vote. This question dominated his presidency, which was renewed in 1888, 1893 and 1898, and led to the Jameson Raid of 1895 to 1896 and the Second Boer War.

He took no part in the fighting, directing the war from Pretoria by telegram. He left South Africa on 11 September 1900, was carried from Mozambique to Marseille on the Dutch warship Gelderland and refused to return after the British victory. He died in Switzerland in 1904, and his body was returned for a state funeral in Pretoria. Admirers see him as a tragic folk hero; critics call him a stubborn defender of an unjust cause and an oppressor of black Africans.
paul-the-deacon: Paul was born Winfrid, son of Warnefrid, about 720 in the Duchy of Friuli; Paulus was his monastic name. An ancestor named Leupichis had come to Italy in 568 in the train of Alboin, King of the Lombards, and received lands at or near Cividale del Friuli. During an invasion by the Avars his five sons were carried off to Pannonia, but one of them returned and restored the family's fortunes. Paul's father Warnefrid was his grandson.

Because his family was possibly noble, Paul received an exceptionally good education, probably at the court of the Lombard king Ratchis in Pavia, where a teacher named Flavian taught him the rudiments of Greek. He was probably secretary to Ratchis's successor, Desiderius.

After Desiderius's daughter Adelperga married Arichis II, duke of Benevento, Paul wrote at her request a continuation of Eutropius's Summary of Roman History. He lived at the court of Benevento for at least several years before 774, when Charlemagne captured Pavia. He eventually entered a monastery on Lake Como, and before 782 the great Benedictine house of Monte Cassino, where he made the acquaintance of Charlemagne.

Around 776 his brother Arichis was carried off to Francia as a prisoner after a revolt in Friuli, and Paul wrote to Charlemagne on his behalf, after which Arichis was freed. Paul became an important contributor to the Carolingian Renaissance. In 787 he returned to Monte Cassino, where he died on 13 April, probably in 799.

His chief work is the Historia Langobardorum, an incomplete history in six books written after 787 and no later than 795 or 796. It covers the Lombards from their origins in the north and their migration to Italy in 568 to the death of King Liutprand in 744, and is written from a Lombard point of view. It is especially valuable for the relations between the Franks and the Lombards. Among his sources were the Origo gentis Langobardorum and the Liber pontificalis, and he drew heavily on Bede, Gregory of Tours and Isidore of Seville.

His Historia Romana continues Eutropius down to 553, with extracts from the Scriptures and ecclesiastical historians added because Adelperga complained that Eutropius said nothing of church affairs. At the request of Angilram, Bishop of Metz, he wrote a history of the bishops of Metz to 766, the first work of its kind north of the Alps. He also compiled a collection of homilies for Charlemagne, much used in the Frankish churches.
peanut: The genus Arachis is native to South America, east of the Andes, around Peru, Bolivia, Argentina and Brazil. The cultivated peanut, Arachis hypogaea, arose from a hybrid between two wild species, thought to be Arachis duranensis and Arachis ipaensis. The first hybrid would have been sterile, but spontaneous chromosome doubling restored its fertility. Genetic analysis suggests the hybridisation happened only once, giving rise to a wild form found in a few places in north-western Argentina, and by artificial selection to the cultivated plant.

Domestication made the plant bushier and more compact, with a different pod structure and larger seeds. Cultivation spread from its centre of origin and formed further centres of diversity in Peru, Ecuador, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay. The oldest known remains of pods, about 7,600 years old, were found in Peru, where dry conditions preserve organic material; cultivation almost certainly began earlier in the moister centre of origin.

The peanut is a legume grown mainly for its seeds, which are held in pods that develop underground, a trait called geocarpy and unusual among legumes. After fertilisation a short stalk grows into the soil, and the fruit ripens there. Botanically the pods are not nuts. Like other legumes, peanuts harbour nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules, which improve soil fertility and make them valuable in crop rotation.

The seeds yield oil and are eaten roasted, boiled or ground into peanut butter and sauces. Peanut sauces are used in Latin America, West Africa and Southeast Asia, and in the Indian subcontinent peanuts are made into chikki, a sweet brittle. The plant tops are used for silage and the oilcake left after pressing is fed to livestock. Between 1.4 and 2 per cent of people in Europe and the United States experience allergic reactions to peanuts, which can be fatal.

Many pre-Columbian cultures, such as the Moche, depicted peanuts in their art, and cultivation was well established in Mesoamerica before the Spanish arrived. The conquistadors found the plant, called tlālcacahuatl in Nahuatl, on sale in the marketplace of Tenochtitlan. European traders later spread it across the tropics and subtropics. In West Africa it substantially replaced the Bambara groundnut, another legume whose pods ripen underground.

In the United States peanuts were introduced in the colonial period and grown as a garden crop; from 1870 they served as animal feed until human consumption grew in the 1930s. George Washington Carver promoted the peanut in the American South, where repeated cotton planting had depleted the soil. Marcellus Gilmore Edson of Montreal patented a process for making peanut butter in 1884, and it became well known after the Beech-Nut company sold it at the St. Louis World's Fair in 1904.
pencil: The word pencil comes from the Old French pincel and the late Latin penicillus, a little tail, and first meant an artist's fine brush of camel hair, which was also used for writing. The Romans used a stylus, a thin metal stick for scratching papyrus or wax tablets. The graphite from Cumbria was called plumbago, Latin for lead ore, and the mistake lives on in the name lead for a pencil core. The German Bleistift and the Irish peann luaidhe both mean lead pen. Because graphite could line the moulds for cannonballs, the Crown took over the mines and guarded them, and flooded them when enough had been stored. The graphite for pencils had at first to be smuggled out.

A pencil leaves marks by abrasion, a trail of solid core material that clings to the paper, which sets it apart from pens that dispense liquid ink. Most cores are graphite mixed with a clay binder, and the ratio of graphite to clay decides how hard the core is. The commonest casing is thin wood, usually hexagonal in section. Other cores include charcoal and carbon for fuller blacks, wax-based coloured cores and greasy cores that write on glass or porcelain. Copying pencils, invented in the late 19th century, held a dye that dissolved into coloured ink when moistened, so that the writing could be pressed onto another sheet.

England kept a monopoly on pencils until a method of reconstituting graphite powder was found in Germany in 1662, and square English pencils were still cut from natural graphite into the 1860s. Keswick still has a pencil factory and the Derwent Pencil Museum. Under the naval blockade of the Napoleonic Wars France could import neither English graphite nor the poorer German substitute, which led Nicolas-Jacques Conté to his clay method.

American colonists imported their pencils from Europe. Benjamin Franklin advertised them in 1729, and George Washington used a three-inch pencil when surveying the Ohio Country in 1762. William Munroe of Concord, Massachusetts, made the first American wood pencils in 1812, and Ebenezer Wood of Acton automated the work, building the first hexagonal casings. Eberhard Faber built a factory in New York. By the end of the 19th century more than 240,000 pencils were used each day in the United States. Hymen Lipman received the first patent for an attached eraser on 30 March 1858.
pennsylvania: Pennsylvania is officially the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. It lies in the Mid-Atlantic, Northeastern, Appalachian and Great Lakes regions, and is bordered by Delaware, Maryland, West Virginia, Ohio, New York, New Jersey and, across Lake Erie, the Canadian province of Ontario. The Mason-Dixon line forms its southern boundary. The Appalachian Mountains run through its centre, and about 59 per cent of the state is forested. Of the original Thirteen Colonies, it is the only one that does not border the Atlantic Ocean, though it has waterfront on Lake Erie and the tidal Delaware River.

Humans lived in what is now Pennsylvania for thousands of years before the colony was founded. The Meadowcroft Rockshelter in Jefferson Township holds the earliest known signs of human activity in the state and perhaps in all of North America, and may pre-date the Clovis culture. By 1000 CE the native population had developed agricultural techniques and a mixed food economy. Between 1638 and 1655 a south-eastern portion of the state was part of New Sweden, a Swedish colony.

In 1681 a royal land grant gave the territory to William Penn, son of the man after whom it is named. The colonial Province of Pennsylvania was known for relatively peaceful relations with native peoples, an innovative system of government and religious pluralism. Philadelphia hosted the First and Second Continental Congress; the latter formed the Continental Army under George Washington in 1775 and unanimously adopted the Declaration of Independence the following year. On 12 December 1787 Pennsylvania was the second state to ratify the United States Constitution, after Delaware. It has been known as the Keystone State since 1802, for its central place among the original colonies.

The capital is Harrisburg, and the largest cities are Philadelphia and Pittsburgh. The 2020 census counted 13,011,844 residents. The state has had five constitutions, in 1776, 1790, 1838, 1874 and 1968. Its industrial past gave it the lesser nicknames of the Coal State, the Oil State and the Steel State, and its five manufacturing centres were Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, Erie, Scranton-Wilkes-Barre and the Lehigh Valley.
pericles: Pericles was born around 495 BCE in Athens, the son of the politician Xanthippus, who commanded the Athenian contingent in the Greek victory at Mycale. His mother, Agariste, belonged to the powerful Alcmaeonid family, and her connections helped to start his political career. His early years were quiet, and he preferred study to public appearances. In the spring of 472 BCE he presented The Persians of Aeschylus at the Greater Dionysia as a liturgy, which shows that he was one of the wealthier men of Athens.

In 463 BCE Pericles was the leading prosecutor of Cimon, the leader of the conservative faction, who was acquitted. Around 461 BCE his mentor Ephialtes proposed reducing the powers of the Areopagus, a council controlled by the aristocracy, and the Assembly adopted the reform, signalling an era of radical democracy. In the same year Cimon was ostracised on the charge of aiding Sparta, and Ephialtes was murdered, which left Pericles the unchallenged leader of the democratic party.

Pericles began a project that produced most of the surviving structures on the Acropolis, including the Parthenon. He proposed the Megarian decree, which excluded Megarian merchants from the market of Athens and its empire and strained the peace with Sparta. In 431 BCE, when the Spartan king Archidamus II invaded Attica, Pericles had already arranged for the whole rural population to move within the walls of Athens, and he refused to meet the Spartan army in battle, relying on the navy.

In summer 430 BCE an epidemic broke out in Athens, whose identity is uncertain. Public anger led Pericles to defend himself in a final speech, which Thucydides records, and his opponents managed to deprive him of the generalship and fine him. His sister and both his legitimate sons, Xanthippus and Paralus, died in the plague, and he died in 429 BCE. Scholars differ over his leadership, with some calling him a populist and a hawk and others admiring him.
periodic-table: In 1817 the German physicist Johann Wolfgang Döbereiner began one of the earliest attempts to classify the elements. In 1829 he found that he could form some of them into groups of three with related properties, which he termed triads. Chlorine, bromine and iodine formed a triad, as did calcium, strontium and barium. Later chemists found more relationships between small groups of elements but could not build one scheme that took in all of them.

In 1864 John Newlands published an article in Chemical News showing that if the elements are arranged by atomic weight, every eighth element repeats the properties of the first, like the eighth note of an octave in music, which he called the Law of Octaves. The same year a book by the German chemist Lothar Meyer contained an early table of 28 elements, grouped into six families by valence, the first grouping of elements in that way.

The periodic table arranges the chemical elements in rows called periods and columns called groups, and elements in the same group tend to show similar chemical characteristics. Each element has a unique atomic number, the number of protons in its nucleus, and the elements are listed in order of increasing atomic number. A new row starts when a new electron shell has its first electron, and the columns are determined by the electron configuration of the atom. The table depicts the periodic law, which states that when elements are arranged by atomic number an approximate recurrence of their properties is evident.

Metallic character increases going down a group and from right to left across a period. The first generally accepted table was that of the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869, who formulated the law as a dependence of chemical properties on atomic mass. Because not all elements were then known, his table had gaps, and he used the law to predict properties of some missing elements. The law was explained early in the 20th century by the discovery of atomic numbers and by work in quantum mechanics, and a recognisably modern form was reached in 1945 with Glenn T. Seaborg's discovery that the actinides are f-block rather than d-block elements.

The periodic law was recognised as a fundamental discovery in the late 19th century, and the table is an icon of chemistry, also widely used in physics and other sciences. In nature only elements up to atomic number 94 exist; later ones are synthetic. By 2010 the first 118 elements were known, completing the first seven rows. Within 100 years of Mendeleev's table, Edward G. Mazurs had collected an estimated 700 different published versions and there is no consensus on whether an optimal form exists.
perpignan: Perpignan lies in the middle of the Roussillon plain at the foot of the Pyrenees, 13 kilometres from the Mediterranean coast, and is the southernmost city of metropolitan France. The Têt, the largest river of Roussillon, and its tributary the Basse cross it. It is the prefecture of the Pyrénées-Orientales department, with 119,656 inhabitants in 2021. Its name appears in 927 as Perpinianum and probably derives from the Roman name Perpennius.

Settlement in the area goes back to Roman times, but the medieval town seems to have been founded around the beginning of the tenth century, and it soon became the capital of the counts of Roussillon. In 1172 Count Girard II bequeathed his lands to the counts of Barcelona. The town gained the institutions of a partly self-governing commune in 1197. When James I the Conqueror founded the Kingdom of Majorca in 1276, Perpignan became the capital of its mainland territories. The decades that followed are regarded as the city's golden age, with cloth, leatherwork and goldsmithery. King Philippe III of France died there in 1285 on his return from a failed crusade against the Crown of Aragon.

Peter IV of Aragon annexed the kingdom in 1344, and a few years later the Black Death took about half the population. Louis XI of France occupied the city in 1463, and a rising against French rule in 1473 was put down after a long siege. Charles VIII restored it to Ferdinand II of Aragon in 1493. The French besieged and captured it again in September 1642, during the Thirty Years' War, and Spain ceded it formally 17 years later in the Treaty of the Pyrenees.

The Palace of the Kings of Majorca, of the thirteenth century, stands on the citadel behind ramparts that Louis XIV's engineer Vauban updated in the seventeenth century. The town walls were razed in 1904, but the Castillet, the main gate, a fourteenth-century fortress later used as a prison, survives. Work on the cathedral began in 1324 and finished in 1509. In 1963 the painter Salvador Dalí declared the railway station the centre of the universe. The city hosts the Visa pour l'Image festival of photojournalism each September, and many street signs are in both French and Catalan.
persian-gulf: The Persian Gulf, sometimes called the Arabian Gulf, is a mediterranean sea in West Asia of some 251,000 square kilometres. It is 989 kilometres long and about 56 kilometres wide at its narrowest, in the Strait of Hormuz, which joins it to the Gulf of Oman. The water is shallow, averaging 50 metres in depth. At its north-western end the Shatt al-Arab delta carries the waters of the Euphrates and the Tigris. Eight states have coasts on it: Bahrain, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

During most of the Last Glacial Period much of the Gulf was dry land, a floodplain where several rivers met. The modern sea formed as sea levels rose between about 12,000 and 6,000 years ago. Seagoing vessels from the mid-sixth millennium BCE have been found at H3 in Kuwait, when the Gulf belonged to a trade network linking Ubaid settlements in Mesopotamia with communities along its coast. At the end of the fourth millennium BCE the Dilmun civilization dominated its southern part. Between 625 BCE and 226 CE a succession of Persian empires held the northern side, and the Achaemenid navy kept bases on the Shatt al-Arab and in Bahrain, Oman and Yemen.

In 1521 a Portuguese force under Antonio Correia invaded Bahrain for its pearl industry, after Afonso de Albuquerque had captured the kingdom of Hormuz. On 29 April 1602 Shah Abbas of the Safavid Empire expelled the Portuguese from Bahrain, and in 1622, with British naval support, he took the island of Hormuz; trade moved to Bandar Abbas. Piracy was prevalent until the nineteenth century, and the British mounted the Persian Gulf campaign of 1819, which led to the General Maritime Treaty of 1820 with the sheikhs of the Pirate Coast. From 1763 until 1971 Britain held varying degrees of political control over several Gulf states.

The name Persian Gulf is the historical and internationally established one, though Arab governments use Arabian Gulf or the Gulf. The Gulf and its coastlands hold very large reserves of petroleum and natural gas, and Qatar and Iran share the largest gas field across the median line.
persian-language: Modern Persian is a continuation of Middle Persian, an official language of the Sasanian Empire (224–651 CE), which was itself a continuation of Old Persian, used in the Achaemenid Empire (550–330 BCE). It originated in the region of Fars in southwestern Iran. Old Persian is attested in cuneiform inscriptions from the 6th to the 4th century BCE, the oldest being the Behistun Inscription from the time of King Darius I (reigned 522–486 BCE). Middle Persian is attested in Pahlavi and Manichaean scripts, and New Persian literature was first recorded in the ninth century, after the Muslim conquest of Persia. Gernot Windfuhr treats New Persian as an evolution of both earlier stages, but states that none of the known Middle Persian dialects is its direct predecessor.

Persian belongs to the Western Iranian group of the Iranian languages. It has three standard varieties: Iranian Persian, Dari in Afghanistan and Tajiki in Tajikistan, all based on classic Persian literature and mutually intelligible to a relatively high degree. Iranian Persian and Dari are written in the Persian alphabet, a modified form of the Arabic alphabet; after the Arab conquest it took about 200 years before Persians adopted the Arabic script in place of Pahlavi. Tajiki is written in a Cyrillic alphabet.

Modern Persian has no grammatical gender and its usual word order is subject–object–verb. Its core vocabulary is of Middle Persian origin, but it also contains a considerable number of Arabic loanwords. John R. Perry estimates that about 20 percent of everyday vocabulary, and around 25 percent of that of classical and modern literature, is of Arabic origin.

Persian was the first language to break the monopoly of Arabic on writing in the Muslim world, and Persian poetry became a tradition in many eastern courts. It served as a language of bureaucracy even for non-native speakers, among them the Ottomans in Anatolia, the Delhi Sultanates and Mughals in the Indian subcontinent, and the Pashtuns in Afghanistan. It influenced Turkic, Armenian, Georgian, Greek and Indo-Aryan languages, as well as other Iranian ones. Works written in it include the Shahnameh by Ferdowsi, the works of Rumi, the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, the Divân of Hafez and the Gulistan and Bustan by Saadi Shirazi. Approximately 130 million people speak it worldwide.
perth: Perth lies mostly on the sandy, relatively flat Swan Coastal Plain, between the Darling Scarp and the Indian Ocean. The Swan River, also known as Derbarl Yerrigan, runs through it; the Dutch captain Willem de Vlamingh named it for the black swans he found there when exploring in 1697. The central business district and the port of Fremantle both stand on the river. Summers are hot, sunny and dry and winters mild and wet, a hot-summer Mediterranean climate. The nearest city of more than 100,000 people is Adelaide, over 2,100 km away, which makes Perth one of the most isolated major cities in the world.

People have lived in the Perth area for at least 48,000 years. Noongar country covers the south-west corner of Western Australia, and the wetlands of the Swan Coastal Plain hold spiritual importance and were a source of food. The Whadjuk Noongar are the traditional owners of the land, and the Noongar name for the place is Boorloo. In 1619 the Dutch explorer Frederick de Houtman sighted the coast near present-day Perth, which he and Jacob Dedel called Dedelsland.

Perth was founded as the administrative centre of the Swan River Colony in 1829, the first comprehensive European settlement in the west of the continent, after New South Wales had set up a convict-supported outpost at King George's Sound in 1826 in response to rumours of French annexation. Stirling's proclamation of the colony was read at Fremantle on 18 June 1829. The name honours Sir George Murray, Secretary of State for War and the Colonies, who sat in the House of Commons for Perthshire. The colony was officially designated Western Australia in 1832.

In 1850, at the request of farmers and businesspeople short of labour, Western Australia accepted convicts, and over eighteen years 9,721 arrived on 43 ships, outnumbering the roughly 7,300 free settlers. Queen Victoria announced Perth's designation as a city in 1856, but it remained a tranquil town. After a referendum in 1900 Western Australia joined the Federation of Australia in 1901, the last colony to agree, and only after concessions that included a transcontinental railway from Port Augusta to Kalgoorlie. From 1927 to 1954 Indigenous people were prohibited from entering large parts of Perth.

Perth is the capital and largest city of Western Australia and the fourth most populous city in Australia, a position it has held since 1984. Mining booms in the late 20th century made it the headquarters of significant mining operations in the state. Kings Park and Botanic Garden is one of the world's largest inner-city parks, and Fremantle Prison is a World Heritage Site.
peru: Peru covers 1,285,216 km2 on the Pacific coast of South America, the third-largest country on the continent. The Andes run parallel to the ocean and define three traditional regions: the costa, a narrow and largely arid coastal plain; the sierra, the highlands, which include the Altiplano and the highest peak, Huascarán at 6,768 metres; and the selva, the Amazon rainforest, which covers almost 60 percent of the country.

The Amazon basin covers 75% of Peruvian territory, and Lake Titicaca, shared with Bolivia, is the largest lake in South America. The name may derive from Birú, a local ruler near the Bay of San Miguel in Panama, and the Capitulation of Toledo of 1529 gave it legal status as the name of the province that was the Inca Empire.

The earliest evidence of people in Peruvian territory, about 12,500 BCE, comes from Huaca Prieta. The Caral-Supe civilization flourished on the coast, and the Chavín culture, from 1500 to 300 BCE, was probably more a religious than a political phenomenon. Later coastal cultures included the Paracas, Nazca, Moche and Chimu. The Chimu flourished from about 1140 to 1450 as a loose confederation of walled cities with its capital at Chan Chan, and in the highlands the Tiahuanaco and Wari cultures developed large urban settlements between 500 and 1000 CE.

The Spanish Empire conquered the region in the 16th century, and Charles V established a viceroyalty, the Kingdom of Peru, with its capital at Lima. According to the historian Noble David Cook, the Amerindian population fell from nearly 5–9 million in the 1520s to around 600,000 in 1620, mainly from infectious disease. The National University of San Marcos was founded in Lima in 1551. Peru proclaimed independence in 1821 and completed it in 1824, with the battle of Ayacucho. Guano exploitation brought relative stability until the War of the Pacific, 1879–1884.

Peru is a unitary semi-presidential republic under its 1993 constitution, with a president elected for five years without immediate re-election. The population was 33,396,698 in estimates to 2022, about 80 percent of them urban, and the Lima metropolitan area has over 9.8 million people. Spanish is the main language, but many Peruvians speak Quechuan languages, Aymara or other Indigenous languages.
pervez-musharraf: Pervez Musharraf was born on 11 August 1943 in Delhi, British India, to an Urdu-speaking family of Sayyids. His father, Syed Musharrafuddin, worked in the foreign office of the British Indian government and became an accounting director, and his mother, Zarin, took a degree in English literature at Delhi University. In 1961, aged 18, he entered the Pakistan Military Academy at Kakul.

Musharraf first saw battle with an artillery regiment during the Second Kashmir War of 1965 and received the Imtiazi Sanad medal for gallantry. In 1987 he commanded a new brigade of the Special Services Group near the Siachen Glacier. Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif promoted him to four-star general and Chief of the Army Staff in October 1998. From March to May 1999 he ordered the secret infiltration of forces into the Kargil district, and a fierce Indian offensive nearly led to a full-scale war. Sharif withdrew support in July under international pressure, which antagonised the army, and Sharif's attempt to dismiss Musharraf was followed by the coup of October 1999.

Musharraf governed as Chief Executive, appointed himself president on 20 June 2001, and in August 2002 issued the Legal Framework Order, which made many amendments to the Constitution. After the attacks of 11 September 2001 he allied Pakistan with the United States against the Taliban. His government liberalised the media and presided over rapid economic growth, while his rule also saw curbs on the judiciary and a growing insurgency in the North-West Frontier Province.

His dismissal of Chief Justice Iftikhar Chaudhry in March 2007 and the state of emergency of November cost him support, and he announced his resignation on 18 August 2008. He founded the All Pakistan Muslim League in 2010. On 17 December 2019 a special court sentenced him in absentia to death for suspending the constitution in November 2007. He died on 5 February 2023, aged 79, of amyloidosis, and was buried with military honours in Karachi. Judgements of his rule are sharply divided between those who credit him with economic stabilisation and those who point to the erosion of democratic institutions.
peter-kropotkin: Pyotr Alexeyevich Kropotkin was born in Moscow on 9 December 1842, the youngest of four children. His father, Alexey, was a royal officer who owned serfs in three provinces. His mother died of tuberculosis when he was three, and he and his brother Alexander were raised mostly by their German nurse. In 1862 he chose to serve with the Amur Cossacks in east Siberia, a post that allowed him to travel and become financially independent of his father. There the exiled poet Mikhail Mikhailov introduced him to anarchism by recommending an essay by Pierre-Joseph Proudhon.

In 1872 Kropotkin travelled to Switzerland, where he met the Jura Federation of followers of Mikhail Bakunin and was converted to anarchism. In 1879 he started the fortnightly Le Révolté in Geneva, which published his articulation of anarchist communism, the idea of distributing the product of work by need. In France he was imprisoned for almost four years. He then lived in England until 1917 and co-founded the monthly Freedom in London in late 1886.

In The Conquest of Bread (1892) he proposed an economy of voluntary cooperation in which everyone could take what they needed from the social product. In Mutual Aid: A Factor of Evolution (1902) he answered the social thinkers who stressed competition by arguing that cooperation made for the success of species. He returned to Russia in June 1917 and refused the Provisional Government's offer of a cabinet seat. He argued with Lenin against the Bolsheviks' hostage policy and centralisation.

Kropotkin died of pneumonia on 8 February 1921. His family refused an offer of a state funeral, and the Bolsheviks permitted a restrained official memorial in Moscow, the last major anarchist demonstration of the period in Russia, since the movement and his writings were suppressed later that year. He had little influence on the Russian Revolution, but his books and pamphlets were the most widely read of anarchist literature and influenced revolutionaries such as Nestor Makhno and Emiliano Zapata.
peter-paul-rubens: Rubens was born on 28 June 1577 to Jan Rubens and Maria Pypelincks, whose family came from Antwerp. His father, a lawyer, converted to Calvinism, and in 1568 the family fled to Cologne, fearing persecution under the Duke of Alba. After Jan Rubens died in 1587 the family moved to Antwerp, where Peter Paul studied Latin and classical literature. In 1590 he had to start working, and after serving as a page to a countess he began an apprenticeship with the landscape painter Tobias Verhaecht in 1592.

In 1600 Rubens travelled to Italy, where in Venice he saw paintings by Titian, Veronese and Tintoretto. He entered the service of Duke Vincenzo I Gonzaga of Mantua, painting portraits of the ducal family and copying works in his collection, and in 1601 went on to Rome, where he studied classical sculpture and the art of Michelangelo, Raphael and Leonardo. He returned to Antwerp in 1608, and in September 1609 was appointed court painter by Archduke Albert and the Infanta Isabella Clara Eugenia, with permission to keep his studio in Antwerp. He married Isabella Brant on 3 October 1609, and from 1610 he lived and worked in a villa he designed, now the Rubenshuis Museum. His pupils and collaborators included Anthony van Dyck.

In 1621 Marie de' Medici commissioned him to paint two cycles for the Luxembourg Palace in Paris, and the one on her own life was installed in 1625. After the Twelve Years' Truce ended in 1621 the Spanish Habsburg rulers entrusted him with diplomatic missions, and between 1627 and 1630 he travelled between the courts of Spain and England to seek peace between the Spanish Netherlands and the Dutch Republic. Philip IV of Spain raised him to the nobility in 1624, Cambridge gave him an honorary degree in 1629, and Charles I of England knighted him in 1630. His output was large: Michael Jaffé's catalogue lists 1,403 works, not counting the many copies made in his workshop.

In 1630 Rubens, whose first wife Isabella had died four years earlier, married the 16-year-old Helena Fourment, who became the model for the full-figured women of many of his paintings of the 1630s. In 1635 he bought the Steen, an estate outside Antwerp, and painted landscapes there. He died on 30 May 1640 of heart failure resulting from chronic gout and was buried in Saint James' Church in Antwerp, where a family chapel was completed in 1650 with an altarpiece he painted himself. He is considered the most influential artist of the Flemish Baroque, and the terms Rubensian and Rubenesque are derived from his name.
peter-the-great: Peter was born on 9 June 1672 and grew up at the Izmaylovo Estate. When his father, Tsar Alexei, died in 1676 the throne passed to Peter's half-brother Feodor III. When Feodor died in 1682 without children, the Miloslavsky and Naryshkin families, the families of Alexei's first and second wives, disputed the succession. Ivan V was next in line but was weak-minded and blind, and the Boyar Duma, the council of nobles, chose the ten-year-old Peter, with his mother Natalya Naryshkina as regent. A hole was cut in the back of the throne so that she could whisper to the two boys, who ruled jointly until Ivan's death in 1696.

In March 1697 Peter travelled to Western Europe on an 18-month journey with a large delegation, the Grand Embassy, hoping to find allies against the Ottoman Empire; he failed to enlarge the anti-Ottoman alliance. In 1699 he moved the new year from 1 September to 1 January and had years counted from the birth of Christ. In 1700 he refused to allow a new patriarch to be elected, and the church later came under a Holy Synod controlled by a procurator.

He declared war on Sweden in the Great Northern War. The Russian army was defeated at Narva in 1700, but the Swedish king Charles XII then turned against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which gave Peter time to reorganise his army. Russia captured Nöteborg, renamed Shlisselburg, and founded Saint Petersburg on the Neva, and in 1712 Peter moved the capital there from Moscow. After his victory Russia annexed much of the eastern Baltic coast and became an empire. He created a Governing Senate in 1711 and a Table of Ranks in 1722, and brutally suppressed rebellions by the Streltsy, the Bashkirs, Astrakhan and the Bulavin Rebellion.

Peter's health was never robust. He began to suffer from problems of the bladder in the winter of 1723 and died early on 8 February 1725 at the age of 52; an autopsy found his bladder infected with gangrene. He is buried in the Saints Peter and Paul Cathedral. A story that he caught his fatal illness rescuing drowning soldiers rests on a single source and is viewed with scepticism by some historians. For Old Believers he was the Antichrist, because of the calendar changes and the poll tax, and mid-19th-century Slavophiles deplored the westernisation of Russia. The so-called Will of Peter the Great was a forgery made in Paris on Napoleon's order in 1812.
peter-tordenskjold: Peter Jansen Wessel was the tenth child of the Trondheim alderman Jan Wessel. An unruly boy, he stowed away on a ship to Copenhagen in 1704 and tried without success to become a naval cadet. The king's chaplain, Peder Jespersen, sent him on a voyage to the West Indies and at last found him a cadetship. After voyages to the East Indies he was made second lieutenant on 7 July 1711. The Norwegian admiral Waldemar Løvendal gave him the four-gun sloop Ormen and in June 1712 the 18-gun Løvendals Galej, against the advice of the Danish admiralty, which thought him unreliable.

He took part in the destruction of Swedish transports at Rügen on 29 September 1712. On 26 and 27 July 1714, off Lindesnes, he fought the 28-gun Swedish privateer Olbing Galley until both ships were badly damaged, then sent to thank her crew and to ask for more ammunition so as to go on. King Frederick IV had him court-martialled for disclosing his lack of ammunition and for risking his ship against a stronger one; he was acquitted on 15 December and made captain on 28 December.

At Kolberg on 24 April 1715 he captured the Swedish Rear-Admiral Hans Wachtmeister and the frigate Hvita Örn, which became his flagship. At Dynekilen on 8 July 1716, with two frigates and five smaller ships, he took or destroyed around 30 Swedish vessels. A failure against the Gothenburg squadron in 1717 brought a second court-martial in 1718, which was quashed after Ulrik Christian Gyldenløve intervened. He became rear-admiral in December 1718 and vice-admiral after partly destroying and partly capturing the Gothenburg squadron on 26 September 1719.

On 12 November 1720, aged 30, he was killed by the sword of the Livonian colonel Jakob Axel Staël von Holstein in a duel at Gleidingen near Hildesheim. The quarrel arose at a dinner where Tordenskiold spoke of a friend cheated at gambling. As duelling was against Danish law, his body was brought to Holmen Church without much ceremony. He is named in the Danish anthem Kong Christian stod ved højen mast of 1778 and the Norwegian anthem Ja, vi elsker dette landet of 1864. A story that at Marstrand his men moved from post to post to seem more numerous gave Danish and Norwegian the phrase Tordenskjold's soldiers.
petra: Petra lies in a basin surrounded by mountains on the eastern flank of the Arabah valley, which runs from the Dead Sea to the Gulf of Aqaba. Flash floods visit the area, but excavations show that the Nabataeans controlled them with dams, cisterns and water conduits, which stored water through long droughts and created an artificial oasis. Enclosed by rocks and watered by a perennial stream, the city had the advantages of a fortress and controlled the commercial routes to Gaza, to Bosra and Damascus, to the Red Sea, and across the desert to the Persian Gulf.

By 7000 BCE some of the earliest recorded farmers had settled at Beidha, just north of Petra. In the Iron Age the area was held by the Edomites. The Nabataeans, a northern Arabian people who had roamed the desert with their herds, settled there in the fourth century BCE, and their name for the city appears to have been Raqēmō. Petra flourished in the first century CE, when its population peaked at an estimated 20,000 and Al-Khazneh, possibly the mausoleum of the king Aretas IV, was built.

In 106 the Romans annexed the Nabataean realm as the province of Arabia Petraea. The native dynasty ended, but the city continued to flourish under Roman rule. Its importance declined as sea-based trade routes grew, and an earthquake in 363 destroyed many buildings and crippled the water system. Petra became the capital of the Byzantine province of Palaestina III, and papyri found in the Byzantine Church show that it still thrived in the sixth century. The site was lost to the outside world until the Swiss traveller Johann Ludwig Burckhardt reached it in 1812.

Petra is a World Heritage Site, called the Rose City for its sandstone. Visitors enter through the Siq, a narrow gorge ending at Al-Khazneh, the Treasury. Other monuments include the Royal Tombs, among them the Urn Tomb, which was made into a church in 446, and the High Place of Sacrifice on Jebel Madbah. The Monastery, Ad Deir, the largest monument, dates from the first century BCE and is thought to have been dedicated to the deified king Obodas I.
petrarch: Petrarch was born on 20 July 1304, the son of Ser Petracco and his wife Eletta Canigiani. His birth name was Francesco di Petracco, which he Latinized to Franciscus Petrarcha. His family followed Pope Clement V to Avignon, where the papacy had moved in 1309. His father, a notary, insisted that he and his brother Gherardo study law, at Montpellier from 1316 to 1320 and at Bologna from 1320 to 1326. Petrarch preferred Latin literature and thought the seven years wasted. His father once threw his books into a fire.

After their parents died, Petrarch and his brother returned to Avignon in 1326, where he held clerical offices that left time for writing. His Latin epic Africa, about the Roman general Scipio Africanus, made him a European celebrity. On 8 April 1341 he was crowned on the Capitoline Hill in Rome by the senators Giordano Orsini and Orso dell'Anguillara, the second poet laureate since classical antiquity. He travelled widely and served as an ambassador.

He collected crumbling Latin manuscripts, and in 1345 he found in the Chapter Library of Verona Cathedral a collection of Cicero's letters not known to have survived, the Epistulae ad Atticum. About 1368 he moved with his daughter Francesca and her family to Arquà in the Euganean Hills near Padua, where he spent his remaining years in religious contemplation. The da Carrara lords of Padua seized his library, and its manuscripts are now scattered across Europe.

Petrarch is best known for the Rerum vulgarium fragmenta, or Canzoniere, a collection of 366 poems, 317 of them sonnets. The poems centre on Laura, whom he said he first saw in the church of Sainte-Claire d'Avignon on 6 April 1327. She may have been Laura de Noves, though he always denied that she was an invented figure. The Petrarchan sonnet still bears his name, and in the 16th century Pietro Bembo made his verse a model for the Italian language.

Most of his writing was in Latin, including the Secretum, an imagined dialogue with a figure inspired by Augustine of Hippo, and a large body of letters. He valued the study of ancient history and literature as the study of human thought and action, and is often called the father of humanism. He is credited with creating the idea of a historical "Dark Ages", a notion most modern scholars find inaccurate and misleading.
pharaoh: The word pharaoh derives from the Egyptian pr ꜥꜣ, meaning great house, which named the royal palace and was long used only in phrases referring to the court. Under the New Kingdom it became a form of address for the king himself. The earliest confirmed use for a ruler is a letter to Akhenaten (reigned c. 1353–1336 BCE), and an inscription referring to Thutmose III (c. 1479–1425 BCE) may be earlier. The first dated attachment of the title to a king's name is in year 17 of Siamun, in the tenth century BCE.

Scholars nevertheless use the word for every ruler of Egypt from the First Dynasty (c. 3150 BCE) to 30 BCE. Early kings bore up to three titles, the Horus name, the Sedge and Bee name and the Two Ladies name; the Golden Horus name, the nomen and the prenomen were added later, and by the Middle Kingdom the formal titulary had five names.

The king was the intermediary between the gods and the people. He owned all the land of Egypt, enacted laws, collected taxes and commanded the army, and he officiated at religious ceremonies and chose the sites of new temples. Officials acted only in his name, by delegated power. From the Pyramid Texts his task was summed up in a maxim, bring Maat and repel Isfet, that is, promote order and repel chaos.

Regalia expressed the office. The red crown, the Deshret, stood for Lower Egypt and the white crown, the Hedjet, for Upper Egypt; the double crown, the Pschent, is first documented in the middle of the First Dynasty. The rearing cobra, the uraeus, appears from the reign of Den. No ancient Egyptian crown has ever been found, not even in the tomb of Tutankhamun.

Egyptians often regarded the pharaoh as divine. In the Early Dynastic Period he was the incarnation of Horus; by the time of Djedefre in the 26th century BCE he was held to have no human father, his mother having been impregnated by the sun god Ra. Under the New Kingdom he was thought to possess the living royal ka of Amun-Re, received at his coronation. Temple texts called Darius the Great (522–486 BCE) a divine being, and such descriptions continued for Alexander the Great and the Ptolemaic rulers.

Herodotus reports that Egyptian priests rejected the divinity of the king, and rabbinic literature later depicted Pharaoh as a man who falsely proclaimed himself a god. Through the Hebrew Bible and the Qur'an, which spells the title firʿawn, it became the usual name for the kings of ancient Egypt.
philadelphia: Philadelphia lies on the Atlantic Seaboard Fall Line, which separates the Atlantic Plain from the Piedmont. The Delaware and Schuylkill rivers are its principal natural bodies of water. The city encompasses about 142.7 square miles, 6 per cent of it water, and its highest point, in Chestnut Hill, is about 446 feet above sea level. The city has been coterminous with its county since 1854.

Before Europeans arrived in the early 17th century, the Lenape, also known as the Delaware Indians, lived in the village of Shackamaxon, in present-day Philadelphia. Most Lenape were pushed out of the region during the 18th century as the Thirteen Colonies expanded, a loss made worse by intertribal conflicts, newly introduced diseases, mainly smallpox, and conflicts with Europeans. In the 1860s the federal government sent most of those remaining in the eastern United States to the Indian Territory, in present-day Oklahoma.

William Penn, an English Quaker and advocate of religious freedom, founded Philadelphia in 1682, and it became the capital of the colonial Province of Pennsylvania. It hosted the First Continental Congress in 1774 and the Second Continental Congress, which formed the Continental Army, elected George Washington as its commander and adopted the Declaration of Independence on 4 July 1776. The British Army occupied the city for nine months, from September 1777 to June 1778. The Constitution of the United States was ratified at the Philadelphia Convention. The city served as the national capital on several occasions until 1800, when the new capital at Washington, D.C. was completed.

Philadelphia is the most populous city in Pennsylvania and the sixth most populous in the United States, with about 1.6 million people in the 2020 census. Independence National Historical Park, which holds Independence Hall and the Liberty Bell, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the city has 67 National Historic Landmarks. It claims many firsts in the United States, among them the first library (1731), hospital (1751), medical school (1765) and zoo (1874).
philippines: The Philippines consists of about 7,641 islands with a total area of about 300,000 km2, stretching 1,850 kilometres from north to south. They fall into three divisions, Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao, and the 11 largest islands make up about 95 percent of the land. The highest mountain is Mount Apo on Mindanao, at 2,954 metres.

The islands lie on the western fringes of the Pacific Ring of Fire, with 23 active volcanoes and about five recorded earthquakes a day, most too weak to be felt. On an expedition of the 16th century Ruy López de Villalobos named Leyte and Samar Felipinas after the Prince of Asturias, later Philip II of Castile, and the name Las Islas Filipinas was later used for the Spanish possessions. The title Republic of the Philippines appeared in the 1935 constitution.

Evidence of early hominins dates to as early as 709,000 years ago, and bones from Callao Cave may represent an unknown species, Homo luzonensis, who lived 50,000 to 67,000 years ago. The first Austronesians reached the islands from Taiwan around 2200 BCE and settled the Batanes Islands and northern Luzon. The earliest known surviving written record is the Laguna Copperplate Inscription of 900 CE, in Old Malay. By the 14th century large coastal settlements had become trading centres, trade with China had begun under the late Tang dynasty and widened under the Song, and Islam was established in the Sulu Archipelago by the 15th century.

Ferdinand Magellan's arrival marked the beginning of Spanish colonization. Catholicism became the dominant religion, and Manila became the western hub of trans-Pacific trade. The Philippine Revolution began in 1896 and became entwined with the Spanish–American War of 1898, after which Spain ceded the territory to the United States and revolutionaries declared the First Philippine Republic. The ensuing Philippine–American War left the United States in control until the Japanese invasion in the Second World War, and the Philippines became independent in 1946.

Ferdinand Marcos ruled under martial law from 1972 to 1981, and the People Power Revolution overthrew him in 1986. The Philippines is a constitutional republic with a presidential system, in which the president serves a six-year term, and its population was 112,729,484 in July 2024. The largest ethnic group in the 2020 census was the Tagalog, at 26.0 percent, and indigenous peoples comprise 110 ethnolinguistic groups. Spanish and American rule left lasting marks, among them the dominance of Catholicism, the use of English and Spanish surnames resulting from an 1849 edict.
phnom-penh: Phnom Penh lies in the south-central region of Cambodia, on the banks of the Tonlé Sap, the Mekong and the Bassac rivers, and is fully surrounded by Kandal province. It is a typical flood plain, and flooding in the monsoon season is a problem when the river sometimes overflows its banks. The city takes its name from Wat Phnom, the hill temple, and from Lady Penh, its founder.

Excavations at Choeung Ek, in the south of the city, uncovered one of the largest kiln pottery centres in Cambodia, which produced ceremonial vessels from the 5th to the 13th century, and suggest settlement from the 5th century. According to a tale first recorded a century after it is said to have taken place, a woman named Penh found a floating koki tree in the river in 1372. Inside it were four Buddha statues and one of Vishnu, and she raised a hill with a shrine to house them, later known as Wat Phnom.

King Ponhea Yat moved the capital here from Angkor Thom after Siam captured and destroyed it. Later kings abandoned Phnom Penh because of fighting between royal pretenders and set up their capitals at places such as Pursat, Longvek and Oudong. Japanese immigrants settled on the outskirts of the city in the 17th century, and a Portuguese community carried on commercial and religious activity there. It became the capital again in 1865 and was the national capital under French colonial rule. After independence it was modernized, and earned the nickname the Pearl of Asia for its French colonial, New Khmer and Art Deco architecture.

During the Vietnam War thousands of refugees fled to the city from the fighting, and by 1975 its population was two to three million. The Khmer Rouge cut off supplies for more than a year before the city fell on 17 April 1975, and then forcibly evacuated all its residents. The city faced persecution, forced labour and genocide, and remained largely uninhabited until Vietnam-backed forces took it in 1979, when people began to return. Reconstruction followed with foreign investment and aid.

Phnom Penh is the capital and most populous city of Cambodia and the seat of its monarchy at the Royal Palace. It is an autonomous municipality with a status equal to that of the provinces. The official language is Khmer, and English and French are also used. Its census population was 2,129,371 in 2019. Its Water Festival marks the reversing of the flow of the Tonlé Sap River, and the city holds buildings of the New Khmer Architecture of the 1950s and 1960s, associated with the architect Vann Molyvann.
piaui: Piauí has the shortest coastline of any coastal Brazilian state, 66 kilometres, and was colonised from the interior towards the ocean, unlike the rest of the region. It is bounded by Maranhão, Ceará, Pernambuco, Bahia and Tocantins. The Parnaíba River forms the boundary with Maranhão along its whole length, and the state lies almost entirely in the basin of the Parnaíba and its tributaries. The coast and lower Parnaíba are low, swampy and historically malarial; to the south the land rises to a plateau of open campos, with flat-topped plateaus called chapadas between the river valleys. The east is dry caatinga shrubland, and cerrado savanna covers the south-west.

The state holds many archaeological sites, among them Serra da Capivara National Park and Sete Cidades National Park, rich in remains of prehistoric Paleo-Indian and settled Indigenous cultures. Among the early settlers was Francisco Dias d'Ávila from Bahia, who brought the first herds of cattle, and Domingos Afonso Mafrense, from Portugal, who founded what is now Oeiras. The first settlement dates from 1674, when Domingos Afonso Mafrense established a number of cattle ranges.

In the 17th century impoverished noblemen and Jesuit priests settled there, together with enslaved Black and Amerindian people. Large estate owners looking for new pasture came from neighbouring states such as Bahia and Maranhão. At the start of the 20th century stock raising remained the principal industry. Goats were a secondary one, and cotton, sugar and tobacco, rubber, carnauba wax and dyewoods were also produced. Hides, skins, rubber, wax, tobacco and cotton were exported.

Teresina was the first planned city in Brazil. An architect designed it in 1852, taking a chessboard as his inspiration. It stands where the Parnaíba and Poti rivers meet and is known as the Green City for the mango trees that line its streets. A battle of Brazil's war of independence was fought at Jenipapo on 13 March 1823, and the date was added to the state flag in 2005.

Piauí is divided into 224 municipalities, and Teresina is its capital and the only capital in the north-east that lies inland. The 2022 census counted 3,271,199 people. Portuguese is the language of schooling. The Serra da Capivara National Park, in the south-east, has more than 400 archaeological sites and a very large concentration of rock paintings, and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
piedmont: Piedmont is one of the 20 regions of Italy, in the northwest, and the second largest in area after Sicily. It borders Liguria, Lombardy, Emilia-Romagna and the Aosta Valley, as well as Switzerland and France. The Alps surround it on three sides, among them Monviso, where the Po rises, and Monte Rosa. The region is 43.3 per cent mountainous, 30.3 per cent hills and 26.4 per cent plain, from the rice paddies of Vercelli and Novara to the hillsides of the Langhe, Roero and Montferrat. The name comes from the medieval Latin Pedemontium, at the foot of the mountains, attested from the end of the 12th century.

Celtic-Ligurian tribes such as the Taurini and the Salassi lived there until the Romans subdued them about 220 BCE and founded colonies including Augusta Taurinorum (Turin) and Eporedia (Ivrea). After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the region was invaded by Burgundians, Ostrogoths, East Romans, Lombards and, in 773, the Franks. In 1046 Otto of Savoy added Piedmont to the County of Savoy, whose capital was Chambéry, though Asti, Alessandria, Saluzzo and Montferrat stayed independent. Duke Emanuele Filiberto moved the seat to Turin in 1563, and in 1720 the Duke of Savoy became King of Sardinia.

France created client republics in Piedmont from 1796 and annexed it in September 1802; the Congress of Vienna restored the Kingdom of Sardinia and gave it the Republic of Genoa as a barrier against France. Piedmont was the springboard of Italian unification in 1859 to 1861, after unsuccessful wars with Austria in 1820 to 1821 and 1848 to 1849. Turin was the first capital of the Kingdom of Italy, from 1861 to 1865; when the capital moved the region lost administrative importance, though the Italian crown prince was still styled Prince of Piedmont, and it was one of the most important regions of early Italian industrialisation.

Piedmont has 4,255,006 inhabitants and Turin as its capital. It is a great winegrowing region, producing Barolo and Barbaresco from the Langhe and sparkling Asti, and the Montferrat wine district was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014. The Residences of the Royal House of Savoy have been World Heritage Sites since 1997. Besides Italian, Piedmontese, Occitan, Franco-Provençal and Walser are spoken.
piracy: Piracy is robbery or criminal violence by ship or boat-borne attackers upon another ship or a coastal area, typically to steal cargo and valuables or to take hostages. It is a specific crime under customary international law and of many states' law. It is usually held apart from privateering, which a state authorised by a letter of marque and reprisal against an enemy's merchant ships. The line was not always clear, since whether a man was a privateer or a pirate could depend on whose custody he fell into. Narrow channels that funnel shipping into predictable routes, such as the waters of Gibraltar, the Strait of Malacca and the English Channel, have long offered opportunities for it.

The earliest documented piracy is that of the Sea Peoples, who threatened ships of the Aegean and Mediterranean civilisations in the fourteenth century BCE. Phoenicians, Illyrians and Tyrrhenians were known as pirates in antiquity, and in the pre-classical era the Greeks accepted piracy as a way of making a living, with the abduction of women and children for sale into slavery common. By the time of Classical Greece it was looked on as a disgrace. The English word comes from Latin pirata and Greek peiratēs, which means anyone who attempts something.

In East Asia, the merchant Chang Pogo, angered that Silla subjects fell victim to coastal pirates in the unstable late Tang period, petitioned King Heungdeok for a garrison. In 828 the Cheonghae Garrison was founded at Wando island with an army of 10,000, and Chang became the arbiter of Yellow Sea commerce. The Sindhi Bawarij, active between 251 and 865, looted two treasure ships from Ceylon, which became the casus belli for the Umayyad conquest of Sindh.

The classic era of Caribbean piracy lasted from about 1650 to the mid-1720s, as France, England and the United Provinces built colonial empires and seaborne trade grew. Pirate crews divided plunder under a hierarchy in which the quartermaster could veto the captain, and the loot was more often food, water, weapons and ship's gear than buried treasure. Caught pirates were usually hanged, in England often at Execution Dock on the Thames.

The two-volume A General History of the Pyrates, published in London in 1724, gave the public its picture of the Golden Age of Piracy and inspired later fiction, notably Treasure Island in 1883 and Peter Pan in 1911.
pisa: Pisa is a city and comune in Tuscany, Central Italy, straddling the Arno just before it empties into the Ligurian Sea, and the capital of the Province of Pisa. Most believe that the name comes from Etruscan and means mouth, since the city lies at the mouth of the Arno. Excavations in the 1980s and 1990s found numerous remains, including the fifth-century BCE tomb of an Etruscan prince, proving the city's Etruscan origin and its role as a maritime city trading with other Mediterranean civilisations.

In the last years of the Western Roman Empire Pisa did not decline as much as other Italian cities, probably because its river system made it easy to defend. It became the main port of the Upper Tyrrhenian Sea and the main trading centre between Tuscany and Corsica, Sardinia and the southern coasts of France and Spain, and its power as a maritime nation reached its apex in the 11th century.

In 1113 Pisa and Pope Paschal II organised, with the count of Barcelona and others, a war to free the Balearic Islands from the Moors. The king and queen of Mallorca were brought to Tuscany in chains, and although the Almoravides soon reconquered the island, the booty financed the cathedral and gave Pisa pre-eminence in the western Mediterranean.

Resentment of Genoa grew again after Frederick II confirmed his supremacy over the Tyrrhenian coast in 1220, and Pisa's strong Ghibelline position set it against the pope, who tried to deprive it of its dominions in northern Sardinia. The decline is said to have begun on 6 August 1284, when the larger Pisan fleet under Albertino Morosini was defeated by the Genoese under Benedetto Zaccaria and Oberto Doria at the Battle of Meloria.

In 1290 the Genoese destroyed the Porto Pisano and covered the land with salt. The loss of thousands of sailors could not easily be made up, and the Arno began to change course, keeping galleys from the port. The end came in 1324, when Sardinia was entirely lost to the Aragonese.

Pisa is best known for the Leaning Tower, the cathedral's bell tower, one of the buildings of the Piazza del Duomo, also called the Piazza dei Miracoli, with the cathedral, baptistery and Campo Santo. The city has more than twenty other historic churches. The University of Pisa has a history going back to the 12th century, and the Scuola Normale Superiore was founded by Napoleon in 1810.
plato: Plato was born in the late fifth century BCE into an aristocratic and influential Athenian family. Through his mother, Perictione, he was a descendant of Solon, the statesman credited with laying the foundations of Athenian democracy. Diogenes Laertius asserted that Plato was a nickname alluding to his robust figure and that his birth name was Aristocles, but modern scholarship widely regards this as false. His brothers Glaucon and Adeimantus appear in the Republic. During his childhood Athens was at war with Sparta in the Peloponnesian War, and both brothers distinguished themselves at the battle of Megara in 409 BCE.

Like all male citizens of Athens, Plato received a traditional education in gymnastics and music. Ancient writers report a tradition that in his youth he wrote poems and tragedies, but burnt them when he met Socrates and turned to philosophy. He soon became a member of Socrates' inner circle. Socrates examined the ideas of his interlocutors by a series of questions, the Socratic method, and turned philosophy from natural philosophy to questions of ethics and politics.

Plato wrote dialogues in which Socrates is usually the primary speaker. Plato never presents himself as a participant. The dialogues discuss religion, human nature, love, perception and reality, and body and soul. His best known contribution is the theory of Forms, first introduced in the Phaedo. It holds that there is an apparent world of material objects grasped by the senses, which constantly changes, and an unchanging and unseen world of Forms, grasped by reason. He also argued for the immortality of the soul, and in the Republic the soul has three parts.

Thirty-five dialogues and thirteen letters have traditionally been ascribed to Plato, though modern scholarship doubts the authenticity of at least some of them. No one knows the exact order in which the dialogues were written. During the Islamic Golden Age, Neoplatonism was revived, and Al-Farabi, inspired by the Republic, proposed an ideal city governed by philosopher-kings. Byzantine scholars reintroduced Plato's texts to Western Europe in the early Renaissance, and about 250 Byzantine manuscripts survive. The edition published by Henricus Stephanus in Geneva in 1578 established the standard Stephanus pagination still in use.
pliny-the-elder: Pliny was the son of an equestrian, Gaius Plinius Celer, and his wife Marcella, names known only from a fragmentary inscription found at Verona. He was born at Como, which he regarded as part of old Gallia Transpadana, and his father took him to Rome to be educated. His dates rest on the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 and a statement by his nephew that he died in his 56th year. He had a sister, Plinia, who was the mother of Pliny the Younger, whose letters describe his uncle's work and study regimen in detail. Pliny the Elder bequeathed his notes to his nephew and adopted him in his will.

In 46 CE, at about 23, Pliny entered the army as a junior officer, as young men of equestrian rank did. He served under Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo in Germania Inferior and took part in the conquest of the Chauci in 47 and the building of a canal between the Maas and the Rhine. He later served in Germania Superior under Publius Pomponius Secundus, and probably joined the campaign against the Chatti in 50.

Under Nero he held no high office, lived mainly in Rome, pleaded cases and wrote on safer subjects such as rhetoric and grammar, and a biography of Pomponius Secundus. After Vespasian became emperor in 69, Pliny was kept in a succession of procuratorships. Scholars propose two to four of them, including Gallia Narbonensis in 70, Africa from 70 to 72, Hispania Tarraconensis from 72 to 74 and Gallia Belgica from 74 to 76. He kept good relations with Vespasian and, according to his nephew, went to the emperor before dawn each day.

Pliny produced seven works in 102 volumes, of which only the Natural History survives. Among the lost works was the twenty-volume Bella Germaniae, used by Plutarch, Tacitus and Suetonius, and a thirty-one-volume history continuing that of Aufidius Bassus, which he held back for publication after his death. The Natural History, in 37 books, drew on personal experience, his earlier works and extracts from other writers. One servant read aloud and another wrote down what he dictated, and the collection reached about 160 volumes. Larcius Licinius offered 400,000 sesterces for them, unsuccessfully.

The work is dedicated to Titus. It became a model for later encyclopedias in its breadth, its practice of citing original authors and its index of contents, and some historians call it the first encyclopedia. Pliny died in the eruption of 79, with the book lacking a final revision. According to the younger Pliny, he sailed from Misenum across the Gulf of Naples to rescue friends at Stabiae, and was overcome by toxic gases there.
plough: A plough, or plow in the US, is a farm tool for loosening or turning soil before sowing or planting. It may have a wooden, iron or steel frame with a blade attached to cut and loosen the soil, and the trenches it cuts are called furrows. Its main purpose is to turn over the uppermost soil, bringing fresh nutrients to the surface while burying weeds and crop remains. The earliest ploughs had no wheels, and the Romans called such a plough an aratrum. A Sumerian disputation poem of the 3rd millennium BCE personifies the plough in a debate with the hoe.

When agriculture began, soil was turned with digging sticks and hoes. The domestication of oxen in Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley Civilisation, perhaps as early as the 6th millennium BCE, gave the draught power to develop the true ard, or scratch plough. A ploughed field of about 2800 BCE has been found at Kalibangan in India.

The heavy iron mould-board plough was invented in China under the Han Empire in the 1st and 2nd centuries and spread from there to the Netherlands. The first mould-board ploughs turned the soil in one direction only, so fields were worked in long strips, and their traditional size, a furlong by a chain, an area of one acre, is the origin of the acre.

The basic mould-board plough was unsuitable for the heavier soils of northern Europe. Wheels allowed heavier ploughs with a larger metal-faced mould board, and these led to greater food production, coinciding with a marked increase in the world's population in the second millennium CE. They needed up to eight oxen, so fields became long and narrow. Four to eight oxen were more than a typical peasant household could muster, so ploughing became a communal effort and contributed to the rise of the manorial system in northern Europe.

By 1837 John Deere, an Illinois blacksmith, was making polished cast steel ploughs for sticky soils. Riding ploughs with multiple mould boards soon followed, and steam engines and then tractors replaced animals as power.
plovdiv: Evidence of habitation in the area goes back to the 6th millennium BCE, when the first Neolithic settlements appeared, and the cultural layers in the city are twelve metres thick. A Thracian settlement named Pulpudeva was later conquered and ruled by Persians, Macedonians, Celts, Romans, Byzantines, Goths, Huns, Bulgarians and Ottoman Turks. Philip II of Macedon settled Thracians and 2,000 Macedonians there in 342 BCE and founded it as Philippopolis. The Roman Republic took it in 168 BCE, and it became the capital of the province of Thracia, at the centre of the road network of inland Thrace. Marcus Aurelius built a new wall around the city.

The Goths under Cniva sacked Philippopolis in 250, and the Huns did so in 441 or 442; the walls were rebuilt each time, and Justinian renewed them again. The city fell to the Bulgars of the First Bulgarian Empire in 863, in the reign of Boris I. Basil II used it as a strategic fortress in the wars against Bulgaria, and the Pechenegs occupied it briefly around 1090. Geoffrey of Villehardouin ranked it the third largest city of the Byzantine Empire after Constantinople and Thessalonica. Kaloyan of Bulgaria destroyed it in 1206, and in 1219 it became the capital of the Crusader Duchy of Philippopolis.

The Ottoman Turks under Lala Shahin Pasha took the city in 1364, though other accounts place its fall after the Battle of Maritsa in 1371. Over about five hundred years it was a sanjak centre at various times, one of the major economic centres of the Balkans beside Constantinople, Edirne, Thessaloniki and Sofia, and its richer citizens built the houses that still stand in the architectural reserve of Old Plovdiv.

The Treaty of San Stefano of 3 March 1878 chose Plovdiv as capital of a restored Bulgaria, but the Congress of Berlin separated the autonomous region of Eastern Rumelia from Bulgaria, and Plovdiv became its capital under a constitution made by the Ottoman Empire. In 1885 Eastern Rumelia joined Bulgaria. A railway linked the city with Constantinople in 1874 and with Sofia in 1888, and in 1892 it hosted the First Bulgarian Fair.

Plovdiv is the second largest city in Bulgaria, on the Maritsa river 144 km southeast of Sofia, spread over seven syenite hills that give it the name City of the Seven Hills. It had a population of 329,489 in 2024. It was the European Capital of Culture in 2019, and the city has more than 200 archaeological sites.
plutarch: Plutarch was born to a prominent family in the small town of Chaeronea, in the Greek region of Boeotia, about 30 kilometres east of Delphi. His family was long established there. His father was named Autobulus and his grandfather Lamprias, and his brothers Timon and Lamprias appear often in his essays and dialogues. He studied mathematics and philosophy in Athens under Ammonius from 66 to 67 CE. At some point he received Roman citizenship, sponsored by Lucius Mestrius Florus, an associate of the emperor Vespasian, and took the name Lucius Mestrius Plutarchus.

Plutarch lived most of his life at Chaeronea, where he served as a magistrate and held the office of archon,. He visited Rome about 70 CE with Florus, who served as a source for his Life of Otho, and he was on familiar terms with Roman nobles including Quintus Sosius Senecio. About 95 CE he became one of the two priests of the temple of Apollo at Delphi, a site that had declined considerably since the classical period. He was also epimeletes of the Amphictyonic League for at least five terms, from 107 to 127, organising the Pythian Games. Plutarch and his wife Timoxena had at least four sons and one daughter. The year of his death is not known.

His best-known work, the Parallel Lives, arranges biographies of illustrious Greeks and Romans in pairs to illuminate their shared virtues and vices. The surviving Lives contain 23 pairs and four single lives, though several others are lost and many survivors are truncated. Plutarch states in his Life of Alexander that he is writing lives and not histories, because a small thing such as a phrase or a jest often reveals character better than battles. His Life of Pyrrhus is the main account of Roman history from 293 to 264 BCE, for which the texts of Dionysius and Livy are lost.

The Moralia is a collection of seventy-eight essays and speeches. It includes a dialogue on the face seen in the orb of the Moon, which served as a source for Galileo, On the Worship of Isis and Osiris, a crucial source on ancient Egyptian religion, and philosophical treatises such as On the Decline of the Oracles. Some works printed with it, including the Lives of the Ten Orators, were falsely attributed to him and are credited to an unknown author called Pseudo-Plutarch.
plzen: Plzeň lies about 78 kilometres west of Prague, at the confluence of four rivers, the Mže, Úhlava, Úslava and Radbuza, which together form the Berounka. The first written mention of Plzeň Castle is from 976. King Wenceslaus II founded the city of New Plzeň nearby in 1295, and it quickly became an important place on the trade routes from Bohemia to Nuremberg and Regensburg. In the fourteenth century it had about 3,000 inhabitants, making it the third largest city in Bohemia after Prague and Kutná Hora.

The first written mention of beer brewing is from 1307. During the Hussite Wars Plzeň was the centre of Catholic resistance; Prokop the Great besieged it three times without success. In 1476 the city printed Statuta by Arnošt of Pardubice, the oldest book printed in Bohemia. In the Thirty Years' War Mansfeld took it in 1618, and Imperial troops did not recapture it until 1621.

From the second half of the nineteenth century the city industrialised rapidly. Emil Škoda founded the Škoda Works in 1869, which became the most important engineering company in the country and a crucial supplier of arms to the Austro-Hungarian Army. The Bavarian brewer Josef Groll produced the first batch of modern Pilsner beer on 5 October 1842, using soft local water, Saaz hops and Bavarian-style lagering. In April 1945 Allied bombing raids caused heavy damage, and on 6 May 1945 the 16th Armored Division of General George Patton's Third Army liberated the city.

Plzeň is the capital of the Plzeň Region, and its historic centre has been an urban monument reservation since 1989. The Cathedral of St Bartholomew, built in the Gothic style in the late thirteenth century, has the highest tower in the Czech Republic at 102.6 metres. Beneath the centre runs a labyrinth of tunnels and cellars with a length of 20 kilometres, partly open to visitors. The city was a European Capital of Culture in 2015, and the Pilsner Urquell Brewery is the largest brewery in the Czech Republic.
podgorica: Podgorica lies in central Montenegro, at the confluence of the Ribnica and Morača rivers, where the southern foothills of the Dinaric Alps meet the northernmost part of the Zeta Plain. The name means under the hill. The city is only 15 kilometres north of Lake Skadar and stands at the crossroads of several historically important routes, in fertile lowlands with a favourable climate.

The oldest physical remains in the area are from the late Stone Age. In the Iron Age the area between the Zeta and Bjelopavlići valleys was populated by two Illyrian tribes, the Labeates and the Docleatae, and the nearby town of Doclea had 8,000 to 10,000 inhabitants. The area later passed through many hands, among them the Roman Empire, the Byzantine Empire, the Serbian Empire and the Republic of Venice.

The Ottoman Empire captured Podgorica in 1474, and in 1479 built a large fortress there. The existing settlement, with its highly developed merchant connections, became the main Ottoman defensive and attacking bastion in the region. After the Congress of Berlin in 1878 the town was annexed to the Principality of Montenegro, ending four centuries of Ottoman rule. Roads were built to all neighbouring towns in 1902, and tobacco became its first significant commercial product.

In World War II Podgorica was bombed over 80 times, first by the Luftwaffe on 6 April 1941; an attack by the USAAF on 5 May 1944 killed about 400 civilians. It was liberated on 19 December 1944, and 1,691 people had been killed there in the course of the war. Josip Broz Tito promised on 12 July 1946 that the destroyed city would be rebuilt. It was renamed Titograd in 1946 and designated capital of the Socialist Republic of Montenegro, and rapid growth turned a small town into the country's primate city. Its original name was restored after a referendum on 2 April 1992.

Podgorica is the capital and largest city of Montenegro, capital of the independent state since 2006. It is a hub of the country's rail and road network and the centre of its education, science and healthcare. Cetinje, capital for much of Montenegrin history, preserves much of the national cultural heritage. Monuments in and around Podgorica include the Clock tower, the ruins of the Ribnica fortress and remnants of the ancient city of Doclea.
poitiers: Poitiers stands on a vast promontory between the valleys of the Boivre and the Clain, on the Seuil du Poitou, a shallow gap that connects the Aquitaine Basin in the south to the Paris Basin in the north. The old town occupies a plateau rising about 40 metres above the streams around it, a strong tactical position that mattered especially before and throughout the Middle Ages.

The Celtic tribe of the Pictones founded the town and gave it its name; before Roman influence it was the oppidum of Lemonum, and after the conquest it was called Pictavium. The Romans built at least three aqueducts and an amphitheatre larger than the one at Nîmes. Hilary of Poitiers, the first bishop, held the see from 350 to 367 and evangelised the town; he was exiled by Constantius II and returned at risk of death. The Visigoths later made it one of their principal residences, until Clovis I defeated Alaric II at Vouillé, not far away, in 507, and the town came under Frankish rule.

In the Early Middle Ages Poitiers benefited from its defensible position far from the centre of Frankish power. It was the seat of a diocese from the 4th century and the capital of the county of Poitou. Charles Martel's troops fought an Umayyad army led by Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi near the city on 10 October 732, a battle also called the Battle of Tours.
