Eleanor of Aquitaine often lived there, embellished and fortified it, and in 1199 gave it communal rights; in 1152 she married the future Henry II of England in the cathedral.

On 19 September 1356 the English defeated a larger French royal army near the town in the Battle of Poitiers and captured King John II of France. From 1418, under Charles VII, the royal parliament sat in exile at Poitiers until 1436, and in 1429 the town was the site of the formal inquest into Joan of Arc. The university was founded in 1431. In 1569 it withstood a siege by Gaspard de Coligny during the Wars of Religion.

Poitiers is the capital of the Vienne department in the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region and has a population of 89,427. It is a university town, and Descartes, Rabelais and Joachim du Bellay are among those associated with it. Its preserved buildings include the 4th-century baptistery of Saint-Jean, the 12th-century Church of Notre-Dame-la-Grande and the cathedral, completed at the end of the 12th century.
pol-pot: Pol Pot was born Saloth Sâr in the village of Prek Sbauv, outside Kampong Thom, the son of a prosperous farmer. He was educated at some of Cambodia's most elite schools, boarding from 1942 at a new junior middle school in Kampong Cham, where fellow pupils such as Hu Nim and Khieu Samphan later served in his government. He arrived in Paris on 1 October 1949 on a scholarship to study radio electronics, and joined the French Communist Party in 1951. He returned to Cambodia in 1953 and worked with the Khmer Việt Minh, then taught in Phnom Penh while remaining a central figure in the Marxist-Leninist movement.

In 1959 the movement was formalised as the Kampuchean Labour Party, later renamed the Communist Party of Kampuchea. To avoid repression by Norodom Sihanouk's government, Pol Pot moved to a jungle camp in 1962, and in February 1963 he was elected party secretary. The war against Sihanouk was launched in January 1968. After Lon Nol deposed Sihanouk in March 1970, Sihanouk allied with the Khmer Rouge, and his support greatly helped recruitment. In May 1973 Pol Pot ordered the collectivisation of villages in Khmer Rouge territory. Phnom Penh fell on 17 April 1975, and he secretly entered the abandoned city three days later.

In January 1976 a new constitution renamed the country Democratic Kampuchea. The Khmer Rouge emptied the cities and moved the urban population to collective farms and labour camps, where mass executions, torture, malnutrition and disease were rampant. Money, religion and private property were abolished, and more than 1.3 million people were executed and buried in mass graves. After repeated border clashes and massacres of Vietnamese villagers, Vietnam launched a full-scale invasion on 25 December 1978, and by January 1979 the Khmer Rouge were toppled.

The Khmer Rouge retreated to the jungles near the Thai border and kept fighting until the Vietnamese withdrew in 1989. In June 1997 Pol Pot ordered the killing of Son Sen, which prompted the commander Ta Mok to turn against him. Pol Pot was placed under house arrest and died shortly afterward in 1998. Some Cambodians still leave offerings at his grave in Anlong Veng, while many call the period samai a-Pot, the era of the contemptible Pot.
poland: Poland covers an administrative area of 312,722 square kilometres, the ninth-largest country in Europe. The central and northern parts bordering the Baltic Sea lie within the flat Central European Plain, while the south is hilly and mountainous. The Sudetes lie in the west and the Carpathians in the east, and the Tatra Mountains hold the highest point, the northwestern summit of Rysy at 2,500 metres. The coastline spans 770 kilometres. The longest rivers are the Vistula, the Oder, the Warta and the Bug, and the country has around ten thousand lakes, mostly in the north-eastern region of Masuria.

The first Stone Age archaic humans settled the area approximately 500,000 years ago. The earliest evidence of European cheesemaking, from 5500 BCE, was discovered in Kuyavia, and a fortified settlement at Biskupin is attributed to the Lusatian culture of the Late Bronze Age. In antiquity many peoples lived in the territory, among them Celtic, Scythian, Germanic, Sarmatian, Baltic and Slavic tribes. Poland began to form into a unitary and territorial entity around the middle of the 10th century under the Piast dynasty, and in 966 the ruler of the Polans, Mieszko I, accepted Western Christianity under the Roman Catholic Church. The Kingdom of Poland emerged in 1025.

In 1569 Poland cemented its long-standing association with Lithuania, forming the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which had an elective monarchy and adopted Europe's first modern constitution in 1791. The country was partitioned by neighbouring states at the end of the 18th century and regained independence in 1918 as the Second Polish Republic.

The invasion of Poland by Germany and by the Soviet Union in September 1939 marked the beginning of World War II, which resulted in the Holocaust and millions of Polish casualties. Forced into the Eastern Bloc, the Polish People's Republic was a signatory of the Warsaw Pact. The Solidarity movement emerged in 1980, and in 1989 Poland re-established itself as a liberal democracy and held free elections.

Poland has over 37 million people and is composed of sixteen voivodeships, with Warsaw as its capital and largest city. It is a unitary parliamentary republic with a bicameral legislature of the Sejm, with 460 members, and the Senate, with 100. The 2021 census found that ethnic Poles comprise 98.84% of the population. It keeps its own currency, the złoty. Poland has 18 UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
polynesia: Polynesia has only about 300,000 to 310,000 square kilometres of land spread over a vast part of the central and southern Pacific, and more than 270,000 of them are in New Zealand. The Hawaiian archipelago makes up about half of the remainder. Most islands, including Hawaii and Samoa, are volcanic and built by hotspots, while New Zealand, Norfolk Island and Ouvéa are the unsubmerged portions of the largely sunken continent of Zealandia. The other main island groups within the triangle are Samoa, Tonga, the Cook Islands, Tuvalu, Tokelau, Niue, Wallis and Futuna and French Polynesia. The French writer Charles de Brosses first used the term Polynésie in 1756 for all the islands of the Pacific, and Jules Dumont d'Urville proposed a narrower definition in 1831.

By linguistic, archaeological and genetic evidence the Polynesians are a subset of the sea-migrating Austronesian people, whose languages trace back through Island Melanesia and Maritime Southeast Asia to Taiwan. The Express Train model, supported by most current data, holds that an expansion out of Taiwan reached Island Melanesia by roughly 1400 BCE and western Polynesia around 900 BCE, followed by a pause of about a thousand years before settlement of central and eastern Polynesia. Two other models, the Entangled Bank and the Slow Boat, stress longer interaction and admixture with peoples in Melanesia. Language, social life and material culture were distinctly Polynesian by 1000 BCE.

The sweet potato, native to the Americas, was widespread in Polynesia when Europeans arrived. Remains in the Cook Islands date to before 1400, and the present consensus is that Polynesians who travelled to South America and back brought it to central Polynesia around 1300. Whether Polynesians reached the Americas, and with what effects, remains contentious. Thor Heyerdahl's claim in the mid-20th century that Polynesians originated in the Americas is regarded as a misconception.

Polynesia is a cultural term for one of the three parts of Oceania, with Melanesia and Micronesia. It divides into West Polynesia, around Tonga and Samoa, and East Polynesia, which includes Tahiti, the Marquesas, Hawaii, Rapa Nui and New Zealand. Polynesian languages belong to the Oceanic branch of the Austronesian family and are similar to one another. The ancestral homeland, from a Proto-Nuclear Polynesian word, appears as Hawaiki in New Zealand and Havaiʻi in the Society Islands, and the largest islands of Hawaii and Samoa are called Hawaiʻi and Savaiʻi. Leaders were generally chosen by hereditary bloodline, though Samoa has a system, fa'amatai, that combines heredity with practical skills.
pompeii: Pompeii stood about 40 metres above sea level on a coastal lava plateau created by earlier eruptions of Mount Vesuvius, beside the mouth of the navigable Sarno River, which served early Greek and Phoenician sailors as a haven port. The first stable settlements on the site date to the 8th century BCE, when the Oscans founded five villages in the area. The Samnites conquered Greek Cumae between 423 and 420 BCE, and it is likely that Pompeii had already been conquered around 424 BCE.

Pompeii rebelled against Rome in the Social Wars, and in 89 BCE Sulla besieged it; the impact craters of thousands of ballista shots can still be seen in its walls. It surrendered and became a Roman colony, its people were granted Roman citizenship and quickly assimilated, and Latin became the main language. Urban development accelerated from about 30 BCE, with an amphitheatre, two theatres and at least four public baths. The city was home to some 11,000 people, and it had at least 31 bakeries.

Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE in one of the deadliest eruptions in history, which lasted two days. The first phase was a rain of pumice lasting about 18 hours, which allowed most inhabitants to escape; only about 1,150 bodies have been found on the site. In the night or early the next day pyroclastic flows began, scorching clouds of ash that knocked down structures in their path and incinerated or suffocated the remaining population. Pompeii lay buried under 4 to 6 metres of ash and pumice. Titus donated large sums to the victims, but no recovery work was done. Survivors reoccupied the site as a small informal settlement that lasted until the fifth century.

The site's name and location were forgotten, though it appeared on the Tabula Peutingeriana of the 4th century. It remained largely undisturbed until its rediscovery in the late 16th century, and major excavations began in the mid-18th century, marking the emergence of modern archaeology. Early efforts were haphazard or marred by looting. Organic remains decayed within the ash, allowing archaeologists to make moulds of figures in their final moments, and graffiti on walls preserve the colloquial Vulgar Latin of the time. Two-thirds of the city has been excavated, and Pompeii is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
pope-francis: Jorge Mario Bergoglio was born on 17 December 1936 in Flores, a neighbourhood of Buenos Aires, the eldest of five children. His father, Mario José Bergoglio, was an accountant and an Italian immigrant from Piedmont; his mother, Regina María Sívori, was a housewife born in Buenos Aires to a family of northern Italian origin. The family left Italy in 1929 to escape the fascist rule of Benito Mussolini. At 21, after life-threatening pneumonia and three cysts, he had part of a lung removed.

Bergoglio entered the Society of Jesus as a novice on 11 March 1958, after three years at the archdiocesan seminary in Villa Devoto, and studied the humanities in Santiago, Chile. He took perpetual vows on 12 March 1960 and taught literature and psychology in Santa Fe and Buenos Aires. He was ordained in 1969 and was Jesuit provincial superior in Argentina from 1973 to 1979. In 1976 the Argentine Navy kidnapped two Jesuit priests, Orlando Yorio and Franz Jalics, during the Dirty War. Bergoglio is widely reported to have failed to protect them; a criminal complaint filed in 2005 was dismissed, but the debate over his conduct has continued.

He became archbishop of Buenos Aires on the death of his predecessor, Quarracino, on 28 February 1998, and was created a cardinal in 2001 by Pope John Paul II. He doubled the number of priests working in the city's shantytowns, which earned him the name villero bishop, and put the archdiocese's finances on a stricter footing. After the resignation of Pope Benedict XVI, the conclave elected him pope on 13 March 2013. He took the name Francis in honour of Francis of Assisi, and was the first Jesuit pope, the first from Latin America and the first from the Southern Hemisphere.

As pope Francis called for decentralised, synodal governance, made women full members of dicasteries of the Roman Curia and convened the Synod on Synodality. He was a behind-the-scenes broker, with the Government of Canada, of the restoration of diplomatic relations between the United States and Cuba announced on 17 December 2014.

His last public appearance was on Easter Sunday, 20 April 2025. He died on Easter Monday, 21 April 2025, aged 88, of a cerebral stroke. His funeral took place on 26 April, and on 8 May the conclave elected Robert Francis Prevost as Pope Leo XIV. Francis had appointed more than 80 per cent of the cardinals who elected his successor, and he formalised the Church's opposition to the death penalty in all cases.
pope-gregory-i: Gregory was born around 540 in Rome, recently reconquered by the Eastern Roman Empire from the Ostrogoths, into a wealthy noble family with close ties to the church. His father, Gordianus, was a patrician and senator who served for a time as Prefect of the City of Rome, and his great-great-grandfather had been Pope Felix III. Gregory was himself prefect of Rome at 30. On his father's death he turned the family villa into a monastery dedicated to Andrew the Apostle, later rededicated as San Gregorio Magno al Celio.

In 579 Pope Pelagius II chose Gregory as apocrisiarius, his ambassador to the imperial court in Constantinople, and he held the post until 586. The Roman delegation had gone to ask the emperor for military aid against the Lombards. Emperor Maurice had long decided to limit his efforts against them to intrigue and diplomacy, and the empire was occupied with the Persians in the East and the Avars and Slavs to the north. There is no evidence that Gregory's tenure accomplished much for the objectives of Pelagius.

He returned to his monastery in 585 and was elected by acclamation in 590, when Pelagius II died of the plague then spreading through Rome. Gregory wrote letters disavowing any ambition for the papacy, and one to Maurice asking him not to confirm his election, though the prefect of Rome intercepted it. He built a system of charitable relief for the poor of Rome, most of them refugees from Lombard incursions, holding that the wealth belonged to the poor and the church was only its steward. He sent missionaries to England, among them Augustine of Canterbury and Paulinus of York, and died on 12 March 604.

Gregory is the only pope between the fifth and the eleventh centuries whose correspondence and writings survive in enough quantity to form a comprehensive body. His Moralia in Job is one of the longest patristic works, based on talks on the Book of Job. His Pastoral Care became the definitive statement of the nature of the episcopal office. The Dialogues are four books on the miracles of holy men of sixth-century Italy, with the second devoted to a life of Saint Benedict.

John the Deacon wrote that Gregory revised the liturgy of the Mass, removing many things, changing a few and adding some. In his own letters Gregory says he moved the Pater Noster to just after the Roman Canon, where it still stands in the Roman Liturgy, and he established the nine Kyries at the beginning of Mass. He is honoured with Augustine, Jerome and Ambrose as one of the four Great Latin Church Fathers.
pope-john-paul-ii: Karol Józef Wojtyła was the youngest of three children of Karol Wojtyła, an ethnic Pole, and Emilia Kaczorowska, a schoolteacher. His mother died in 1929, when he was eight. In his youth he worked occasionally as a stage actor, and during the Second World War he took work in a quarry to avoid being sent to a German forced labour camp. Adam Stefan Sapieha, the Archbishop of Kraków, encouraged him to study theology and ordained him on 1 November 1946. On 4 July 1958 Pope Pius XII appointed him auxiliary bishop of Kraków, and at 38 he became the youngest bishop in Poland.

After Pope John Paul I died following only 33 days as pope, a second conclave opened on 14 October 1978, split between Cardinal Giuseppe Siri and Cardinal Giovanni Benelli. Cardinal Franz König suggested Wojtyła as a compromise, and he won on the eighth ballot on 16 October, taking his predecessor's name. He wrote 14 encyclicals, completed a reform of the Church's legal system and the Roman Curia, and saw the 1983 Code of Canon Law and the Catechism of the Catholic Church promulgated. He beatified 1,344 people and canonised 483 saints.

On 13 May 1981 he was shot in the abdomen in St. Peter's Square by Mehmet Ali Ağca, lost nearly three-quarters of his blood and underwent five hours of surgery. As pope he made public apologies for more than 100 wrongdoings, among them the trial of Galileo Galilei (31 October 1992) and the silence of many Catholics during the Holocaust (1998).

He died on 2 April 2005 and was succeeded by Pope Benedict XVI. He was beatified on 1 May 2011 and canonised on 27 April 2014 by Pope Francis, alongside Pope John XXIII. He has been credited with helping to end communist rule in Poland and the rest of Europe, and under him the Church greatly expanded its influence in Africa and Latin America. He has also been criticised for allegedly not acting against, or being insufficiently harsh with, the sexual abuse of children by priests, both as archbishop in the Polish People's Republic and as pope.
pope-leo-xiii: Gioacchino Pecci was born on 2 March 1810 at Carpineto Romano, near Rome, the sixth of seven children of Count Domenico Ludovico Pecci, a colonel in Napoleon's French army, and Anna Francesca Prosperi-Buzzi. He studied at the Jesuit College in Viterbo until 1824. In 1837 Pope Gregory XVI appointed him a prelate, and he was ordained a priest on 31 December that year. He then served as papal legate to Benevento, and in 1843, aged 33, as nuncio to Belgium, where he was made an archbishop and developed excellent relations with the royal family.

From 1846 Pecci was Archbishop of Perugia. In 1849 he called a provincial council to reform religious life, enlarged the seminary and hired Thomist professors and founded shelters and soup kitchens. He became a cardinal in the consistory of 19 December 1853. When Pope Pius IX died on 7 February 1878, the conclave assembled on 18 February, and Pecci was elected on the third ballot and took the name Leo XIII. He was crowned on 3 March 1878.

The Holy See had lost the Papal States, and under Leo it sought to regain international standing by acting as an arbiter of disputes. He opened the Vatican Archives to qualified researchers, among them the historian Ludwig von Pastor,. He created 147 cardinals in 27 consistories, among them John Henry Newman.

Leo wrote 86 encyclicals. In Aeterni Patris of 4 August 1879 he made the revival of the theology of Thomas Aquinas the charter of Catholic teaching, to be followed in the training of priests and in universities. Humanum genus of 1884 reaffirmed condemnations of Freemasonry, arguing that its principles were incompatible with Catholic doctrine. He issued eleven encyclicals on the rosary and was called the Rosary Pope.

His encyclical Rerum novarum of 1891 addressed social inequality for the first time with papal authority, discussing the rights and duties of capital and labour. It affirmed workers' rights to a fair wage, safe conditions and trade unions, and the rights to property and free enterprise, and it rejected both atheistic communism and laissez-faire capitalism. It is thought to have laid the foundations of modern Catholic social teaching, and Leo was called the Pope of the Workers.

Leo XIII died on 20 July 1903, aged 93, of pneumonia followed by hemorrhagic pleurisy. He was buried in the Vatican Grottoes, and in 1924 his remains were moved to the Archbasilica of Saint John Lateran. He had the fourth-longest reign of any pope.
pope-pius-xi: Ambrogio Damiano Achille Ratti was born in Desio, in the province of Milan, in 1857, the son of the owner of a silk factory. He was ordained a priest in 1879 and selected for a life of academic study, obtaining three doctorates in philosophy, canon law and theology at the Gregorian University in Rome. From 1882 to 1888 he was a professor at a seminary in Padua, with expert paleography as his speciality, and from 1888 to 1911 he worked at the Ambrosian Library in Milan.

In 1918 Pope Benedict XV appointed him apostolic visitor in Poland, and in 1919 papal nuncio and titular archbishop. During the Bolshevik advance on Warsaw in August 1920 he was the only foreign diplomat who refused to flee the city. Benedict created him cardinal and Archbishop of Milan on 3 June 1921, and Benedict XV died on 22 January 1922.

Ratti was elected pope and headed the Catholic Church from 6 February 1922. His first encyclical, Ubi arcano, of December 1922 inaugurated the Catholic Action movement, aimed at Christianizing increasingly secular societies. Divini illius Magistri (1929) asserted the need for Christian influence over education, and Casti connubii (31 December 1930) praised Christian marriage and prohibited contraception. Quadragesimo anno (1931) restated Leo XIII's warnings against both socialism and unrestrained capitalism and called international capitalism materially and spiritually exploitative. He also wrote Quas primas, establishing the feast of Christ the King.

He was the first sovereign of Vatican City, created on 11 February 1929, when the Lateran Treaty ended the long hostility with the Italian government. Pius XI took a pragmatic approach to forms of government, stating that the Church is never bound to one form more than another, and concluded a record number of concordats, including the Reichskonkordat with Nazi Germany, whose betrayals he condemned four years later in the encyclical Mit brennender Sorge. He canonised Thomas More, Peter Canisius, Bernadette of Lourdes and Don Bosco.

The end of his pontificate was dominated by his speaking out against Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini and by his defence of the Church against outside interference. Pius XI died on 10 February 1939 in the Apostolic Palace and was buried in the Papal Grotto of Saint Peter's Basilica. He took a strong interest in fostering the participation of laypeople in the Church, especially through Catholic Action.
port-au-prince: Port-au-Prince lies on the Gulf of Gonâve, whose bay acts as a natural harbour and has sustained economic activity since the Taíno. The city's layout resembles an amphitheatre, with commercial districts near the water and residential neighbourhoods on the hills above. The name means 'Prince's Port', but it is unclear which prince was meant: one theory points to Le Prince, a ship that arrived in 1706, though the islets in the bay were called les îlets du Prince as early as 1680.

The area was part of the Taíno chiefdom of Xaragua. Under Spanish rule the governor Nicolas Ovando, from 1503, had Taíno leaders killed at a feast, and violence and disease decimated the native population. The Spanish administration abandoned the region in 1606, and French filibusters arrived around 1650, setting up a hospital that gave the region the name Hôpital. Spain renounced its claims in 1697. Petit-Goâve was too malarial and Léogâne hard to defend, so Port-au-Prince was built in 1749, and in 1770 it replaced Cap-Français as capital of Saint-Domingue.

In 1804 it became the capital of independent Haiti. After the assassination of Jean-Jacques Dessalines in 1806 it was capital of the southern republic under Alexandre Pétion, and it became capital of all Haiti when the country was unified in 1820. American forces occupied Haiti from 1915 to 1934. On 12 January 2010 a magnitude 7.0 earthquake destroyed most of the central historic area, including the cathedral and the National Palace; Haiti's government estimated the death toll at 230,000.

Port-au-Prince is the capital and most populous city of Haiti, with a population estimated at 1,200,000 in 2022. It is the seat of the State University of Haiti, established in 1920, and the Presidential Palace stands on the Champ de Mars. Its cultural sites include the National Museum, founded in 1938, the National Archives and the National Library. Each November the national cemetery fills with people celebrating Fet Gede, a Vodou festival of the dead.
port-louis: Dutch settlers used the site as a harbour from 1606 and called the area the Harbour of Tortoises. Under French government it became the administrative centre of Mauritius, then called Ile de France, and a major reprovisioning halt for French ships passing between Asia and Europe around the Cape of Good Hope. The port is named in honour of King Louis XV, and the French governor Bertrand-François Mahé de La Bourdonnais contributed to the development of the city. Because the Moka Mountain Range shelters it from cyclone winds, it was chosen to house both the main harbour and the fort.

The port kept its value during the British occupation of the island in the Napoleonic Wars, when it helped Britain control the Indian Ocean. Port calls fell drastically after the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869, but rose during the canal's seven-year closure from 1967. Modernisation in the late 1970s helped it remain the central point for all imports and exports of Mauritius.

Port Louis is the capital and most populous city of Mauritius, with 147,066 inhabitants at the 2018 census. The main harbour is the only official port of entry and exit for sea vessels in the country, and ships must be cleared there before visiting any other anchorage. It is the biggest port facility in the Indian Ocean region, with specialised terminals for sugar, fish and containers.

Many buildings reflect the city's colonial history, among them French colonial buildings of the 18th century such as Government House, the Jummah Mosque, Saint James Cathedral, a Tamil temple and the five-tier Port Louis Theatre. The Aapravasi Ghat is the remains of the immigration depot built by the British government to import labourers from India, Eastern Africa, Madagascar, China and Southeast Asia to work on the island's sugar estates. The Intercontinental Slavery Museum deals with slavery and indentured labour.
port-moresby: Port Moresby lies on the shores of the Coral Sea, on the south-western coast of the Papuan Peninsula of the island of New Guinea. The place where the city was founded has been inhabited by the Motu-Koitabu people for centuries. When Europeans first came, the largest settlement, Hanuabada, consisted of five villages of Motu and Koita people, who were organised into units called iduhu, somewhat like clans. Port Moresby was already an important centre of trade, visited by distant tribes of New Guinea.

In February 1873 the crew of HMS Basilisk, surveying the southern shore of New Guinea, reached the harbour. Captain John Moresby named it for his father, Admiral of the Fleet Sir Fairfax Moresby. Missionaries of the London Missionary Society arrived in 1873 and 1874. In 1883 the Premier of Queensland ordered the police magistrate Henry Chester to take possession of the eastern half of New Guinea, and on 4 April the Union Jack was raised at Port Moresby. A protectorate over the south-eastern coast was proclaimed in October 1884, and Special Commissioner Peter Scratchley chose the site as the colonial capital.

In 1906 the Papua Act transferred Papua, with Port Moresby as capital, to direct Australian rule. In the Second World War it was a prime objective of Imperial Japanese forces in 1942 and 1943, and by September 1942 it was an important Allied complex of bases. General Douglas MacArthur had his headquarters there from November 1942 to October 1944. It was granted city status in 1972 and became the capital of independent Papua New Guinea in September 1975.

Port Moresby is the capital and largest city of Papua New Guinea, with 756,754 inhabitants at the 2024 census. Although surrounded by Central Province, it forms its own National Capital District, and the Motu and Koitabu landowners are represented by the Motu Koita Assembly. The National Parliament Building, opened in 1984, and the National Museum and National Library stand in the suburb of Waigani.
port-of-spain: Port of Spain measures about 10.4 square kilometres and lies in the north-west of the island of Trinidad, between the Gulf of Paria, the Northern Range and the Caroni Swamp. The Laventille Hills form its eastern boundary. The climate is tropical monsoon, with little seasonal variation, a wet season from May to December and a dry season from January to April. The city proper is small. It forms the western end of a continuous built-up area, the East-West Corridor, which runs about 24 kilometres east to Arima.

The Spanish founded the town as Puerto España. The first settlement stood near an Amerindian fishing village called Cumucurapo, meaning place of the silk cotton trees, in the area now known as Mucurapo. The name Conquerabia is also recorded for an Amerindian settlement here. It may have been a separate village, another name for Cumucurapo, or the result of a misunderstanding by early Spanish settlers, who set up a port called Puerto de los Españoles, later Puerto de España. In 1560 a Spanish garrison was posted near the foot of the Laventille Hills.

Queen's Park Savannah, once sugar land, was bought by the town council in 1817 from the Peschier family. After an election in 1887 Michel Maxwell Philip became mayor, a post previously held only by white men, which the historian Bridget Brereton wrote perhaps marked the emergence of the coloured man as a political force in Trinidad. The city was also the de facto capital of the short-lived West Indies Federation.

Port of Spain is the capital and chief port of Trinidad and Tobago, with a municipal population of 49,867 in 2017. It is a retail and administrative centre, with most government offices, and a financial centre for the Caribbean. The Trinidad and Tobago Stock Exchange, the Central Bank, the Red House and Independence Square are in the downtown district. Queen's Park Savannah, about 110 hectares, is the largest open space. The pre-Lenten Carnival is the city's main annual festival, and the city was among the hosts of the 2007 Cricket World Cup.
port-vila: Port Vila lies on the west coast of the island of Efate, in Shefa Province, and is the capital and largest city of Vanuatu. Locally it is called simply Vila. The name of the area is Efil in the native South Efate language and Ifira in the neighbouring Mele-Fila language, of which Vila is a variant. Ifira is a small island in Vila Harbour where many traditional landowners live. The climate is tropical and maritime, with nearly constant trade winds, a wettest month in March and a driest in September.

Port Vila is the most important harbour and the centre of trade of Vanuatu. It is home to many languages: the daily lingua franca is Bislama, English and French are widely spoken, and many of Vanuatu's 138 indigenous languages are heard as people from rural areas move to the city.

Melanesian people have occupied the area for thousands of years. In 2004 an archaeological expedition at Teouma found a burial site of 25 tombs holding about three dozen skeletons of members of the Lapita culture; ceramics from the site were dated to the 13th century BCE. James Cook charted Efate in 1774 and named it Sandwich Island. His expedition did not land, but noted the good harbours and land suitable for European settlement.

In the late 19th century, when the islands were known as the New Hebrides, the economic balance began to favour the French by the 1890s, and they established large plantations. The French citizen Ferdinand Chevillard bought and cleared land around Port Vila for what was to be the largest French plantation on the island; it became instead the municipality of Franceville, which declared independence on 9 August 1889 and lasted only until June of the following year. After 1887 the territory was jointly administered by the French and the British, formalised in 1906 as an Anglo-French Condominium. During the Second World War Port Vila was an American and Australian airbase.

Port Vila had 49,034 inhabitants at the 2020 census, 16.3 per cent of the population of Vanuatu. The people are predominantly Melanesian, with small Polynesian, Asian, Australian and European populations. Christianity is the main religion in Vanuatu, and the city has a Roman Catholic cathedral, the Cathédrale du Sacré-Cœur, seat of the Diocese of Port Vila.

The Vanuatu Cultural Centre, which hosts the Vanuatu National Museum and the National Audiovisual Archives, stands at Saralana Park in front of the National Parliament. The city is one location of the University of the South Pacific, and is served by Bauerfield International Airport. It has been damaged by cyclones: Cyclone Uma in 1987 and Cyclone Pam on 13 March 2015, whose eye wall passed just east of the town.
porto: Porto stands on the Douro River estuary in northern Portugal, about 280 kilometres north of Lisbon, and its western part reaches the Atlantic coast. It is the capital of the Porto District. Its historic core, with the Luiz I Bridge and the Monastery of Serra do Pilar, was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996, and has been a National Monument since 2001.

Before the Roman conquest the region was inhabited by the Gallaeci, a Celtic people, and findings suggest settlement at the mouth of the Douro as early as the eighth century BCE. As Portus Cale the town became a significant commercial hub under the Roman Empire, and its combined Celtic-Latin name has been cited as the origin of the name Portugal. In the Suebian and Visigothic periods it was a key centre for the spread of Christianity.

The Methuen Treaty of 1703 strengthened ties with England, and by 1717 English firms dominated the port wine trade. The Marquis of Pombal created a state-controlled wine company and demarcated the Douro, Europe's first protected wine region, which led in 1757 to the Revolta dos Borrachos, suppressed brutally by the authorities.

On 29 March 1809, during the Peninsular War, the Ponte das Barcas, a pontoon bridge, collapsed as civilians fled French forces, with an estimated 4,000 deaths. Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, then retook the city, crossing the Douro in wine barges. On 19 January 1919 monarchists declared the Monarchy of the North in Porto, which briefly served as the capital of the restored monarchy.

Porto is the second-largest city in Portugal, after Lisbon, with a metropolitan area of about 1.9 million people. Port wine takes its name from the city, since the cellars of Vila Nova de Gaia packaged and exported the fortified wine. In 2001 it shared the title of European Capital of Culture with Rotterdam.
porto-novo: Porto-Novo lies in the south of Benin on an inlet of the Gulf of Guinea, 13 kilometres from the Atlantic, from which it is separated by a lagoon. It stands about 30 kilometres east of Cotonou and 12 kilometres from the Nigerian border. Its commune covers 52 square kilometres. The city sits at the edge of the Dahomey Gap, which makes its climate drier than its nearness to the equator would suggest.

Porto-Novo was once a tributary of the Yoruba Oyo Empire, which offered it protection from the neighbouring Fon, who were expanding their power. The Yoruba called the city Ajashe, and the Gun called it Hogbonu. The first inhabitants were Yoruba-speaking, but a wave of migration from the region of Allada in the 1600s brought Te-Agbalin and his group to Ajashe in the late 16th century. In 1730 the Portuguese Eucaristo de Campos named the city Porto-Novo, because it resembled the city of Porto. It developed as a port for the transatlantic slave trade led by the Portuguese Empire.

In 1861 the British, who were active in nearby Nigeria, bombarded the city, and in 1863 the Kingdom of Porto-Novo accepted a French offer of protection. The neighbouring Kingdom of Dahomey objected to French involvement, and war broke out between the two states. In 1883 Porto-Novo was incorporated into the French colony of Dahomey and its dependencies, and in 1900 it became Dahomey's capital. The French sought to impose their language in every sphere of life and to stamp out the indigenous languages. Kings continued to rule in the city, officially and unofficially, until the death of the last, Alohinto Gbeffa, in 1976; from 1908 the king held the title of Chef supérieur.

Many Afro-Brazilians settled in Porto-Novo after returning to Africa following emancipation in Brazil, and Brazilian architecture and foods remain important to its cultural life. Under French rule, people often fled across the new border into British-ruled Nigeria to avoid harsh taxation, military service and forced labour. The border cuts through contiguous Yoruba- and Egun-speaking areas.

Porto-Novo is the official capital of Benin and the second-largest city, with 264,320 people at the census of 2013. The national parliament sits there, while the presidency and most other government institutions are in Cotonou. Its residents are mostly Yoruba and Gun. King Toffa's Palace, now a museum, and its surrounding district were added to UNESCO's Tentative List in 1996. The Da Silva Museum tells of the returning Afro-Brazilians, and the Alexandre Sènou Adandé Ethnographic Museum holds a large collection of Yoruba masks.
portuguese-language: Portuguese belongs to the Ibero-Romance group, which evolved from several dialects of Vulgar Latin in the medieval Kingdom of Galicia and the County of Portugal. Before the Roman conquest the territory of modern Portugal was inhabited by the Gallaeci, Lusitanians, Celts, Iberians, Phoenicians, Greeks and Ligurians, whose languages were gradually replaced but left words behind, many of them about nature, agriculture and material culture. The Roman presence began in 218 BCE and full consolidation came in 19 BCE under Augustus. Latin spread outward from the cities and was tied to Roman citizenship. In the 5th century the Suebi and Visigoths conquered the peninsula and contributed about 500 Germanic words, many to do with warfare.

Portuguese has a rich system of nasal vowels, and its spelling is largely phonemic but shaped by etymology and tradition. Its verbs have kept more inflections from classical Latin than any other major Romance language, and it has features that other Romance languages, except Galician and Fala, lack, among them the future subjunctive and the personal infinitive. Its lexicon of around 228,500 entries comes largely from Latin, with more than 3,000 words traced to pre-Roman Celtic sources and loanwords from Germanic, Arabic, African, Amerindian and Asian languages. It is fully mutually intelligible with Galician, with which it shares its origin in the medieval language Galician-Portuguese. Two standard varieties are used for learning, European and Brazilian Portuguese.

Colonial expansion carried Portuguese across the world. It is the official language of eight countries: Portugal, Brazil, Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau, São Tomé and Príncipe and Timor-Leste, and shares official status in Macau and Equatorial Guinea. There are about 267 million speakers in all, some 200 million of them in South America and 30 million in Africa. In Cape Verde and Guinea-Bissau a Portuguese-based creole is also widely spoken. The Community of Portuguese Language Countries unites all the officially Lusophone nations, and recent spelling agreements have tried to give the language one spelling everywhere.
potato: The potato is the underground stem tuber of Solanum tuberosum, a perennial in the nightshade family. Its tubers are not roots but stems that form from thickened rhizomes at the tips of long thin stolons. Wild potato species occur from the southern United States to southern Chile. Genetic studies show that the cultivated potato has a single origin, in the area of present-day southern Peru and extreme northwestern Bolivia, around Lake Titicaca, where pre-Columbian farmers domesticated it about 7,000 to 10,000 years ago from a species in the Solanum brevicaule complex.

The earliest archaeologically verified tuber remains come from the coastal site of Ancon in central Peru and date to 2500 BCE. The most widely cultivated variety, Solanum tuberosum tuberosum, is indigenous to the Chiloé Archipelago and has been grown by the local indigenous people since before the Spanish conquest.

The English word potato comes from the Spanish patata, in turn from the Taíno batata, which meant sweet potato and not the plant now called simply the potato. The name spud comes from spudde, a short and stout knife or dagger in the 15th century, and was transferred to the tuber from around 1840.

The Spanish introduced potatoes to Europe in the second half of the 16th century. Selective breeding has since produced over 5,000 varieties, about 3,000 of them in the Andes, mainly in Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, Chile and Colombia. Over 100 cultivars might be found in a single valley, and a dozen or more might be maintained by a single agricultural household. Most potatoes are self-incompatible and bear no useful fruit when self-pollinated, which makes crop breeding difficult, since all sexually produced plants must be hybrids.

The potato has been an essential crop in the Andes since the pre-Columbian era. The Moche culture of northern Peru represented it in ceramics, both naturally and as human figures. In Inca mythology Axomamma, a daughter of the earth mother Pachamama, is the goddess of potatoes, who ensured the fertility of the soil and the growth of the tubers. In Haudenosaunee mythology the first potatoes grew out of the feet of Earth Woman after she died giving birth to her twin sons, Sapling and Flint. Chuño, a freeze-dried potato product, is traditionally made by Quechua and Aymara communities of Peru and Bolivia.

In Europe the potato became an essential crop, especially in Northern and Eastern Europe. In the late 19th century numerous images of potato harvesting appeared in European art, including the works of Willem Witsen and Anton Mauve. Raw potatoes contain toxic glycoalkaloids, chiefly solanine and chaconine, and tubers exposed to light can become toxic.
potsdam: Potsdam lies on the River Havel, a tributary of the Elbe, about 25 kilometres south-west of Berlin's city centre. The area was formed from a series of large moraines left after the last glacial period, and the hilly landscape holds about 20 lakes and rivers in and around the city, among them the Griebnitzsee, Templiner See and Jungfernsee. Only a quarter of the city is built up, the rest remaining green space. The highest point is the Kleiner Ravensberg, at 114 metres. The name of the city and of many of its boroughs is of Slavic origin; it seems originally to have been Poztupimi, perhaps from a West Slavonic term meaning beneath the oaks.

The area shows signs of occupation since the Bronze Age. After the migrations of the Germanic peoples, Slavs moved in, and Potsdam was probably founded after the 7th century as a settlement of the Hevelli tribe centred on a castle. It was first mentioned in 993, when Emperor Otto III gave the territory to Quedlinburg Abbey, and it received its town charter in 1345. In 1573 it was still a small market town of about 2,000 people, and the Thirty Years' War cost it nearly half its population. It had been a Hohenzollern possession since 1415, and in 1660 the Elector of Brandenburg chose it as a hunting residence.

The Edict of Potsdam of 1685 offered religious freedom and made the city a centre of European immigration, drawing Huguenots and settlers from Russia, the Netherlands and Bohemia. The royal residences were built mainly under Frederick the Great, including Sanssouci, by Georg Wenzeslaus von Knobelsdorff, in 1744.

When Berlin was capital of Prussia and then of the German Empire, the court remained in Potsdam, and in 1914 Emperor Wilhelm II signed the Declaration of War in the New Palace. The city lost its status as a second capital in 1918. On 21 March 1933 Paul von Hindenburg and Adolf Hitler shook hands in Potsdam's Garrison Church in the ceremony known as the Day of Potsdam. Allied bombing raids, notably on the Old Town on 14 April 1945, severely damaged the city.

Potsdam is the capital and largest city of the German state of Brandenburg and part of the Berlin/Brandenburg Metropolitan Region. Its parks and palaces, among them Sanssouci and Cecilienhof Palace, form Germany's largest World Heritage Site. Babelsberg in the south-east has a film studio founded in 1912, the oldest large-scale film studio in the world, and Potsdam was named a UNESCO City of Film in 2019. The city became a centre of science in the 19th century, and it has the University of Potsdam and more than 30 research institutes.
pound-sterling: The basic unit of currency in medieval England was the silver penny, or sterling, weighing about one 240th of a tower pound. Two hundred and forty of these coins made a pound of sterlings, a term later shortened to pound sterling and kept in accounting even after the sterling had ceased to circulate. The earliest known instances occur in Orderic Vitalis's 12th-century Historia Ecclesiastica, which mentions librae sterilensium. The sign £ derives from the capital L for the Roman libra, the pound weight, which became an English unit defined as the tower pound. A pound sterling was literally a tower pound of sterling silver.
The pound emerged after the adoption of the Carolingian monetary system in England about 800, and by the ninth century it was a unit of account equal to 240 silver pence.

In 1158 King Henry II introduced a new coinage, the Tealby penny, in which a tower pound of 92.5 per cent silver was minted into 240 pennies. This alloy, called sterling silver, is harder than the 99.9 per cent fine silver traditionally used, and its coins wore down less quickly. Under Edward III the introduction of gold coins received from Flanders as payment for English wool brought economic and trade opportunities but also unsettled the currency for the next 200 years, and the first changes of 1344 reduced the penny to about 20 grains of sterling silver. The demands of the Hundred Years' War led to further debasements towards the end of the reign of Henry IV.

Before decimalisation in 1971 the pound was divided into 20 shillings and each shilling into 12 pence, making 240 pence to the pound. The abbreviations £sd, for pounds, shillings and pence, recall the Roman libra, solidus and denarius. Coins had special names, among them florin, crown, farthing, sovereign and guinea. On Decimal Day in 1971 the pound was divided into 100 pence.

Sterling is the currency of the United Kingdom and of nine of its dependent territories, and it was formerly the currency of the Kingdom of England. It is the world's oldest currency in continuous use since its inception. The Bank of England is its central bank. Sterling was historically also used to varying degrees by the colonies and territories of the British Empire, and the currency of the Crown Dependencies and of a third of the British Overseas Territories is either sterling or pegged to it at par. In wholesale foreign exchange markets the sterling and US dollar rate is called cable, from the mid-19th century, when it was transmitted by transatlantic cable.
poznan: Poznań lies on the River Warta in west Poland, within the Greater Poland region. Its highest point, at 157 metres, is the summit of Morasko hill in the north, within the Morasko meteorite nature reserve, and its lowest, at 60 metres, lies in the Warta valley. The name probably derives from the Polish verb poznać, 'to meet' or 'to know', marking the area as a meeting place. The earliest references are in the chronicle of Thietmar of Merseburg, which mentions a bishop of Poznań in 970 and the city in 1005.

For centuries before the Christianization of Poland, Poznań was an important cultural and political centre of the Western Polans. A fortified stronghold stood between the Warta and Cybina rivers on what is now Ostrów Tumski, and Mieszko I built one of his main gords there. His baptism in 966, seen as a defining moment in the Christianization of the Polish state, may have taken place in Poznań.

After the baptism construction began of Poznań's cathedral, the first in Poland, and the city was the main seat of Bishop Jordan, the first missionary bishop sent to Poland. The Congress of Gniezno in 1000 established the country's first permanent archbishopric at Gniezno, though Poznań kept bishops of its own. The cathedral was the burial place of early Piast monarchs, among them Mieszko I, Bolesław I the Brave, Casimir I, Przemysł I and Przemysł II. The Town Hall was rebuilt in Renaissance style after a fire in 1536 and finished in 1560.

In the later 17th and most of the 18th century wars and occupations devastated the city. Prussian authorities later merged the walled city with its suburbs and took down the old walls in the early 19th century. The Treaty of Versailles awarded Posen to the new Poland. From 1939 to 1945 Poznań was the capital of the Reichsgau Wartheland, part of Nazi Germany, and many Polish inhabitants were executed, arrested, expelled or used as forced labour.

Poznań is the administrative capital of the Greater Poland Voivodeship and the seat of the oldest Polish diocese. It is home to Adam Mickiewicz University and hosts the Poznań International Fair. Its Old Town, Town Hall, cathedral and the Baroque Fara church are among its main heritage sites.
prague: Prague is situated on the Vltava River, into which the Berounka flows in the suburb of Lahovice. Most of the city lies on the Prague Plateau. Its highest point is the hill Teleček on the western border, at 399 metres, and its lowest is the Vltava at Suchdol, at 172 metres. The city grew from a settlement stretching from Prague Castle in the north to the fort of Vyšehrad in the south. Its archaeological deposits are over 10 metres deep. The name Praha has been explained in several ways, among them as meaning a threshold, a ford or rapid, or a burned forest cleared for settlement.

The region was settled as early as the Paleolithic. Around the fifth and fourth centuries BCE a Celtic tribe, the Boii, appeared there and gave Bohemia its name, meaning home of the Boii. They built the largest Celtic oppidum in Bohemia, at Závist, and in the last century BCE Germanic tribes slowly drove them out. The 2nd-century map of Ptolemaios mentions a Germanic city called Casurgis near the site of present-day Prague.

Prague became the capital of the Kingdom of Bohemia and the residence of several Holy Roman Emperors, most notably Charles IV, who reigned from 1346 to 1378, and Rudolf II, who reigned from 1575 to 1611. Charles University, founded in 1348, is the oldest university in Central Europe. The city played major roles in the Bohemian and Protestant Reformations and in the Thirty Years' War. It was an important city to the Habsburg monarchy and to Austria-Hungary, and the capital of Czechoslovakia in the interwar period and in the Communist era after World War II.

Prague suffered considerably less damage in World War II than some other major cities in the region, which allowed most of its historic architecture to stay true to form. The city contains buildings in many styles, from Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque to Art Nouveau and Cubist. The Estates Theatre was the venue of the premieres of Mozart's Don Giovanni and La clemenza di Tito.

Prague is the capital and largest city of the Czech Republic and the historical capital of Bohemia, with a population of about 1.4 million. It has had the status of a statutory city again since 24 November 1990. The historic centre has been on the UNESCO list of World Heritage Sites since 1992. Among its landmarks are Prague Castle, Charles Bridge, the Old Town Square with the astronomical clock, the Jewish Quarter and Vyšehrad. It has been nicknamed the City of a Hundred Spires.
praia: The island of Santiago was discovered by António da Noli in 1460, and its first settlement was Ribeira Grande, now called Cidade Velha. A village named Praia de Santa Maria was first mentioned around 1615 and grew beside the natural harbour. The ports of Santiago were calls for ships sailing between Portugal and its colonies in Africa and South America. Between the end of the 16th century and the end of the 18th, both Ribeira Grande and Praia were attacked by privateers several times, among them Sir Francis Drake in 1585 and Jacques Cassard in 1712.

Praia's position on a plateau gave it better protection against such raids, and it gradually overtook Ribeira Grande. A naval battle was fought in Praia harbour on 16 April 1781 between Great Britain and France, while Portugal was neutral; it ended in a tactical draw and a French strategic victory. Charles Darwin's voyage with HMS Beagle made Praia its first stop in 1832. In the 19th century the Plateau was rebuilt on a grid plan, lined with colonial buildings and mansions, and Praia officially became a city in 1858.

Resistance to Portuguese rule rose in the 1950s, but there was no open independence war as in Guinea-Bissau. After the Carnation Revolution of 1974 in Portugal, Cape Verde declared independence in July 1975, and Praia then grew quickly as people moved in from all the islands.

Praia is a set of plateaus and the valleys around them. The plateaus are generally called achada, a Portuguese word for a volcanic plateau, and the central one is simply the Plateau. For a long time only the Plateau counted as the city, with the paved streets and services, while the other neighbourhoods were treated as outlying suburbs and grew in a more haphazard way. After independence they merged with it into the city as it is understood now. The climate is arid, with about 210 millimetres of rain a year, most of it in August, September and October.

Praia is the capital and largest city of Cape Verde and its political, economic and cultural centre, the seat of Praia Municipality, which holds some 29 per cent of the country's population. The city's own population was estimated at 151,436 in 2015. Landmarks of the old centre include Albuquerque Square, the Presidential Palace, built at the end of the 19th century to house the Portuguese governor, and the Monumento de Diogo Gomes. The Museu Etnográfico was founded in 1997, and since 2016 the historic centre has been on the tentative list of World Heritage Sites.
prayagraj: Prayagraj lies in the south of Uttar Pradesh, at the Triveni Sangam, the confluence of the Ganges, the Yamuna and the mythical Sarasvati, which according to Hindu legend wells up from underground. The place was known in ancient times as Prayāga, meaning place of a sacrifice in Sanskrit, since the god Brahma was believed to have performed the first sacrifice there.

The name Prayag alone is still used for the city. Geographically it is part of the Ganga-Yamuna Doab, at the mouth of the Yamuna. The Prayag Kumbh Mela is held at the Sangam every 12 years, and the ashes of several national leaders, among them Mahatma Gandhi in 1948, have been immersed there.

The earliest mention of Prayāga as a pilgrimage is in the Rigveda Pariśiṣṭa, a supplement of about 1200 to 1000 BCE. The Pali canon records the Buddha saying that bathing there cannot wash away cruel deeds, and the Mahabharata describes a bathing pilgrimage at Prayag as atonement for past wrongs. The city is also sacred to Jains, who believe their first Tirthankara, Rishabhanatha, attained kevala jnana there.

Some recent studies trace the Gupta dynasty to the Prayaga region, where the Allahabad Pillar Inscription indicates its early centre of power. In 644 the Chinese traveller Xuanzang described Prayaga as a great city with hundreds of temples, two Buddhist institutions to its south, and a Grand Place of Almsgiving where wealthy people and kings gave alms.

Abul Fazal records in the Ain-i-Akbari that on 13 November 1583 the Mughal emperor Akbar reached the spot where the rivers meet, laid the foundations of a city and planned four forts. It was called Ilahabas or Ilahabad, later Allahabad. British troops were first stationed in the fort in 1765 under the Treaty of Allahabad, signed by Robert Clive, the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II and Shuja-ud-Daula, Nawab of Awadh. The East India Company acquired the city in 1801.

In 1857 Maulvi Liaquat Ali raised the banner of revolt there, and Allahabad was the scene of a massacre of European troops. It became the capital of the North-Western Provinces in 1858, and for a day the capital of India, and was capital of the United Provinces from 1902 to 1920. The Civil Lines quarter, built in 1857, was the largest town-planning project in India before New Delhi.

The city is the judicial capital of Uttar Pradesh, with the Allahabad High Court, and the administrative headquarters of Prayagraj district. Hindi is the most widely spoken language. Its landmarks include the Triveni Sangam, Allahabad University, All Saints Cathedral and Anand Bhavan, and it has buildings in Indo-Islamic and Indo-Saracenic styles. The Kumbh Mela held there is among the largest peaceful gatherings in the world.
premier-league: Despite major European success in the 1970s and early 1980s, the mid and late 1980s were a low point for English football. Stadiums were ageing with poor facilities, hooliganism was rife, and after the Heysel Stadium disaster of 1985 all English clubs faced a five-year ban from European competition, with Liverpool given an extra year. The Football League First Division, the top level since 1888, lagged behind Italy's Serie A and Spain's La Liga in attendance and revenue, and several top English players had moved abroad.

At the close of the 1990-91 season a proposal was tabled for a new league that would bring more money into the game. The Founder Members Agreement, signed on 17 July 1991 by the top-flight clubs, set the principles of the FA Premier League, which was founded on 20 February 1992.

The league began with 22 clubs, a number the top flight had reached only at the start of 1991-92, and was reduced to 20 in 1995, when four teams were relegated and only two promoted. In the 2000s Arsenal, Chelsea, Liverpool and Manchester United dominated and were called the Big Four; from 1999-2000 to 2008-09 three of them finished in the top four every season. Manchester United won six titles in the decade, Arsenal two and Chelsea two under José Mourinho. Arsenal's unbeaten 2003-04 season earned them the nickname the Invincibles, the only such season of the Premier League era.

After 2009 Tottenham Hotspur and Manchester City regularly reached the top four, forming what came to be called the Big Six. Manchester City's title in 2011-12 was the first by a club outside the Big Four since Blackburn Rovers in 1994-95. Video assistant referees were introduced from the 2019-20 season, the season in which Liverpool won their first Premier League title, ending a 30-year wait for a top-flight championship. In October 2020 Manchester United and Liverpool announced Project Big Picture, a proposal for closer alignment between top clubs and the English Football League, which the league's leadership and the Department for Culture, Media and Sport criticised.

The Football Association Premier League Limited is a corporation owned by its member clubs, each a shareholder with one vote on rule changes and contracts. The clubs choose a chairman, a chief executive and a board. The Football Association is not involved in daily operations but holds a veto as a special shareholder over the choice of chairman and chief executive and over new rules. Each club plays the others twice, home and away, for 38 games, with three points for a win and one for a draw, and the lowest-placed teams are relegated to the EFL Championship.
pretoria: Pretoria stands about 56 kilometres north-northeast of Johannesburg, at an altitude of about 1,339 metres. It lies in a warm, sheltered, fertile valley in the transitional belt between the plateau of the Highveld to the south and the lower-lying Bushveld to the north, surrounded by the hills of the Magaliesberg range, and straddles the Apies River. It is called the Jacaranda City for the roughly 60,000 to 70,000 jacaranda trees along its streets.

Pretoria was founded in 1855 by Marthinus Pretorius, a leader of the Voortrekkers, who named it after his father Andries Pretorius and chose a spot on the banks of the Apies as the new capital of the South African Republic. The elder Pretorius had become a national hero of the Voortrekkers after his victory over Dingane and the Zulus in the Battle of Blood River in 1838, and had negotiated the Sand River Convention of 1852, in which the United Kingdom acknowledged the independence of the Transvaal. Pretoria became the capital of the republic on 1 May 1860, superseding Potchefstroom.

In the First Boer War, Republican forces besieged the city in December 1880 and March 1881, and the peace treaty was signed in Pretoria on 3 August 1881 at the Pretoria Convention. In the Second Boer War the city surrendered to British forces under Frederick Roberts on 5 June 1900, and the conflict ended in Pretoria with the Peace of Vereeniging, signed on 31 May 1902 at Melrose House. That war ended the Transvaal Republic and began British hegemony in South Africa.

In 1910 the Boer republics of the South African Republic and the Orange River Colony were united with the Cape Colony and Natal Colony as the Union of South Africa. Pretoria became the administrative capital of the whole country, with Cape Town as the legislative capital and Bloemfontein as the judicial capital, and from 1910 to 1994 it was also the capital of the province of Transvaal. It achieved official city status on 14 October 1931 and remained the administrative capital when South Africa became a republic in 1961.

Pretoria is the executive capital of South Africa, seat of the executive branch and home to all foreign embassies. It forms the central part of the City of Tshwane Metropolitan Municipality. It is an academic and research centre, with the University of Pretoria, the University of South Africa and the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research. The Voortrekker Monument and Kruger House, residence of the president of the South African Republic, are among its museums and monuments.
prince-edward-island: Prince Edward Island lies in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, about ten kilometres across the Northumberland Strait from both Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. It has a land area of 5,686 square kilometres and is the only Canadian province consisting entirely of islands. Its bedrock is sedimentary. When the Pleistocene glaciers receded about 15,000 years ago a strip of land still joined the area to the mainland, and rising seas flooded it and formed the island. The Mi'kmaq call it Abegweit or Epekwitk, roughly land cradled on the waves.

The Mi'kmaq are the Indigenous inhabitants, and the island formed part of Mi'kma'ki, their homeland. Jacques Cartier was the first known European to see it, in 1543. In 1604 France claimed the Maritimes as the colony of Acadia and named the island Île Saint-Jean. The Mi'kmaq never recognised the claim but welcomed the French as trading partners and allies. It passed to Britain in 1763 and became a separate colony in 1769.

In the mid-1760s a survey led by Samuel Holland divided the island into 67 lots, allocated by lottery on 1 July 1767 to supporters of King George III. Ownership stayed with landlords in England, which angered settlers who could not gain title to the land they worked. Islanders spent decades trying to persuade the Crown to confiscate the lots. The Charlottetown Conference was held from 1 to 7 September 1864, but the island stayed out of Confederation in 1867. Facing railway debts, it joined Canada on 1 July 1873, and Canada financed a buy-out of the last absentee landlords.

Prince Edward Island is the smallest Canadian province by area and population but has the highest population density. Its capital and largest city is Charlottetown, and it is one of the three Maritime provinces. Farming is central to the economy, and the island produces about a quarter of Canada's potatoes. Surnames of its earliest settlers are still mostly Acadian, Scottish, Irish and English. Its nicknames include Birthplace of Confederation. A law of 1982 limits non-resident ownership of land, a legacy of the colonial land question.
prince-vijaya: The Mahavamsa gives Vijaya a marvellous ancestry. His grandmother Suppadevi, daughter of the king of Vanga and a princess of Kalinga, was carried off by Sinha, the lion, whom some modern interpreters take to have been an outlaw living in the forest. Their son Sinhabahu escaped with his mother and sister, killed his father, founded the city of Sinhapura in the Lala country and married his sister Sinhasivali. Vijaya was the eldest of their thirty-two sons. Where Sinhapura lay is uncertain: it has been placed in Bengal, Odisha, Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh, among other places.

Made prince regent by his father, Vijaya became notorious with his followers for violent deeds, and prominent citizens demanded his death. Sinhabahu instead expelled them: their heads were half shaved and they were put on a ship, their wives and children being sent off on separate ships.

In the Mahavamsa's telling the kingdom was named Tambapanni, copper-red hands, because the red soil coloured the hands of Vijaya's men, and his people were called Sinhala after Sinhabahu. His ministers founded villages, among them Upatissagama. To be crowned he needed a queen of noble house, and the Pandya king of Madhura, identified with Madurai, sent his daughter with a hundred noble maidens, craftsmen and a thousand families of eighteen guilds, who landed at the port of Mahatittha.

Vijaya then sent Kuveni away, since his people feared supernatural beings. She went with their two children, Jivahatta and Disala, to the Yakkha city of Lankapura, where she was killed as a traitor. The children fled to Sumanakuta, and from them the chronicle derives the Pulinda, identified with the Vedda people. Vijaya, crowned, is said to have given up his evil ways and ruled in peace and justice.

Having no heir, Vijaya in old age sent for his twin brother Sumitta, but died before a reply came. His ministers governed for a year until Panduvasudeva, Sumitta's youngest son, arrived from Sinhapura to rule. The older Dipavamsa tells a similar story without Kuveni or the South Indian princess, and two other versions of the legend, one recorded by Xuanzang and one a Jataka painted at Ajanta, give the founding prince other names.

There is no archaeological evidence for the story. In Sri Lanka it is often treated as history and used in political argument: Sinhalese scholars such as K. M. de Silva have cited it for the Indo-Aryan origins of the Sinhalese, while Tamil authors such as Satchi Ponnambalam have dismissed it as fiction serving Sinhalese territorial claims.
pristina: Pristina lies on an alluvial plain in the regions of Llap and Kosovo, across the Gollak Hills in central and eastern Kosovo. The area has been inhabited since the Neolithic, and the earliest recognised traces were found at Gračanica, Matiçan and Ulpiana. In antiquity it belonged to the Dardanian Kingdom, and the nearby settlement of Ulpiana represents the heritage of the classical era. The origin of the city's name is unknown; Eric P. Hamp connected it with an Indo-European word for a ford and a word cognate with English stone.

After the division of the Roman Empire the area stayed within the Byzantine Empire between the 5th and 9th centuries. It was ceded to the First Bulgarian Empire in the middle of the 9th century, fell again to the Byzantine Empire in the early 11th century, when it was part of a theme called Bulgaria, and passed several times to the Second Bulgarian Empire. The Kingdom, later Empire, of Serbia held it through the 13th and 14th centuries. King Stefan Milutin founded the nearby Gračanica monastery in 1315, and Pristina is first recorded in 1342, as a village, in the reign of Stefan Dušan.

In 1455 it had a small population of 300 households. In the following century it became an important mining and trading centre because of its position near Novo Brdo, known for its trade fairs and for goatskin, goat hair and gunpowder. During the Austro-Turkish War of the late 17th century, townspeople under the Catholic Albanian priest Pjetër Bogdani pledged loyalty to the Austrian army, and he supplied a force of 6,000 Albanian soldiers. According to Noel Malcolm the town then had a majority of about 15,000 Muslims, probably Albanian.

Albanians pillaged and partly burned Pristina in May 1901. Serb forces took it on 22 October 1912, and Bulgaria occupied it in 1915. In 1948 it was chosen as the capital of the province of SAP Kosovo within Yugoslavia, and it remained the capital after Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008.

Pristina is the capital and largest city of Kosovo, with 227,466 residents at the census of 2024, most of them Albanians. It holds the Parliament, the courts and the residences of the president and prime minister. The University of Pristina, founded in the 20th century, is the largest and oldest in the city, and the National Theatre of Kosovo dates from 1946. Of 426 protected monuments in Kosovo, 21 are in Pristina, many of them from the Byzantine and Ottoman periods.
protestant-reformation: Europe suffered a series of calamities from the early 14th century, culminating in the Black Death, which killed about a third of its population. Humanism, with its slogan ad fontes, back to the sources, brought enthusiasm for textual criticism: Lorenzo Valla showed that the Donation of Constantine, a basic document of papal authority, was a medieval forgery. Many of Luther's ideas were anticipated by Wycliff, Hus, Erasmus and others, and scholars now see the Reformation as in important respects a continuation of trends within late medieval Catholicism.

Pope Leo X announced a new plenary indulgence in 1515 to finance the building of St Peter's Basilica, and the friar Johann Tetzel sold indulgences in Germany with unusually aggressive methods. The Reformation is usually dated from Martin Luther's publication of the Ninety-five Theses in 1517.

Printing carried the new ideas quickly: Luther was responsible for about one fifth of all works printed in Germany in the first third of the 16th century. Huldrych Zwingli led reform in Zürich from 1522, and John Calvin shaped the Continental Reformed tradition. Radical reformers such as the Swiss Brethren demanded believers' baptism and a church free of the state. The Peasants' War of 1524 and 1525 drew on the new excitement against authority. In April 1525 Albert of Brandenburg-Ansbach turned the Teutonic Order's Prussia into a hereditary duchy, and the Reformation was introduced in Electoral Saxony on Christmas Day 1525. At the Diet of Augsburg in 1530 the Protestants presented the Augsburg Confession, written by Melanchthon.

Elsewhere the kings of Denmark and Sweden took the lead in Scandinavia. In England, William Tyndale's New Testament had more than 15,000 copies in secret circulation by about 1535, and under Edward VI Thomas Cranmer's Book of Common Prayer replaced the Mass with a vernacular liturgy. Disputes in Germany led to the Schmalkaldic War, and later came the French Wars of Religion and the revolt in the Netherlands, where more Protestants were persecuted between 1523 and 1555 than in any other country.

The Catholic response, the Counter-Reformation, included new orders, above all the Jesuits, whose establishment Paul III sanctioned in 1540. The Council of Trent met from December 1545 to 1563, reaffirmed that apostolic tradition was as authentic a source of faith as the Bible, and stressed good works in salvation, rejecting two important elements of Luther's theology. Historians often use the plural to stress that the movement was not uniform but the result of parallel movements: Lutheranism, Calvinism, the Radical Reformation and the Catholic Reformation. It is considered one of the events that signified the end of the Middle Ages, and the end of the Reformation era is disputed among scholars.
protestantism: Protestantism follows the theology of the Protestant Reformation, a movement that began in the 16th century with the aim of reforming the Catholic Church of perceived errors and abuses. It began in the Holy Roman Empire in 1517, when Martin Luther published his Ninety-five Theses in reaction to abuses in the sale of indulgences. Luther argued against buying or earning forgiveness and claimed instead that salvation is a gift God gives to those who have faith.

The name comes from a protest. Six princes of the Holy Roman Empire and the rulers of fourteen Imperial Free Cities issued a protest against the edict of the Diet of Speyer in 1529 and were the first to be called Protestants. Lutheranism spread into Denmark–Norway, Sweden, Finland, Livonia and Iceland, and Calvinist churches spread in Germany, Hungary, the Netherlands, Scotland, Switzerland, France, Poland and Lithuania. The separation of the Church of England from the Catholic Church under King Henry VIII began Anglicanism.

Protestants hold to justification by faith alone, the priesthood of all believers, and the Bible as the highest authority for faith and practice. They reject papal supremacy, and early Protestants rejected transubstantiation. Lutherans affirmed a corporeal presence of Christ in Holy Communion, along with Catholics, while the Reformed affirmed a real spiritual presence.

The movement soon divided into branches: Lutheranism, Anglicanism, Calvinism or Reformed Christianity, and later Methodism, which grew from a revival within the 18th-century Church of England under John Wesley, and the Baptists, who hold that baptism should be given only to professing believers. The Radical Reformation, which had no state sponsorship and faced intense persecution from both Catholics and mainstream Protestants, gave rise to Anabaptism, whose descendants include the Amish, Hutterites and Mennonites.

The Reformation affected marriage and family, education, the political and social order, the economy and the arts. Protestant churches reject a celibate priesthood and allow their clergy to marry. Freedom of conscience gained priority after Luther refused to recant at the Diet of Worms in 1521, and Rhode Island, Connecticut and Pennsylvania combined democratic constitutions with freedom of religion. Protestants founded hospitals, schools and aid organisations, and in the 19th century many took part in the abolition of slavery, prison reform and woman suffrage. Estimates of the number of Protestants worldwide range from 600 million to 1 billion, because scholars disagree on which denominations count.
providence-rhode-island: Providence lies at the head of Narragansett Bay, at the mouth of the Providence River, which is formed in the middle of the city by the confluence of the Moshassuck and Woonasquatucket rivers. Its limits enclose a small area of about 20.5 square miles, of which roughly a tenth is water. Like Rome, it is one of many cities claimed to stand on seven hills. The city grew up before the automobile, and its streets run irregularly, radiating from old gathering places such as Market Square.

Roger Williams settled Providence in June 1636. As a minister in the Massachusetts Bay Colony he had advocated the separation of church and state and condemned the colonists' confiscation of land from the Indians, and for these and other opinions described as diverse, new and dangerous he was convicted of sedition and heresy and banished. He and his companions first settled at Rumford, then moved down the Seekonk River, around Fox Point and up the Providence River to the meeting of the Moshassuck and Woonasquatucket. They named the settlement after God's merciful Providence. It grew into one of the original Thirteen Colonies.

Williams founded the First Baptist Church in America there in 1638, and the Old State House served as the state's capitol from 1762 to 1904. Providence developed as a busy port and was one of the first cities in the country to industrialise, becoming noted for textile manufacturing and then for machine tools, jewellery and silverware. Its population peaked in the 1940s, just before the nationwide movement to the suburbs.

Providence is the capital and largest city of Rhode Island and the county seat of Providence County; its population was 190,934 at the 2020 census. The State House houses the General Assembly and the offices of the governor. The East Side has the largest contiguous area of buildings on the National Register of Historic Places in the U.S., many of them from before the Revolution. The city has Italian, Portuguese and Irish neighbourhoods, and is home to Brown University, the Rhode Island School of Design, Providence College and other institutions of higher education.
pskov: Pskov stands on the Velikaya River in north-western Russia, about 20 kilometres east of the Estonian border. Its name was originally Pleskov, which may be loosely translated as the town of purling waters. The earliest mention, under 903, records that Igor of Kiev married a local lady, Olga, later Saint Olga of Kiev. Pskovians sometimes take that year as the city's foundation, and in 2003 they marked its 1,100th anniversary.

The first prince of Pskov was Sudislav, the youngest son of Vladimir the Great. In the 12th and 13th centuries the town adhered politically to the Novgorod Republic. The Teutonic Knights took it in 1241, and Alexander Nevsky recaptured it several months later. To secure their independence from the knights the Pskovians elected a Lithuanian prince, Daumantas, known in Russia as Dovmont, as their leader in 1266. He fortified the town, and the core of the citadel still bears the name Dovmont's town.

Novgorod formally recognised Pskov's independence in 1348, and it became the capital of the Pskov Republic. Its most powerful force was the merchants who traded with the Hanseatic League. The veche promulgated a law code, the Pskov Charter, which was one of the principal sources of the all-Russian law code of 1497. The Kremlin withstood twenty-six sieges in the 15th century alone, and a local school of icon-painting flourished.

The Grand Duchy of Moscow annexed the city in 1510. Three hundred families were deported to central Russia and merchants and military families from Muscovy were settled there. In the Livonian War it withstood a prolonged siege in 1581 and 1582 by a Polish-Lithuanian army of 50,000 under King Stephen Báthory, defended mainly by civilians. It also withstood a Swedish siege in 1615. Peter the Great's conquest of Estonia and Livonia ended its traditional role as a border fortress.

Pskov is the administrative centre of Pskov Oblast and preserves much of its medieval walls, built from the 13th century onwards. Within the Krom, the medieval citadel, stands Trinity Cathedral, founded in 1138 and rebuilt in the 1690s, which holds the tombs of the saint princes Vsevolod and Dovmont. The Churches of the Pskov School of Architecture were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019.
